b: Simple definition# AI engineering is the discipline of building applications on top of foundation models that someone else has usually trained. Instead of collecting data and training a model first, you start from a model that already works, then adapt it — with prompts, context, tools, fine-tuning — and wrap it in the product, evaluation and operations it needs. The shift is from &ldquo;can we build a model?&rdquo; to &ldquo;can we build a reliable product with this model?&rdquo; Why this is a distinct discipline# Three things made AI engineering grow out of machine-learning engineering: Models became general-purpose. One model can summarise, classify, extract, translate, write code and plan. A team no longer needs a model per task. Models became a service. Strong models are available behind an API, so a small product team can ship AI features without an ML research group. The bottleneck moved. When anyone can call the same model, the advantage lies in evaluation, context, data, user experience and operations — the engineering around the model. Key conceptThe one idea to keep In AI engineering the model is a component you adapt and evaluate, not an artefact you build. Most of the work — and most of the competitive advantage — sits in the system around it. AI engineering vs ML engineering# Concern Traditional ML engineering AI engineering with foundation models Starting point Your data, then train a model An existing model, then adapt it Model adaptation Feature engineering, training Prompting, retrieval, tools; fine-tuning when needed Model size Often small, cheap to serve Large; inference cost and latency dominate Outputs Closed (a label, a score) Open-ended (text, code, actions) — much harder to evaluate Evaluation Accuracy against a labelled test set Rubrics, AI judges, human review, online feedback Data work Labelling and features Curating instructions, examples, preferences; synthetic data Interface Usually invisible (a score in a pipeline) Often conversational; the UX is the product The two converge in practice: a production AI team still needs ML skills for fine-tuning, dataset engineering and inference optimisation. AI engineering vs full-stack engineering. Because so much work is now product and interface work, AI engineering has moved closer to full-stack engineering. The common workflow has inverted: build the product first, then invest in data and models once the product shows promise — the opposite of the classic ML order. The three layers of the AI engineering stack# The AI engineering stack flowchart TB subgraph APP[&#34;Application development&#34;] A1[&#34;Prompt and context engineering&#34;] A2[&#34;Evaluation&#34;] A3[&#34;AI interface and UX&#34;] end subgraph MOD[&#34;Model development&#34;] M1[&#34;Fine-tuning and post-training&#34;] M2[&#34;Dataset engineering&#34;] M3[&#34;Inference optimisation&#34;] end subgraph INF[&#34;Infrastructure&#34;] I1[&#34;Model serving&#34;] I2[&#34;Data and compute management&#34;] I3[&#34;Monitoring&#34;] end APP --&gt; MOD --&gt; INF Layer What happens here Read more Application development Prompts, context construction, evaluation, the user interface Prompt engineering, Evaluating AI systems Model development Fine-tuning, dataset engineering, inference optimisation Fine-tuning in depth, Dataset engineering, Inference optimisation Infrastructure Serving, compute, data, monitoring Inference and serving, LLMOps Most enterprise teams spend the majority of their time in the top layer. The lower layers become relevant as scale, cost or customisation grows. What foundation models are used for# Use cases cluster into a handful of archetypes. Knowing the archetype tells you how hard evaluation will be and how much risk is involved. Archetype Examples Typical difficulty Coding Code completion, test generation, migration, code review Output is checkable (does it compile, do tests pass?) Image and video production Marketing assets, product images Subjective quality; brand and IP risk Writing Drafting emails, reports, product descriptions Subjective; tone and factuality Education Tutoring, quiz generation, explanation Correctness and pedagogy Conversational bots Customer support, internal help desks, companions Open-ended; safety and escalation Information aggregation Summarising documents, meetings, research Faithfulness to sources Data organisation Extraction from documents, classification, tagging Structured; measurable against labels Workflow automation Agents that complete multi-step tasks Highest risk; actions have side effects Enterprises usually start with internal, lower-risk use cases (knowledge search, drafting, extraction) before external ones, because mistakes are cheaper and the data is under their control. Planning an AI application# 1. Why build it at all?# Rank the motivation by how much risk it addresses: Motivation What it implies Existential — competitors using AI could make you obsolete Highest priority; consider building core capability in-house Opportunity — higher productivity, lower costs, more revenue Normal business case; buying is often cheaper and faster Exploration — you do not know where AI fits yet Small, time-boxed R&amp;D; learn before committing Then ask whether you must build it yourself. If an off-the-shelf product already does it well, building is a cost, not an advantage. See build, buy or embed. 2. What role does AI play?# Three questions shape requirements more than any model choice: Question Options Consequence Is AI critical or complementary? Product fails without it vs works without it Critical AI needs higher accuracy and fallbacks; complementary AI can tolerate more errors Is AI reactive or proactive? Responds to a request vs offers help unprompted Reactive needs low latency; proactive can run in batch but must clear a higher quality bar, or it becomes noise Is AI dynamic or static? Updates continuously with user feedback vs updated with releases Dynamic needs per-user data, privacy controls and

b: Why a review framework# AI designs fail in predictable places: unclear success criteria, missing permissions in retrieval, agents with too much autonomy, no evaluation, no cost model. A shared framework lets architects, security, risk and product owners review any AI design — your own before you build it, or a team&rsquo;s at an architecture board — consistently and quickly. The eight review areas# AI architecture review in 8 areas flowchart TB S1[&#34;1 · Problem &amp; value&lt;br/&gt;users, tasks, success, is AI right?&#34;] --&gt; S2[&#34;2 · Requirements&lt;br/&gt;functional, non-functional, risk&#34;] S2 --&gt; S3[&#34;3 · Estimates&lt;br/&gt;volume, tokens, cost, limits, data&#34;] S3 --&gt; S4[&#34;4 · Architecture&lt;br/&gt;components, one request traced&#34;] S4 --&gt; S5[&#34;5 · AI components&lt;br/&gt;knowledge, models, prompts,&lt;br/&gt;agents, tools, frameworks&#34;] S5 --&gt; S6[&#34;6 · Evaluation&lt;br/&gt;datasets, metrics, gates&#34;] S6 --&gt; S7[&#34;7 · Security &amp; governance&lt;br/&gt;permissions, injection, HITL, compliance&#34;] S7 --&gt; S8[&#34;8 · Operations&lt;br/&gt;scaling, resilience, cost, rollout&#34;] 1. Problem and value# Who are the users and what exact tasks will the system do? What is the success metric (deflection, time saved, accuracy, CSAT) and its baseline? Would search, rules, a form or a fixed workflow solve it more simply? Red flags: &ldquo;use AI for X&rdquo; with no measurable outcome; no owner. 2. Requirements# Type Check Functional Inputs/outputs, channels, languages, citations, actions, hand-off to humans Non-functional Latency (TTFT, total), availability, knowledge freshness, throughput Quality Accuracy targets, tolerable error types, &ldquo;I don&rsquo;t know&rdquo; behaviour Security &amp; privacy Data classification, permissions, PII, residency, provider terms Risk &amp; compliance Regulatory tier (EU AI Act), human oversight, auditability Cost Budget per request or per month Red flags: no latency or quality targets; data classification unknown. 3. Estimates# Requests/day and peak per second; tokens per request (system + context + history + question; output). Cost/day and per outcome; peak tokens/minute vs provider limits. Corpus size → chunks → vector storage; ingestion rate. Red flags: no token or cost estimate; peak load above provider quotas with no plan. Worked numbers: knowledge assistant, quick reference. 4. Architecture# Ask for a diagram and one request traced end to end — identity, retrieval with filters, gateway, model, tools, guardrails, response, tracing. Reference shape most GenAI designs should resemble flowchart LR U[&#34;Clients&#34;] --&gt; GW[&#34;API gateway&lt;br/&gt;auth, rate limit&#34;] GW --&gt; APP[&#34;Orchestrator / agent&lt;br/&gt;framework&#34;] APP --&gt; GR[&#34;Guardrails&lt;br/&gt;in / out&#34;] APP --&gt; RET[&#34;Retrieval&lt;br/&gt;hybrid + rerank + ACL&#34;] RET --&gt; IDX[(&#34;Index&#34;)] APP --&gt; TOOLS[&#34;Tools / MCP gateway&#34;] APP --&gt; MEM[(&#34;State &amp; memory&#34;)] APP --&gt; AIGW[&#34;AI gateway&#34;] AIGW --&gt; LLM[&#34;Models&lt;br/&gt;primary, fallback, small&#34;] ING[&#34;Ingestion pipeline&#34;] --&gt; IDX APP -.-&gt; OBS[&#34;Tracing, evals, cost&#34;] Red flags: apps calling model providers directly with shared keys; no gateway; state held in one pod. 5. AI components# Component Review questions Knowledge Prompt, RAG or fine-tuning — and why? Chunking, hybrid search, reranking, ACL filters, freshness, deletes? GraphRAG justified? Models Which tier and why? Routing, fallback, context window, data residency? Prompts Versioned templates? Structured output with validation? Citations? Agents Workflow or agent — justified? Autonomy level per action? Step and cost budgets? Memory and checkpoints? Tools Task-level tools? MCP servers owned by domain teams? Identity from session, not model? Frameworks Fit for language, control and platform? Lock-in mitigations (MCP, A2A, Git-managed prompts/evals, OpenTelemetry)? Red flags: multi-agent design without a reason per agent; fine-tuning to teach facts; 50 retrieved chunks in the prompt. 6. Evaluation# Golden dataset: source, size, coverage (no-answer, adversarial, permission-boundary cases), owner. Retrieval metrics (recall@k, MRR) and generation metrics (faithfulness, relevance, correctness); agent outcome, trajectory and pass^k. CI gate against a baseline; online sampling; user feedback; business A/B metrics. Red flags: &ldquo;we&rsquo;ll test it manually&rdquo;; only end-to-end scores; uncalibrated LLM judge. 7. Security and governance# Retrieval and tool permissions per user; effective permission = user ∩ agent ∩ task (agent identity). Prompt-injection defences: isolation of untrusted content, lethal-trifecta check, tool gating, output sanitisation. Human approval thresholds; limits enforced in services, not prompts. PII handling in prompts and logs; provider terms; AI inventory entry; risk tier; transparency to users. Red flags: agent service account with admin rights; &ldquo;the prompt tells it not to&rdquo;; prompt logs with customer data and no retention policy. 8. Operations# Scaling (stateless services, index sharding, provider quotas), timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, fallback models, degraded mode. Cost levers (caching, routing, context trimming, budgets) and cost alerts. Rollout plan: shadow → canary → progressive autonomy; kill switch; rollback of prompts and models. Red flags: no degraded mode; no owner on call; autonomy at full level on day one. Scoring rubric# Score each area 0–3 and record the evidence: Score Meaning 0 Missing — not considered 1 Mentioned — no concrete design 2 Designed — concrete choices, some gaps 3 Evidenced — concrete choices with numbers, tests or prototypes A design is ready to build when no area scores 0, the high-risk areas for its risk tier (usually 6 and 7) score 3, and open gaps have owners and dates. One-page review template# System: Owner: Risk tier: Decision requested:

b: Simple definition# Anthropic sells Claude in tiers. Bigger tiers reason better and cost more; smaller tiers are faster and cheaper. Inside each model you also choose an effort level — how hard the model thinks before it answers. Model selection for Claude is therefore a two-dimensional choice: which tier and how much effort, made per task and checked against your own evaluation set. Why it matters# Between the cheapest and the most capable current Claude model the price differs by 100× per token. Effort changes token use within one model by several times again. Teams that pick &ldquo;the best model, maximum effort&rdquo; for everything overspend; teams that pick the cheapest for everything ship wrong answers. The general method is in Model selection for the enterprise; this article applies it to Claude. The model family (November 2026)# Model API model ID Context Max output Input / output price per 1M tokens Positioning Claude Fable 5.1 claude-fable-5-1 1M 128K $10 / $50 Most capable widely released model: hardest reasoning, long-horizon autonomous work Claude Opus 5.5 claude-opus-5-5 1M 128K $4 / $20 The default for serious work: complex coding, agents, analysis Claude Sonnet 5.5 claude-sonnet-5-5 1M 128K $2 / $10 Speed and capability for everyday coding, agents and enterprise workloads Claude Haiku 5.5 claude-haiku-5-5 1M 128K $0.10 / $0.50 (≤100K-token prompts) High-volume, latency-sensitive tasks: classification, extraction, routing, sub-agents Prices are Anthropic first-party API list prices; Microsoft Foundry bills at the same rates, while Amazon Bedrock and Google Vertex AI publish their own pricing. Previous generations (Claude Fable 5, Opus 5, Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, Haiku 4.5 and others) remain available for a time but should not be chosen for new work. Claude Mythos 5.1 has Fable-level capability but is available only to Project Glasswing participants. TipNever hard-code what you can look up The Models API (GET /v1/models) returns each model&rsquo;s context window, output limit and capabilities. Read limits from it in tooling, and keep model IDs in configuration — not scattered through code — so an upgrade is a one-line change plus an evaluation run. Discounts that change the arithmetic# Mechanism Effect Use it for Prompt caching Cache reads are billed at a small fraction of the input price (for example $0.20 per 1M on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5) Long, stable system prompts, documents and tool definitions reused across requests Message Batches 50% off, results within 24 hours Offline work: back-fills, evaluations, bulk classification, nightly reports Fast mode (Opus 5.5, Claude API only) Up to 2.5× faster output at 2× the price ($8 / $40) Interactive coding sessions where waiting costs more than tokens Thinking and effort# Current Claude models think before they answer — they reason internally, then respond. You do not set a thinking-token budget any more; instead: Adaptive thinking lets the model decide how much to think per request. On Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 thinking is always on; on Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 it is on by default. Effort (low, medium, high, xhigh, max) sets the overall thoroughness: how much it thinks, how many tool calls it makes, how much it writes. It is the main quality-versus-cost dial within one model. Effort Typical use low Chat, classification, simple extraction, sub-agents doing narrow reading tasks medium Default on Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5; most product features; agentic coding on Sonnet 5.5 high Intelligence-sensitive work: design, analysis, tricky debugging; default on Sonnet 5.5 xhigh Long agentic coding and multi-step tool use; the default in Claude Code max When correctness matters far more than cost and measurement shows headroom above xhigh Key conceptTry a better model at lower effort before a cascade The newest models at low or medium effort often match or beat older models at high effort. Before building a multi-model cascade, measure the single most capable model at a lower effort on the same tasks — one model is simpler, and prompt caches are per model, so a cascade forfeits cache reuse. Which model for which task# Choosing a Claude model and effort flowchart TD A{&#34;Is it a hard, open-ended problem&lt;br/&gt;where one wrong answer is expensive?&lt;br/&gt;(architecture, novel algorithms,&lt;br/&gt;multi-day autonomous work)&#34;} --&gt;|&#34;yes&#34;| F[&#34;Fable 5.1 · high–max&lt;br/&gt;or Opus 5.5 · xhigh–max&#34;] A --&gt;|&#34;no&#34;| B{&#34;Multi-step reasoning, agentic coding,&lt;br/&gt;non-trivial analysis or writing?&#34;} B --&gt;|&#34;yes&#34;| O[&#34;Opus 5.5 · medium–xhigh&lt;br/&gt;(Sonnet 5.5 · high if cost/latency bound)&#34;] B --&gt;|&#34;no&#34;| C{&#34;High volume, latency-sensitive,&lt;br/&gt;or a well-specified narrow task?&#34;} C --&gt;|&#34;yes&#34;| H[&#34;Haiku 5.5 · low–medium&#34;] C --&gt;|&#34;no&#34;| S[&#34;Sonnet 5.5 · medium–high&#34;] F --&gt; E[&#34;Confirm on your own evaluation set,&lt;br/&gt;then fix model + effort per route&#34;] O --&gt; E H --&gt; E S --&gt; E Task Starting point Why Architecture options, threat models, migration strategy Opus 5.5 high/xhigh; Fable 5.1 for the hardest Reasoning quality dominates cost; volume is low Agentic coding (feature work, refactors, bug fixes) Opus 5.5 xhigh in Claude Code; Sonnet 5.5 medium–high for routine changes Long tool loops reward capability; routine edits do not need the top tier Code review on every pull request Sonnet 5.5 high; Opus 5.5 for security-critical repos Runs often; must be good but not maximal Test generation, documentation, changelogs Sonnet 5.5 medium Well-specified, verifiable output Log and ticket triage, classification, routing Haiku 5.5 low High volume, short outputs, latency matters RAG answer generation for employees Sonnet 5.5 medium; Haiku 5.5 for simple FAQ Grounded answers rarely need frontier reasoning Bulk extraction from documents Haiku 5.5 or Sonnet 5.5 via Batches 50% batch discount; quality checked by sampling Sub-agents
d: The Claude model family in November 2026 — Fable, Opus, Sonnet and Haiku — with context windows and prices, how adaptive thinking and effort levels work, a task-to-model guide for product and engineering work, routing and fallbacks, and how to run your own selection.

b: Simple definition# An agent framework is a library or SDK that implements the plumbing every agent needs — the loop that calls the model, executes tools and feeds results back — plus state, memory, multi-agent coordination, human-in-the-loop, guardrails and tracing. You write the instructions, tools and business logic; the framework runs them. What a framework gives you# Capability Without a framework With a framework Agent loop Hand-written loop over model responses and tool calls agent.run(...) with step limits Tools JSON Schemas written by hand Generated from functions/annotations; MCP client built in State &amp; checkpoints Your own tables and resume logic Pluggable checkpointers, sessions, durable runs Multi-agent Custom routing code Handoffs, supervisors, graphs, crews Human-in-the-loop Custom pause/resume Interrupts, approvals, resumable runs Guardrails Ad-hoc checks Input/output guardrail hooks, middleware Observability Manual logging Tracing (often OpenTelemetry) out of the box Protocols Your own integrations MCP, A2A and AG-UI adapters TipYou may not need one A single tool-calling loop is 30–50 lines with a provider SDK. Frameworks pay off when you need durable state, human approval, multi-agent coordination, standard tracing and team-wide conventions. Where frameworks sit in the platform# Where agent frameworks sit in an enterprise platform · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. &copy; 2026 Samir Kumar Sahoo, all rights reserved. Open full screen ↗ The framework is one layer. Around it: the agent UI (connected with AG-UI or a custom stream), the AI gateway that governs model calls, MCP servers for tools, remote agents via A2A, and a runtime that keeps state and traces — either your own Kubernetes deployment or a managed agent platform. b: Simple definition# Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) answers a question in two steps: first retrieve the most relevant pieces of your own documents, then ask the LLM to generate an answer using those pieces as context. Analogy: an open-book exam. The model is a smart student who has not read your company handbook. RAG hands them the right pages before they answer. The problem RAG solves# An LLM on its own: does not know your private data (policies, contracts, tickets, product docs); does not know anything after its training cutoff; cannot tell you where an answer came from; invents plausible answers when it does not know. Fine-tuning does not fix these well (see prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning). RAG does: knowledge stays in your systems, is updated by re-indexing, can be filtered per user, and every answer can cite its sources. The two pipelines# RAG is really two systems: an offline ingestion (indexing) pipeline and an online query pipeline. RAG architecture: ingestion and query flowchart TB subgraph Ingestion[&#34;Ingestion pipeline — offline, continuous&#34;] direction LR S[&#34;Sources&lt;br/&gt;SharePoint, Confluence, PDFs,&lt;br/&gt;databases, tickets&#34;] --&gt; L[&#34;Load &amp; parse&lt;br/&gt;text, tables, metadata&#34;] L --&gt; C[&#34;Clean &amp; chunk&lt;br/&gt;split into passages&#34;] C --&gt; E1[&#34;Embed chunks&lt;br/&gt;embedding model&#34;] E1 --&gt; I[(&#34;Vector store&lt;br/&gt;+ keyword index&lt;br/&gt;+ metadata &amp; ACLs&#34;)] end subgraph Query[&#34;Query pipeline — online, per request&#34;] direction LR Q[&#34;User question&#34;] --&gt; E2[&#34;Embed query&lt;br/&gt;same embedding model&#34;] E2 --&gt; R[&#34;Retrieve top-k&lt;br/&gt;similar chunks + filters&#34;] R --&gt; A[&#34;Augment prompt&lt;br/&gt;instructions + chunks + question&#34;] A --&gt; G[&#34;Generate&lt;br/&gt;LLM&#34;] G --&gt; O[&#34;Answer + citations&#34;] end I --&gt; R Ingestion, step by step# Load — connectors pull documents from source systems, with metadata (title, URL, owner, date, permissions). Parse — extract clean text from PDF, Word, HTML, slides; handle tables and images (OCR, or a vision model for complex layouts). Chunk — split into passages of a few hundred tokens so each chunk is about one topic. See chunking. Enrich — add metadata: section headings, document type, product, region, access-control lists; optionally summaries or keywords. Embed — convert each chunk into a vector with an embedding model. Index — store vector, text and metadata in a vector database, usually also a keyword (BM25) index. Keep fresh — detect changes and deletions in sources and re-index incrementally. Query, step by step# Understand the question — optionally rewrite it (resolve &ldquo;it&rdquo; from chat history, fix typos, expand acronyms). Embed the question with the same embedding model used for chunks. Retrieve the top-k most similar chunks, applying metadata filters (user permissions, region, date). Rerank (advanced RAG) — reorder candidates with a more precise model and keep the best few. Augment — build the prompt: instructions, numbered sources, question. Generate — the LLM writes the answer, citing sources. Post-process — validate citations, apply output guardrails, log the trace. What the augmented prompt looks like# SYSTEM: Answer using only the sources below. Cite sources like [2]. If the sources do not answer the question, say you don&#39;t know. &lt;sources&gt; [1] (Travel Policy 2026, §4.2) Economy class is required for flights under 6 hours... [2] (Travel Policy 2026, §4.3) Business class may be booked for flights over 6 hours with director approval... [3] (FAQ: Travel) Approval requests are submitted in the Expenses portal... &lt;/sources&gt; USER: Can I fly business class to Singapore? Naive, advanced and modular RAG# Evolution of RAG designs flowchart LR N[&#34;Naive RAG&lt;br/&gt;chunk → embed → top-k → generate&#34;] --&gt; A[&#34;Advanced RAG&lt;br/&gt;+ query rewriting, hybrid search,&lt;br/&gt;reranking, better chunking,&lt;br/&gt;metadata filters&#34;] A --&gt; M[&#34;Modular / agentic RAG&lt;br/&gt;routing across sources, iterative retrieval,&lt;br/&gt;self-checking, tools, GraphRAG&#34;] Naive RAG Advanced RAG Modular / agentic RAG Retrieval Single vector search Hybrid + rerank + filters Multiple sources, chosen dynamically Query handling As typed Rewritten, expanded Decomposed into sub-questions, iterative Good for Prototypes Most production assistants Complex research, multi-hop questions Cost / latency Lowest Moderate Highest Details: advanced retrieval, GraphRAG, agentic RAG. Where RAG fails# Failure points along the pipeline flowchart LR A[&#34;Missing content&lt;br/&gt;answer not in corpus&#34;] --&gt; B[&#34;Bad parsing&lt;br/&gt;tables garbled, headers lost&#34;] B --&gt; C[&#34;Bad chunking&lt;br/&gt;answer split across chunks&#34;] C --&gt; D[&#34;Missed retrieval&lt;br/&gt;right chunk not in top-k&#34;] D --&gt; E[&#34;Lost in context&lt;br/&gt;right chunk present but ignored&#34;] E --&gt; F[&#34;Unfaithful answer&lt;br/&gt;model adds facts not in sources&#34;] F --&gt; G[&#34;Wrong format&lt;br/&gt;or missing citation&#34;] Each failure needs a different fix, which is why you evaluate retrieval and generation separately. Symptom Likely cause Fix &ldquo;I don&rsquo;t know&rdquo; but the answer exists Retrieval miss Hybrid search, better chunking, query rewriting, more candidates + reranking Wrong answer citing the right document Ambiguous or conflicting chunks; poor prompt Rerank, add metadata (dates, versions), instruct to prefer latest Answer mixes products or regions No metadata filtering Filter by product/region; ask clarifying question Confident answer with no support Unfaithful generation Stricter prompt, faithfulness check, lower temperature User sees content they should not Missing access control Filter by ACL at retrieval time — never rely on the prompt Security: permissions in RAG# The retrieval step must only return chunks the current user is

b: Simple definition# Spring AI is the Spring project for building AI applications in Java. It gives you portable APIs for chat, embeddings, images, audio and vector stores across many providers, plus higher-level building blocks — a fluent ChatClient, advisors for RAG and memory, tool calling, MCP, structured output and observability — all configured the Spring Boot way. It plays the role in Java that LangChain or LlamaIndex play in Python, with Spring idioms: auto-configuration, dependency injection, Micrometer observability and starters. Why architects use it# Provider portability — switch between Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Amazon Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, Mistral, Ollama and more mostly through configuration. Fits existing Java estates — security, transactions, data access, messaging and observability you already run. Enterprise patterns built in — RAG advisors, chat memory repositories, MCP client and server starters, evaluation helpers. Core abstractions# Spring AI building blocks flowchart TB APP[&#34;Your service / controller&#34;] --&gt; CC[&#34;ChatClient&lt;br/&gt;fluent API&#34;] CC --&gt; ADV[&#34;Advisor chain&lt;br/&gt;memory, RAG, logging, safeguards,&lt;br/&gt;tool calling, custom&#34;] ADV --&gt; CM[&#34;ChatModel&lt;br/&gt;portable interface&#34;] CM --&gt; P1[&#34;AnthropicChatModel&#34;] CM --&gt; P2[&#34;OpenAiChatModel&#34;] CM --&gt; P3[&#34;Bedrock / Google GenAI /&lt;br/&gt;Ollama / Mistral ...&#34;] CC -.-&gt; TOOLS[&#34;Tools&lt;br/&gt;@Tool methods, MCP tool callbacks&#34;] ADV -.-&gt; VS[&#34;VectorStore&lt;br/&gt;pgvector, OpenSearch, Redis ...&#34;] VS -.-&gt; EM[&#34;EmbeddingModel&#34;] ADV -.-&gt; MEM[&#34;ChatMemory&lt;br/&gt;JDBC, Redis, Cassandra ...&#34;] Abstraction Purpose ChatModel / StreamingChatModel Low-level portable interface to a chat LLM ChatClient High-level fluent API: prompts, options, advisors, tools, structured output Prompt, Message, PromptTemplate Messages with roles; templates with variables ChatOptions Portable options (model, temperature, max tokens) or provider-specific options EmbeddingModel Text → vectors VectorStore Store and search embeddings with metadata filters Advisor Interceptors around the model call (like servlet filters or AOP) ToolCallback / @Tool Functions the model can call ChatMemory Conversation history management Getting started# Add the BOM and a model starter (Maven): &lt;dependencyManagement&gt; &lt;dependencies&gt; &lt;dependency&gt; &lt;groupId&gt;org.springframework.ai&lt;/groupId&gt; &lt;artifactId&gt;spring-ai-bom&lt;/artifactId&gt; &lt;version&gt;2.0.x&lt;/version&gt; &lt;!-- use the latest 2.0 release --&gt; &lt;type&gt;pom&lt;/type&gt; &lt;scope&gt;import&lt;/scope&gt; &lt;/dependency&gt; &lt;/dependencies&gt; &lt;/dependencyManagement&gt; &lt;dependency&gt; &lt;groupId&gt;org.springframework.ai&lt;/groupId&gt; &lt;artifactId&gt;spring-ai-starter-model-anthropic&lt;/artifactId&gt; &lt;/dependency&gt; spring.ai.anthropic.api-key=${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY} spring.ai.anthropic.chat.model=claude-sonnet-4-5 Swap spring-ai-starter-model-anthropic for -openai, -bedrock-converse, -google-genai, -ollama and so on to change providers. ChatClient: the fluent API# @RestController class SupportController { private final ChatClient chatClient; SupportController(ChatClient.Builder builder) { this.chatClient = builder .defaultSystem(&#34;&#34;&#34; You are a concise support assistant for ACME Retail. Answer in at most 120 words. If unsure, say you don&#39;t know. &#34;&#34;&#34;) .build(); } @GetMapping(&#34;/ask&#34;) String ask(@RequestParam String question) { return chatClient.prompt() .user(question) .call() .content(); } } prompt() starts a request; .system(), .user(), .messages() add content. .call() is synchronous; .stream() returns a reactive Flux. .content() returns text; .chatResponse() returns metadata (token usage, finish reason); .entity(...) returns a Java object. Prompt templates# String answer = chatClient.prompt() .user(u -&gt; u .text(&#34;Summarise the following incident for {audience} in 3 bullet points:\n{incident}&#34;) .param(&#34;audience&#34;, &#34;executives&#34;) .param(&#34;incident&#34;, incidentText)) .call() .content(); Templates use the StringTemplate engine by default. Keep templates in files (for example classpath:/prompts/summarise.st) so they are versioned and reviewed. Streaming# @GetMapping(value = &#34;/ask/stream&#34;, produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE) Flux&lt;String&gt; stream(@RequestParam String question) { return chatClient.prompt().user(question).stream().content(); } Options per request# chatClient.prompt() .user(question) .options(ChatOptions.builder().temperature(0.1).maxTokens(400).build()) .call() .content(); Structured output# Map model output straight into Java types. Spring AI generates a JSON Schema from the type, adds format instructions (or uses the provider&rsquo;s native structured output), and parses the response. record InvoiceData(String supplier, LocalDate invoiceDate, String currency, BigDecimal total, List&lt;LineItem&gt; lines) {} record LineItem(String description, int quantity, BigDecimal amount) {} InvoiceData invoice = chatClient.prompt() .system(&#34;Extract invoice data. Use ISO dates and 3-letter currency codes.&#34;) .user(invoiceText) .call() .entity(InvoiceData.class); For generic types use .entity(new ParameterizedTypeReference&lt;List&lt;LineItem&gt;&gt;() {}). Always validate business rules after parsing (totals add up, dates plausible); see structured output. Spring AI 2.0 also includes a StructuredOutputValidationAdvisor that can validate against the schema and retry. Advisors: the interception chain# Advisors wrap every call, like servlet filters. They can modify the request (add memory, retrieved documents, safety rules), the response, or both. Advisor chain around a ChatClient call sequenceDiagram participant App participant M as MessageChatMemoryAdvisor participant Q as QuestionAnswerAdvisor (RAG) participant L as SimpleLoggerAdvisor

b: Simple definition# An AI agent is a system where an LLM decides what to do next, does it by calling tools, observes the result, and repeats until the goal is reached or it must stop. A chatbot answers. An agent acts: it can look up an order, check a policy, issue a refund, and email the customer — choosing the steps itself. From LLM to agent# Levels of LLM systems flowchart LR A[&#34;Single LLM call&lt;br/&gt;prompt → answer&#34;] --&gt; B[&#34;Augmented LLM&lt;br/&gt;+ retrieval, tools, memory&#34;] B --&gt; C[&#34;Workflow&lt;br/&gt;LLM calls and tools in a&lt;br/&gt;path defined by code&#34;] C --&gt; D[&#34;Agent&lt;br/&gt;LLM decides the path&lt;br/&gt;in a loop&#34;] D --&gt; E[&#34;Multi-agent system&lt;br/&gt;several agents&lt;br/&gt;coordinate&#34;] The most useful distinction: Workflow Agent Who decides the steps? Your code (predefined path) The LLM (dynamic) Predictability High Lower Testing Like normal software Needs scenario-based evaluation Cost and latency Bounded, known Variable Best for Well-understood, repeatable tasks Open-ended tasks where steps cannot be predicted Key conceptStart with the simplest thing Most enterprise &ldquo;agent&rdquo; use cases are better built as workflows with a few LLM steps. Use a true agent only when the path really cannot be known in advance. The agent loop# The agent loop: think, act, observe flowchart TD G[&#34;Goal from user&#34;] --&gt; T[&#34;THINK&lt;br/&gt;LLM reasons about the state&lt;br/&gt;and picks the next action&#34;] T --&gt; D{&#34;Done?&#34;} D --&gt;|&#34;No&#34;| A[&#34;ACT&lt;br/&gt;call a tool with arguments&#34;] A --&gt; O[&#34;OBSERVE&lt;br/&gt;tool result added to context&#34;] O --&gt; T D --&gt;|&#34;Yes&#34;| R[&#34;Final answer to user&#34;] T --&gt;|&#34;budget exceeded,&lt;br/&gt;needs approval, or stuck&#34;| H[&#34;Stop: ask human / escalate&#34;] In code, the loop is short: messages = [system_prompt, user_goal] for step in 1..MAX_STEPS: response = llm(messages, tools) if response has no tool calls: return response.text # final answer for call in response.tool_calls: check permissions / ask for approval if risky result = execute(call.name, call.arguments) messages.append(tool_result(call.id, result)) return &#34;Stopped: step limit reached&#34; # always bound the loop ReAct: Reason + Act# ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) interleaves reasoning and actions. The model writes a thought, chooses an action, reads the observation, and continues: Thought: The customer asks why order 8812 is late. I need the order status. Action: get_order(order_id=&#34;8812&#34;) Observation: {&#34;status&#34;: &#34;held&#34;, &#34;reason&#34;: &#34;address_verification_failed&#34;} Thought: Address verification failed. I should check the address on file. Action: get_customer_address(customer_id=&#34;C-301&#34;) Observation: {&#34;postcode&#34;: &#34;SW1A 1AA&#34;, &#34;verified&#34;: false} Thought: I can explain and offer to update the address. Final answer: Your order is on hold because we could not verify the delivery address... Modern models do this natively through tool calling: the &ldquo;Action&rdquo; is a structured tool call, not text to parse. Components of an agent# Anatomy of an agent flowchart TB subgraph Agent M[&#34;Model&lt;br/&gt;reasoning engine&#34;] P[&#34;Instructions&lt;br/&gt;role, goals, rules, stop conditions&#34;] TL[&#34;Tools&lt;br/&gt;APIs, search, code, MCP servers&#34;] MEM[&#34;Memory&lt;br/&gt;short-term context, long-term store&#34;] PL[&#34;Planning&lt;br/&gt;decompose, reflect, re-plan&#34;] GR[&#34;Guardrails&lt;br/&gt;permissions, approvals, budgets&#34;] end U[&#34;User / trigger&#34;] --&gt; Agent Agent --&gt; ENV[&#34;Environment&lt;br/&gt;business systems, data, people&#34;] ENV --&gt; Agent Component Role Read more Model Chooses actions, reasons over results Model selection Instructions Define goal, scope, tone, rules, when to stop Prompt engineering Tools The agent&rsquo;s hands: read and change the world Tool calling, MCP Memory Conversation state, user preferences, past cases Memory and state Planning Break goals into steps; reflect and correct Workflow patterns Guardrails Limit what it can do and spend Reliability, AI security Levels of autonomy# Level Description Example 0 — Assist Suggests; human does everything Draft an email reply 1 — Act with approval Proposes actions; human approves each &ldquo;Refund €40? [Approve]&rdquo; 2 — Act within limits Acts alone below thresholds; escalates above Auto-refund ≤ €50, else approval 3 — Autonomous with oversight Completes whole tasks; humans review samples and exceptions Overnight reconciliation agent 4 — Fully autonomous No routine human involvement Rare in regulated enterprises Choose the level per action by impact and reversibility: reading is safe, writing needs limits, irreversible or high-value actions need human approval. This table is about the authority you grant. For the matching scale of capability — from rule-based automation to fully autonomous agents — and the sense–plan–act–reflect cycle, see levels, SPAR and the three keystones. When to use an agent# Good fit: open-ended tasks with many possible paths (investigation, research, troubleshooting, coding), tasks spanning several systems, and tasks where a human currently follows judgment rather than a fixed procedure. Poor fit: fixed procedures (use a workflow or plain code), strict latency or cost budgets, tasks needing guaranteed exact outcomes, and high-risk actions without a review step. Common mistakes# Common mistakeAn agent where a workflow would do Letting the LLM decide steps that are always the same adds cost, latency and failure modes. If you can draw the flowchart, code it. Common mistakeUnbounded loops Without a maximum number of steps, tokens and time, an agent can loop on a failing tool and burn budget. Always bound it. Common mistakeToo many tools Giving one agent 80 tools confuses tool selection. Group tools, load them on demand, or split into specialised agents. Review

Simple definition# Chunking is splitting documents into smaller passages so that search can return just the relevant part, and so it fits in the prompt. An embedding is a list of numbers (a vector) that represents the meaning of a piece of text. Texts with similar meaning have vectors that are close together. Together they decide what your RAG system can find. Embeddings, simply# Meaning becomes position flowchart LR A[&#34;&#39;How do I reset my password?&#39;&#34;] --&gt; EM[&#34;Embedding model&#34;] B[&#34;&#39;I forgot my login credentials&#39;&#34;] --&gt; EM C[&#34;&#39;Quarterly revenue grew 8%&#39;&#34;] --&gt; EM EM --&gt; VA[&#34;[0.12, -0.48, 0.33, ...]&#34;] EM --&gt; VB[&#34;[0.10, -0.45, 0.31, ...]&#34;] EM --&gt; VC[&#34;[-0.71, 0.22, -0.05, ...]&#34;] VA &lt;--&gt;|&#34;close: similar meaning&#34;| VB VA &lt;--&gt;|&#34;far&#34;| VC The first two sentences share no keywords, yet their vectors are close — this is semantic search, and why RAG finds answers phrased differently from the question. Similarity metrics# Metric Idea Notes Cosine similarity Angle between vectors (1 = same direction) The default for text Dot product Cosine × lengths Equal to cosine when vectors are normalised; fastest Euclidean (L2) distance Straight-line distance Lower = more similar Use the metric the embedding model was trained for (its documentation says). Choosing an embedding model# Factor Consideration Retrieval quality Check the MTEB leaderboard retrieval scores, then test on your data Language Multilingual model if documents or users are not English-only Domain Code, legal or medical text may benefit from specialised or fine-tuned models Dimensions 384–3,072 typical. More dimensions → more storage and slower search Max input length Must exceed your chunk size Hosting API (OpenAI, Cohere, Voyage, Google, Amazon Titan) or open-weight (BGE, E5, GTE, Nomic) Cost Embedding is cheap per token but the whole corpus is embedded, and re-embedded on model change Matryoshka embeddings can be truncated (for example from 3,072 to 512 dimensions) with modest quality loss, trading accuracy for storage and speed. Key conceptVersion your embeddings Store the embedding model name and version with the index. Changing models means re-embedding everything, usually into a new index, then switching over (blue/green). Why chunk at all?# Precision — a 40-page PDF embedded as one vector blurs dozens of topics into one point; a question about one paragraph will not match it well. Context budget — you want to send the 5 most relevant paragraphs, not 5 whole documents. Model limits — embedding models have a maximum input length. Too small is also bad: a chunk with one sentence lacks the context to be understood (&ldquo;It must be approved by a director&rdquo; — what must?). Chunking strategies# Chunking strategies from simple to sophisticated flowchart TB F[&#34;Fixed-size&lt;br/&gt;every N tokens + overlap&#34;] --&gt; R[&#34;Recursive&lt;br/&gt;split on paragraphs → sentences → words&lt;br/&gt;until under size&#34;] R --&gt; S[&#34;Structure-aware&lt;br/&gt;split on headings, sections,&lt;br/&gt;Markdown/HTML elements, code functions&#34;] S --&gt; SE[&#34;Semantic&lt;br/&gt;split where meaning changes&lt;br/&gt;embedding similarity between sentences&#34;] SE --&gt; PC[&#34;Hierarchical / parent-child&lt;br/&gt;search small chunks, return big parent&#34;] Strategy How Pros Cons Fixed-size + overlap 500 tokens, 50–100 overlap Simple, predictable Cuts mid-sentence and mid-topic Recursive character/token Try 

, then 
, then . , … Respects paragraphs; good default Ignores document structure Structure-aware Split by headings, list items, tables, code blocks Chunks match the author&rsquo;s topics; headings become metadata Needs good parsing per format Semantic Break where adjacent sentences&rsquo; embeddings diverge Coherent topics Slower; variable sizes Parent-child (small-to-big) Index small child chunks; return their larger parent section Precise matching and rich context More storage and logic Sentence window Index sentences; return sentence ± neighbours Very precise retrieval Many vectors Late chunking Embed the whole long document with a long-context model, then pool token vectors per chunk Each chunk&rsquo;s vector carries document context Needs a suitable model Contextual chunk headers Prepend document title and section path, or an LLM-written summary, to each chunk before embedding Big quality gains for little effort Extra tokens; LLM cost if summarised Parent-child retrieval# Small-to-big retrieval flowchart LR Q[&#34;Query&#34;] --&gt; V[&#34;Search child chunks&lt;br/&gt;~150 tokens each&#34;] V --&gt; H[&#34;Best child: §4.3 sentence&lt;br/&gt;about business class&#34;] H --&gt; P[&#34;Look up parent&lt;br/&gt;whole §4 Air Travel, ~1,200 tokens&#34;] P --&gt; LLM[&#34;Send parent to LLM&#34;] Practical starting point# Structure-aware or recursive chunking, ~300–800 tokens, 10–20% overlap. Prepend the document title and section heading path to every chunk (&ldquo;Travel Policy 2026 &gt; Air travel &gt; Business class&rdquo;). Keep tables whole where possible; convert them to Markdown or describe each row. Store rich metadata: source, URL, section, page, date, version, language, ACL. Then measure retrieval recall on your evaluation set and tune size, overlap and strategy. Parsing: the hidden half of quality# Content Challenge Approach Native PDFs Columns, headers/footers, hyphenation Layout-aware parsers; strip boilerplate Scanned PDFs No text layer OCR, or a vision-capable model Tables Row/column meaning lost when flattened Extract as Markdown/HTML; keep whole; or one chunk per row with headers Slides Fragmented text, meaning in images Combine slide title + text + speaker notes; describe diagrams with a vision model Web/Confluence Navigation, cookie banners Extract main content; keep heading hierarchy Code Functions and classes Split by syntax (AST), not by characters Tools include Apache Tika, PDF-specific

b: Simple definition# The Claude API is one HTTP endpoint, POST /v1/messages: you send a model ID, optional system instructions, a list of messages and optional tools; Claude returns content blocks (text, tool calls, thinking). Everything else — tools, structured output, caching, citations, files — is a feature of that one endpoint or a small supporting API (Batches, Files, Models, Token counting). Official SDKs exist for Python, TypeScript, Java, Go, Ruby, C# and PHP. Start simple: pick the right surface# Need Surface You own Classify, summarise, extract, answer Single Messages call The prompt and output handling Multi-step pipeline with fixed steps Messages + your code (a workflow) The orchestration Agent with your own tools Messages + tool runner (SDK helper that runs the loop) Tools and hosting Coding/filesystem agent on your infrastructure Claude Agent SDK (the Claude Code harness as a library) Hosting and sandboxing Hosted, stateful agent with a sandbox, schedules, memory Claude Managed Agents (Anthropic runs the loop and the container) Agent configuration and tools you expose Key conceptThe least code you own wins Choose the simplest surface that meets the need. Most features are a single call or a short workflow. Reach for an agent only when the task is genuinely open-ended, valuable enough to pay for many calls, and safe to get wrong because errors are caught (tests, review, rollback). A first request# import anthropic client = anthropic.Anthropic() # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or an `ant auth login` profile response = client.messages.create( model=&#34;claude-opus-5-5&#34;, max_tokens=16000, output_config={&#34;effort&#34;: &#34;medium&#34;}, # low | medium | high | xhigh | max system=&#34;You are a senior reviewer for a Java payments platform.&#34;, messages=[{&#34;role&#34;: &#34;user&#34;, &#34;content&#34;: &#34;Explain the risk in this diff: ...&#34;}], ) if response.stop_reason == &#34;refusal&#34;: ... # handle; see fallbacks below print(next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == &#34;text&#34;)) print(response.usage) # input, output and cache token counts — log them Things to know from the first day: Thinking is built in. Current models think adaptively; control depth with effort, not a token budget (fixed budget_tokens is rejected on current models). No prefill. You cannot start the assistant&rsquo;s reply for it on current models; use structured outputs or instructions instead. Stream long work. For large max_tokens or long tasks, use client.messages.stream(...) and get_final_message() to avoid HTTP timeouts. Sampling parameters are going away. temperature, top_p and top_k are rejected on the newest API version; steer with instructions and effort. Tools and agents# Define tools with a name, description and JSON schema (or a typed function), and let the SDK&rsquo;s tool runner drive the call–execute–repeat loop: from anthropic import beta_tool @beta_tool def get_order(order_id: str) -&gt; str: &#34;&#34;&#34;Look up an order by ID and return status, amount and customer tier as JSON. Args: order_id: The order identifier, e.g. &#34;ORD-10294&#34;. &#34;&#34;&#34; return orders_service.find(order_id).to_json() runner = client.beta.messages.tool_runner( model=&#34;claude-sonnet-5-5&#34;, max_tokens=16000, tools=[get_order], messages=[{&#34;role&#34;: &#34;user&#34;, &#34;content&#34;: &#34;Why was ORD-10294 not refunded?&#34;}], ) final = runner.until_done() Design rules (detail in tool calling): Descriptions are prompts. Say what the tool does, when to use it, and what it returns. Keep the set small and non-overlapping; with many tools, use the tool search tool so definitions load on demand. Use strict: true on tool definitions to guarantee schema-valid arguments; validate again on the server side anyway. Return errors as data (is_error: true) so the model can recover, and return all parallel tool results in one message. Server tools run on Anthropic&rsquo;s side with no loop code: web search, web fetch, code execution. MCP servers can be attached directly through the MCP connector. On the newest models, forced tool choice (any / a named tool) is not supported — use auto plus a clear instruction, or structured outputs if you only wanted JSON. Structured outputs# When you need JSON, constrain the response to a schema instead of asking politely: from pydantic import BaseModel class Triage(BaseModel): component: str severity: str # &#34;S1&#34;..&#34;S4&#34; duplicate_of: str | None summary: str result = client.messages.parse( model=&#34;claude-haiku-5-5&#34;, max_tokens=2000, messages=[{&#34;role&#34;: &#34;user&#34;, &#34;content&#34;: f&#34;Triage this bug report:\n{report}&#34;}], output_format=Triage, ) ticket = result.parsed_output # a validated Triage instance Prompt caching: the biggest free win# Caching stores a prefix of the request (tools → system → messages) so later requests that start with the same bytes pay a fraction of the input price and get faster time to first token. response = client.messages.create( model=&#34;claude-sonnet-5-5&#34;, max_tokens=4000, system=[{ &#34;type&#34;: &#34;text&#34;, &#34;text&#34;: CODING_STANDARDS_AND_ARCHITECTURE_GUIDE, # large and stable &#34;cache_control&#34;: {&#34;type&#34;: &#34;ephemeral&#34;}, }], messages=[{&#34;role&#34;: &#34;user&#34;, &#34;content&#34;: diff_to_review}], # varies per call ) print(response.usage.cache_read_input_tokens) # should be &gt; 0 on repeat calls Put stable content first and volatile content last. A timestamp, request ID or unsorted JSON in the system prompt silently breaks the cache. To add operator instructions mid-conversation on current models, append a system-role message to messages rather than editing the top-level system prompt — the cached prefix survives. Verify with cache_read_input_tokens; if it stays at zero, something in the prefix is changing. Batches, files, citations and documents# Feature What it does Typical engineering use Message Batches Up to tens of thousands of

b: Simple definition# A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained to predict the next piece of text. Given &ldquo;The capital of France is&rdquo;, it assigns a probability to every possible next token and &ldquo;Paris&rdquo; scores highest. Repeating that prediction one token at a time produces sentences, code, plans and answers. Everything else — chat, reasoning, tool use — is built on that single ability. Why architects need to know this# You do not need to train models, but the mechanics explain the constraints you design around: Mechanic Consequence for your architecture Text is split into tokens Cost, latency and limits are measured in tokens, not characters or words. The model sees a fixed context window Anything not in the prompt does not exist for the model. You must retrieve knowledge and manage memory. Output is sampled from probabilities Responses are non-deterministic. You need evaluation, validation and retries. Knowledge is frozen at the training cutoff Recent or private facts must come from RAG or tools. The model is stateless Conversation history is re-sent on every call; your application stores it. It generates the most plausible text It can be fluently wrong (hallucination). Grounding and citations are a design concern. The pipeline from text to text# One generation step inside an LLM flowchart LR A[&#34;Input text&#34;] --&gt; B[&#34;Tokenizer&lt;br/&gt;text → token IDs&#34;] B --&gt; C[&#34;Embedding layer&lt;br/&gt;IDs → vectors&#34;] C --&gt; D[&#34;Transformer blocks × N&lt;br/&gt;self-attention + feed-forward&#34;] D --&gt; E[&#34;Output layer&lt;br/&gt;scores for every token in vocabulary&#34;] E --&gt; F[&#34;Sampling&lt;br/&gt;temperature, top-p&#34;] F --&gt; G[&#34;Next token&#34;] G --&gt;|&#34;append and repeat&#34;| B 1. Tokens# A tokenizer splits text into sub-word units using an algorithm such as Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE). Common words become one token; rare words split into several. Rule of thumb for English: 1 token ≈ 4 characters ≈ 0.75 words. 1,000 tokens ≈ 750 words. Code, non-English text and numbers usually take more tokens per word. Each model family has its own tokenizer, so the same text has different token counts on different models. Review tipWhy do LLMs struggle to count letters in a word? The model never sees letters. &ldquo;strawberry&rdquo; may be one or two tokens, so &ldquo;how many r&rsquo;s?&rdquo; asks about structure the model does not directly observe. 2. Embeddings# Each token ID is mapped to a vector of a few thousand numbers. Vectors for tokens with similar meaning end up close together. The same idea — meaning as a position in space — powers the embedding models used for search in RAG. 3. The transformer and attention# The core of every modern LLM is the transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017). It is a stack of identical blocks. Each block has two parts: Self-attention — every token looks at every earlier token and decides how much each one matters to it. In &ldquo;The bank raised its rates because it …&rdquo;, attention lets &ldquo;it&rdquo; link to &ldquo;bank&rdquo;. Feed-forward network — transforms each token&rsquo;s vector independently; this is where much of the model&rsquo;s stored knowledge lives. Inside one transformer block (decoder-only) flowchart TB IN[&#34;Token vectors from previous block&#34;] --&gt; ATT[&#34;Masked multi-head self-attention&lt;br/&gt;each token attends to earlier tokens&#34;] ATT --&gt; ADD1[&#34;Add &amp; normalise&lt;br/&gt;residual connection&#34;] ADD1 --&gt; FFN[&#34;Feed-forward network&lt;br/&gt;per-token transformation&#34;] FFN --&gt; ADD2[&#34;Add &amp; normalise&#34;] ADD2 --&gt; OUT[&#34;To next block&#34;] How attention works, simply. Each token produces three vectors: a query (&ldquo;what am I looking for?&rdquo;), a key (&ldquo;what do I contain?&rdquo;) and a value (&ldquo;what do I pass on?&rdquo;). A token&rsquo;s query is compared with every earlier token&rsquo;s key; the similarity scores become weights; the output is the weighted sum of the values. Multi-head attention runs several of these in parallel so different heads can track grammar, references, facts and so on. Why it matters: attention compares every token with every other token, so cost grows roughly with the square of the sequence length. That is why long contexts are expensive and why inference engines cache keys and values (the KV cache). Decoder-only. Chat models (GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Mistral) are decoder-only: each token can only attend to tokens before it (&ldquo;causal masking&rdquo;), which is exactly what next-token generation needs. Encoder-only models such as BERT see the whole text at once and are used for classification and embeddings. Mixture of Experts (MoE). Many large models replace the single feed-forward network with several &ldquo;expert&rdquo; networks and a router that sends each token to only a few of them. The model has many parameters in total but uses a fraction per token, so it is cheaper to run than a dense model of the same size. 4. Sampling: turning scores into text# The output layer produces a probability for every token in the vocabulary. Decoding picks one. Setting What it does Typical use Temperature Sharpens (low) or flattens (high) the distribution. 0 ≈ always pick the most likely token. 0–0.3 for extraction, classification, code; 0.7–1.0 for creative text Top-p (nucleus) Sample only from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p. 0.9–1.0 Top-k Sample only from the k most likely tokens. Rarely tuned in enterprise apps Max tokens Hard limit on output length. Always set it: it caps cost and latency Stop sequences Strings that end generation. Structured formats Common mistake&ldquo;Temperature 0 makes it deterministic&rdquo; It makes it more repeatable, not guaranteed. Batching, floating-point arithmetic and provider-side changes can still change outputs. Design for variation: validate outputs and evaluate on datasets, not single runs. 5. The context

b: Simple definition# Generative AI produces content when asked. Agentic AI pursues a goal: it plans, uses tools, takes actions across systems, remembers, and improves from results — with as little human prompting as the task allows. Agentic capability is not on or off. It is a progression, from rule-based automation to fully autonomous agents, and each step needs stronger sensing, planning, acting and reflecting. Generative AI vs agentic AI# Dimension Generative AI Agentic AI Core capability Generate text, images, code from a prompt Plan, decide and execute multi-step work Memory The current context only Persistent memory across sessions; plans adapt to it Autonomy Waits for a human prompt each time Runs workflows with minimal human input Integration Mostly standalone; occasional API use Deep integration with APIs, databases, business systems, sometimes physical systems Learning Changes only when retrained Improves from interactions and feedback Typical use Drafting, summarising, coding help, brainstorming Workflow automation, operations, assistants that complete tasks Business effect Faster, better individual work Automated processes, reduced workload, scalable operations Key conceptThe one idea to keep Generative AI makes people faster at tasks; agentic AI takes over parts of processes. That shift moves the design questions from content quality to control, integration, accountability and failure recovery. The progression: six levels from manual to autonomous# A useful mental model borrows from self-driving cars: autonomy grows in levels, and most real systems today sit in the middle. The agentic AI progression flowchart LR L0[&#34;Level 0&lt;br/&gt;Manual operations&lt;br/&gt;humans do everything&#34;] --&gt; L1[&#34;Level 1&lt;br/&gt;Rule-based automation&lt;br/&gt;RPA, scripts&#34;] L1 --&gt; L2[&#34;Level 2&lt;br/&gt;Intelligent process automation&lt;br/&gt;ML, NLP, OCR + RPA&#34;] L2 --&gt; L3[&#34;Level 3&lt;br/&gt;Agentic workflows&lt;br/&gt;LLMs plan and adapt&lt;br/&gt;in a defined domain&#34;] L3 --&gt; L4[&#34;Level 4&lt;br/&gt;Semi-autonomous agents&lt;br/&gt;adapt strategies,&lt;br/&gt;learn across sessions&#34;] L4 --&gt; L5[&#34;Level 5&lt;br/&gt;Fully autonomous agents&lt;br/&gt;any task, any domain&#34;] Level Car analogy What the system does Typical technology 0 — Manual No assistance People perform every step with basic digital tools Spreadsheets, email 1 — Rule-based automation Cruise control Follows fixed rules on structured inputs; logs errors, does not learn RPA, scripts, rule engines 2 — Intelligent process automation Lane keeping and adaptive speed, supervised Adds perception — reads documents, classifies, extracts — within a fixed process ML, NLP, computer vision, orchestration + RPA 3 — Agentic workflows Highway autopilot; human takes over in complex situations Generates content, reasons, plans and chains tools within a defined domain; limited memory LLMs, tool calling, memory stores 4 — Semi-autonomous agents Self-driving in specific conditions Sets its own sub-goals, recovers from errors, remembers across sessions and learns from experience Advanced reasoning models, long-term memory, real-time adaptation 5 — Fully autonomous agents Self-driving anywhere Handles any task, learns across domains, formulates goals with no human involvement Not yet achieved Most production enterprise agents in 2026 sit at level 3, with selected level-4 behaviour in narrow domains (coding, IT operations, research). Level 5 remains an aspiration. TipTwo different &ldquo;levels&rdquo; scales This progression describes the capability of a system. The levels of autonomy in What is an agent? describe how much authority you grant it per action. A level-4-capable agent can — and in regulated work usually should — run with approval gates. The SPAR loop: how an agent takes action# People act by perceiving a situation, deciding what to do, doing it and learning from the result. Agents follow the same cycle, called SPAR: SPAR: sense, plan, act, reflect flowchart LR S[&#34;SENSE&lt;br/&gt;gather inputs:&lt;br/&gt;requests, events,&lt;br/&gt;data, documents&#34;] --&gt; P[&#34;PLAN&lt;br/&gt;reason about the goal,&lt;br/&gt;break it into steps,&lt;br/&gt;choose tools&#34;] P --&gt; A[&#34;ACT&lt;br/&gt;call tools and APIs,&lt;br/&gt;change systems,&lt;br/&gt;communicate&#34;] A --&gt; R[&#34;REFLECT&lt;br/&gt;check results,&lt;br/&gt;learn, update memory,&lt;br/&gt;adjust the plan&#34;] R --&gt; S How each capability grows across the levels: Capability Level 1–2 Level 3 Level 4–5 Sense Predefined triggers, structured or semi-structured data Natural-language understanding, context awareness Multimodal perception; at level 5, full environmental awareness and goal formulation Plan If-then rules, decision trees, basic ML decisions Reasoning with foundation models; orchestrating multi-step workflows Dynamic strategies, goal decomposition, original problem-solving Act Deterministic actions, error handling Chaining tools, multi-step tasks Autonomous tool selection, error recovery Reflect Logging, monitoring, no adaptation Short-term feedback, limited long-term memory Context across sessions, learning from experience, continuous self-improvement SPAR is the business-friendly name for the agent loop (think → act → observe) with an explicit reflection and learning step. The three keystones: action, reasoning, memory# Agentic capability rests on three keystones. A weakness in any one limits the whole agent. Keystone Question it answers Read more Action Can it do things — use tools reliably, and cope when they fail? Tool calling, Agent planning and failure modes Reasoning Can it think — plan, decompose, judge, recover? Workflow patterns Memory Can it learn — remember context, facts, experience and feedback? Memory and state Action: plans and tool resilience# Ask a capable model to plan a task — &ldquo;summarise a 30-page report and share it with the team, tracking who read it&rdquo; — and it will produce a

b: How to read this page# Each profile answers the same questions: what is the core idea, what does minimal code look like, what is it good at, and what should you watch out for. Code is deliberately minimal and uses a placeholder MODEL; check each project&rsquo;s documentation for current model identifiers and options. Version noteStatus as of November 2026 LangChain and LangGraph reached 1.0 in October 2025. Microsoft Agent Framework 1.0 (successor to AutoGen and Semantic Kernel) shipped in April 2026. Agent Skills became an open standard in December 2025. Other version numbers move monthly — verify before you adopt. LangGraph and LangChain# Core idea. Three layers from the same team: LangChain is the framework (models, tools, create_agent with middleware), LangGraph is the runtime (state graphs with durable checkpoints, interrupts and streaming), and Deep Agents is a batteries-included harness on top (planning, file system, sub-agents, skills, context management). LangChain, LangGraph and Deep Agents flowchart TB DA[&#34;Deep Agents — harness&lt;br/&gt;sub-agents, file system, skills&#34;] --&gt; CA[&#34;LangChain create_agent&lt;br/&gt;agent + middleware&#34;] CA --&gt; LG[&#34;LangGraph runtime&lt;br/&gt;state graph, checkpoints, interrupts&#34;] CUSTOM[&#34;Your custom graphs&lt;br/&gt;deterministic + agentic steps&#34;] --&gt; LG Quick agent with create_agent: from langchain.agents import create_agent def get_order(order_id: str) -&gt; str: &#34;&#34;&#34;Return status of a customer&#39;s order, e.g. A-10293.&#34;&#34;&#34; return orders_api.status(order_id) agent = create_agent(model=MODEL, tools=[get_order], system_prompt=&#34;You are a concise support agent.&#34;) agent.invoke({&#34;messages&#34;: [{&#34;role&#34;: &#34;user&#34;, &#34;content&#34;: &#34;Where is A-10293?&#34;}]}) Explicit control with a LangGraph state graph: from typing import TypedDict from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver class Claim(TypedDict): text: str category: str decision: str def classify(s: Claim): return {&#34;category&#34;: llm_classify(s[&#34;text&#34;])} def auto_settle(s: Claim): return {&#34;decision&#34;: &#34;settled&#34;} def to_adjuster(s: Claim): return {&#34;decision&#34;: &#34;queued for adjuster&#34;} g = StateGraph(Claim) g.add_node(&#34;classify&#34;, classify) g.add_node(&#34;auto_settle&#34;, auto_settle) g.add_node(&#34;to_adjuster&#34;, to_adjuster) g.add_edge(START, &#34;classify&#34;) g.add_conditional_edges(&#34;classify&#34;, lambda s: &#34;auto_settle&#34; if s[&#34;category&#34;] == &#34;simple&#34; else &#34;to_adjuster&#34;) g.add_edge(&#34;auto_settle&#34;, END) g.add_edge(&#34;to_adjuster&#34;, END) app = g.compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver()) # use a Postgres checkpointer in production app.invoke({&#34;text&#34;: claim_text}, config={&#34;configurable&#34;: {&#34;thread_id&#34;: &#34;claim-881&#34;}}) Good at: precise control flow, durable execution, human interrupts (interrupt()), streaming, time-travel debugging; huge integration ecosystem; LangSmith tracing. Watch out: more concepts to learn; keep graphs small and readable; pin versions. OpenAI Agents SDK# Core idea. A small set of primitives: Agents (instructions + tools), handoffs (transfer to another agent), guardrails (input/output checks running in parallel), sessions (conversation memory) and built-in tracing. Uses the Responses API by default. from agents import Agent, Runner, function_tool @function_tool def get_order(order_id: str) -&gt; str: &#34;&#34;&#34;Look up an order&#39;s status.&#34;&#34;&#34; return orders_api.status(order_id) billing = Agent(name=&#34;Billing&#34;, instructions=&#34;Handle refunds and invoices.&#34;, tools=[get_order]) triage = Agent(name=&#34;Triage&#34;, instructions=&#34;Route the customer to the right specialist.&#34;, handoffs=[billing]) result = Runner.run_sync(triage, &#34;I was charged twice for A-10293&#34;) print(result.final_output) Good at: minimal abstractions, clean handoff-based multi-agent apps, tracing on by default, voice/realtime agents. Watch out: best experience with OpenAI models; for complex durable workflows add your own state or a workflow engine. Claude Agent SDK# Core idea. The agent harness behind Claude Code, available as a library: automatic context management and compaction, built-in tools (files, shell, web), sub-agents, hooks around tool calls, permission modes, MCP servers and Agent Skills (folders with a SKILL.md loaded on demand). from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions options = ClaudeAgentOptions( system_prompt=&#34;You are an SRE agent. Investigate, then propose a fix; never deploy.&#34;, allowed_tools=[&#34;Read&#34;, &#34;Grep&#34;, &#34;Bash&#34;], # least privilege mcp_servers={&#34;metrics&#34;: metrics_server_config}, # company MCP server ) async for message in query(prompt=&#34;Why did checkout latency spike at 14:05?&#34;, options=options): print(message) Good at: long-running, open-ended tasks (coding, research, operations) where a capable harness matters more than custom control flow; strong permission and hook model. Watch out: opinionated harness centred on Claude models; give it a sandbox and narrow permissions. See agent harnesses. Google Agent Development Kit (ADK)# Core idea. LLM agents with tools plus deterministic workflow agents — SequentialAgent, ParallelAgent, LoopAgent — composed into hierarchies. Native A2A support; deploy locally, on Cloud Run or on Vertex AI Agent Engine. Available in Python, Java, Go and TypeScript. from google.adk.agents import Agent, SequentialAgent def get_policy(topic: str) -&gt; dict: &#34;&#34;&#34;Return the relevant policy text.&#34;&#34;&#34; return policy_store.lookup(topic) researcher = Agent(name=&#34;researcher&#34;, model=MODEL, instruction=&#34;Find the policy that applies.&#34;, tools=[get_policy]) writer = Agent(name=&#34;writer&#34;, model=MODEL, instruction=&#34;Write a short answer citing the

b: Answers are deliberately short — enough to check your understanding. Each section links to the article with the full explanation. TipHow to use this page Cover the answer, explain it in your own words, then compare. Mark questions you hesitated on and reread the linked article. 1. LLM fundamentals# Full explanations: How LLMs work, Inference &amp; cost, Prompt engineering. What is an LLM, in one sentence? A transformer neural network trained on huge text corpora to predict the next token, which — repeated — generates text, code and structured output. What is a token and why do architects care? A sub-word unit (~4 characters of English). Cost, latency, rate limits and context limits are all measured in tokens. Explain self-attention simply. Each token compares its query vector with the key vectors of other tokens to decide how much to use each one&rsquo;s value vector. It lets tokens draw on relevant context anywhere in the sequence; cost grows quadratically with length. What is the context window? Does a 1M-token window remove the need for RAG? The maximum tokens per call, input plus output. No: long prompts are costly and slow, models use the middle of long contexts less reliably, and corpora are much bigger — retrieval still selects the right context. What do temperature and top-p do? Temperature sharpens or flattens the next-token distribution (low = focused, high = varied). Top-p samples only from the smallest set of tokens whose probability sums to p. Why do LLMs hallucinate? How do you reduce it? They generate plausible text even without the facts. Ground with RAG, require citations, allow &ldquo;I don&rsquo;t know&rdquo;, lower temperature, use tools for facts and maths, and check faithfulness automatically. Base vs instruction-tuned vs reasoning model? Base: next-token predictor only. Instruction-tuned: SFT and preference tuning to follow instructions safely. Reasoning: further RL training to think step by step before answering — better on hard multi-step tasks, slower and costlier. What are prefill and decode? Prefill processes the prompt in parallel and determines time to first token; decode generates one token at a time and determines total generation time. What is the KV cache? Stored attention keys and values of processed tokens, so decode does not recompute them; it consumes GPU memory and limits concurrency. How does prompt caching work and how do you design for it? The provider reuses computation for an identical prompt prefix, cutting cost and TTFT. Put stable content (system prompt, tools, documents) first and variable content last. How do you estimate LLM cost? Requests × (input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price), with realistic token counts including system prompt, retrieved context and history. How do you get reliable structured output? Schema-constrained structured output from a typed class, parse into the type, validate business rules, retry or escalate on failure. 2. Model selection and customisation# Full explanations: Model selection, Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning. How do you choose a model for a use case? Define metrics; apply hard filters (data residency, licence, capabilities, context); shortlist via benchmarks and price; evaluate on our own dataset for quality, latency and cost; weighted scoring; choose primary and fallback; re-evaluate on new releases. Open-weight or proprietary? Proprietary: top quality, no ops, data leaves your network under contract. Open-weight: full control and customisation, cheaper at high steady volume, but you operate it. Many enterprises use both. What is model routing? Sending each request to the cheapest model that can handle it, via rules or a classifier, sometimes with escalation on low confidence. RAG or fine-tuning? RAG for knowledge — private, changing, citable, permissioned. Fine-tuning for behaviour — format, style, domain language, or making a small model good at one high-volume task. Start with prompting. What is LoRA? Parameter-efficient fine-tuning: freeze the base model and train small low-rank adapter matrices; cheap to train and swap. What is distillation? Training a small model on a large model&rsquo;s outputs to get most of its quality on a narrow task at lower cost and latency. How do you avoid vendor lock-in? Abstraction layer or AI gateway, model-agnostic prompts and tool schemas, a reusable evaluation suite, a tested fallback provider. 3. Enterprise AI stack and LLMOps# Full explanations: Enterprise AI stack, LLMOps. Describe an enterprise AI reference architecture. Infrastructure and models; an AI gateway; a knowledge layer (ingestion, hybrid search, graphs); orchestration and agents with a tool/MCP registry; applications; cross-cutting LLMOps and governance. What does an AI gateway do? Central entry to all models: authentication, quotas, guardrails, caching, routing and fallback, logging, cost metering and chargeback. What is LLMOps and how is it different from MLOps? Operating LLM apps: versioned prompts, evaluation of non-deterministic output, token cost control, safety guardrails, tracing of chains and agents, and handling provider model changes. What would you put on an LLM dashboard? Requests, errors, 429s; p95 TTFT and latency; tokens and cost per feature/user; retrieval empty-rate; online faithfulness and relevance; guardrail triggers; user feedback. How do you release a prompt change safely? Version it, run the evaluation suite in CI against the baseline, review, canary or A/B with feature flags, monitor, keep rollback. What resilience patterns apply to LLM calls? Timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads, fallback models/providers, queues for batch, degraded mode. 3a. Adoption, deployment and financial services# Full explanations: GenAI adoption strategy, On-prem &amp; hybrid deployment, Hybrid AI in financial services. What are the stages of GenAI adoption maturity? Explore (policy, approved tools, literacy), experiment (measured pilots), formalise
