b: Simple definition# Fine-tuning continues training a pre-trained model on your own examples so that it changes its behaviour — format, style, task skill, domain vocabulary. It is the most powerful adaptation technique and the most expensive one to run and maintain. Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning covers the decision. This article covers what happens underneath: memory, efficiency techniques and the knobs that matter. When to fine-tune — and when not to# Good reasons Poor reasons A consistent output format or structure prompting cannot hold Adding facts that change — use RAG A style or tone that is hard to describe but easy to show You have not yet tried a strong prompt with examples A narrow, high-volume task where a small tuned model beats a large general one on cost and latency You have no evaluation set to show it helped Distilling a large model&rsquo;s behaviour into a smaller one You cannot maintain it when the base model is updated Domain-specific reasoning patterns or jargon The team has no ML capacity to run training and serving Key conceptForm vs facts Fine-tuning is for form — how the model answers. RAG is for facts — what it answers with. Most production systems that fine-tune also use RAG. Risks to weigh: fine-tuning for one task can degrade others (catastrophic forgetting); you take on training and serving infrastructure; and when a better base model appears, you must decide whether to re-tune on it. A sensible progression: prompt → prompt with examples → RAG → fine-tune a small model (often with LoRA) → full fine-tuning only if justified. Memory math# Memory, not compute, is usually what stops a fine-tuning or serving plan. These rules of thumb make it estimable. Inference# memory ≈ parameters × bytes_per_parameter × 1.2 The 1.2 factor is a rough allowance for activations and KV cache at modest context and batch size. A 13B model in 16-bit needs about 13B × 2 bytes = 26 GB for weights and roughly 31 GB in total. A 70B model needs about 140 GB for weights alone. Long contexts and large batches need much more — see KV cache sizing. Training# training memory = weights + activations + gradients + optimizer states Gradients and optimizer states scale with the number of trainable parameters: Optimizer Extra values per trainable parameter SGD 1 (gradient) SGD with momentum 2 (gradient + momentum) Adam / AdamW 3 (gradient + two moment estimates) Full fine-tuning of a 13B model with Adam at 2 bytes per value needs about 13B × 3 × 2 = 78 GB just for gradients and optimizer state — on top of weights and activations. If only 1B parameters are trainable, that drops to about 6 GB. This is the whole case for parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Activations can dwarf the weights for long sequences. Gradient checkpointing (activation recomputation) stores fewer activations and recomputes them during the backward pass — less memory, more time. Numerical formats and quantisation# Format Bits Notes FP32 32 Full precision; rarely used for LLM inference BF16 16 Same range as FP32 with less precision; the default for training FP16 16 More precision, smaller range; overflow risk in training FP8 8 Supported by recent accelerators for training and inference INT8 8 Common for inference INT4 / 4-bit formats 4 Large savings; quality loss is task-dependent Two things to keep separate: Range vs precision. Fewer exponent bits shrink the range (risk of overflow); fewer mantissa bits reduce precision. Quantisation vs reduced precision. Reduced precision uses a smaller floating-point format; quantisation maps values to integers with a scale factor. Both reduce memory. What to quantise: weights most often, activations sometimes, the KV cache increasingly. When: post-training quantisation (after training, cheap) or quantisation-aware training (simulate low precision during training, better quality at very low bits). Mixed precision training keeps a high-precision master copy of the weights while computing in lower precision. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT)# PEFT trains a small number of new or selected parameters and freezes the rest, getting close to full fine-tuning quality with a fraction of the memory and data. Family Idea Examples Adapter-based Add small trainable modules to the frozen model Bottleneck adapters, LoRA, QLoRA Soft-prompt-based Train continuous &ldquo;virtual tokens&rdquo; prepended to the input Prefix tuning, prompt tuning LoRA# Low-Rank Adaptation freezes a weight matrix W and learns its update as the product of two small matrices, A and B, with a small rank r: LoRA: learn a low-rank update next to a frozen weight flowchart LR X[&#34;Input x&#34;] --&gt; W[&#34;Frozen weight W&lt;br/&gt;d × k&#34;] X --&gt; A[&#34;A&lt;br/&gt;d × r (trainable)&#34;] A --&gt; B[&#34;B&lt;br/&gt;r × k (trainable)&#34;] W --&gt; S((&#34;+&#34;)) B --&gt; S S --&gt; Y[&#34;Output = Wx + BAx&#34;] Why it works well: Few trainable parameters. With r = 8 or 16, the update has a tiny fraction of the original parameters. No inference latency if you merge BA into W before serving. Modular. Each task becomes a small adapter file you can swap. Practical configuration: apply LoRA to the attention projections (query, key, value, output) and, for more capacity, the MLP layers; ranks between 4 and 64 are typical; higher rank is not always better. QLoRA# QLoRA keeps the frozen base model in 4-bit and trains LoRA adapters in higher precision. It makes fine-tuning a large model possible on a single GPU, at the cost of slower training from de-quantising on the fly. Serving many adapters# Strategy Pros Cons Merge each adapter into a full model copy No extra latency One full model per task — memory-heavy Keep adapters separate and apply at request time One base model, many tiny adapters; swap per request Small added latency Multi-LoRA serving engines batch requests for different adapters on the same base model — ideal for per-customer or per-task specialisation. Model merging and multi-task fine-tuning# When you need one

b: Simple definition# LLMs are stateless: each call knows only what is in its prompt. Memory is everything your system stores and feeds back so an agent can continue a conversation, remember a user&rsquo;s preferences, learn from past cases, and resume a long task after a crash. Types of memory# Memory types flowchart TB M[&#34;Agent memory&#34;] --&gt; ST[&#34;Short-term / working memory&lt;br/&gt;current conversation and task state&lt;br/&gt;lives in the context window&#34;] M --&gt; LT[&#34;Long-term memory&lt;br/&gt;persists across sessions&lt;br/&gt;stored outside the model&#34;] LT --&gt; SEM[&#34;Semantic&lt;br/&gt;facts: &#39;customer prefers email&#39;,&lt;br/&gt;&#39;uses product X v3&#39;&#34;] LT --&gt; EPI[&#34;Episodic&lt;br/&gt;past interactions and outcomes:&lt;br/&gt;&#39;last month&#39;s ticket was solved by …&#39;&#34;] LT --&gt; PRO[&#34;Procedural&lt;br/&gt;how to do things: learned instructions,&lt;br/&gt;playbooks, improved prompts&#34;] Type Human analogy Storage Example Working / short-term What you are thinking about now Context window + session store Last 10 messages, current plan, tool results Semantic Facts you know Database / vector store / profile &ldquo;User is in the Munich office; prefers German&rdquo; Episodic Remembering past events Vector store of past episodes Summary of a similar resolved incident Procedural Skills Prompts, playbooks, tool definitions &ldquo;For VPN issues, check certificate first&rdquo; TipDon&rsquo;t forget the feedback layer Beyond short- and long-term memory, production agents need a third layer: a feedback loop that records outcomes and user reactions and feeds them back into prompts, memory and models. See the three layers of memory and user feedback. Managing short-term memory# Conversation history grows each turn and is re-sent every call. Strategies: Keeping history within budget flowchart LR H[&#34;Full history&lt;br/&gt;40 turns, 30K tokens&#34;] --&gt; W[&#34;Sliding window&lt;br/&gt;keep last N turns&#34;] H --&gt; SUM[&#34;Summarise older turns&lt;br/&gt;+ keep recent verbatim&#34;] H --&gt; TR[&#34;Trim tool results&lt;br/&gt;keep only key fields&#34;] H --&gt; RET[&#34;Retrieve relevant past turns&lt;br/&gt;vector search over history&#34;] W --&gt; P[&#34;Prompt within budget&#34;] SUM --&gt; P TR --&gt; P RET --&gt; P Sliding window — simplest; loses early details (like the user&rsquo;s name or order number). Summary + window — a running summary of older turns plus the last few turns verbatim. The usual production choice. Pin key facts — extract and keep important entities (order ID, decision made) in a structured &ldquo;state&rdquo; section. Clear tool results — old, bulky tool outputs can be dropped or shortened once used. Long-term memory: write and read# Long-term memory flow sequenceDiagram participant U as User participant A as Agent participant MS as Memory service participant DB as Memory store U-&gt;&gt;A: new message A-&gt;&gt;MS: recall(user_id, current query) MS-&gt;&gt;DB: profile facts + semantic search over memories DB--&gt;&gt;MS: relevant memories MS--&gt;&gt;A: &#34;Prefers email, had failed payment 2 weeks ago&#34; A-&gt;&gt;A: respond using memories A--&gt;&gt;U: answer A-)MS: extract new memories from this turn (async) MS-&gt;&gt;MS: dedupe, resolve conflicts, check policy MS-&gt;&gt;DB: upsert memories with source, timestamp, TTL Write policy — what is worth remembering? Extract stable facts and preferences, not every message. Resolve conflicts (new address replaces old). Record source and time. Read policy — retrieve only memories relevant to the current task (by user, recency and similarity), and show them to the model as data, clearly labelled. Forget policy — expiry (TTL), user-requested deletion, and correction. State machines and workflow state# For structured processes, model the agent&rsquo;s progress as explicit state, not just chat history: Claims agent as a state machine stateDiagram-v2 [*] --&gt; Intake Intake --&gt; GatherEvidence: claim details complete Intake --&gt; AwaitCustomer: details missing AwaitCustomer --&gt; Intake: customer replies GatherEvidence --&gt; Assess Assess --&gt; AwaitApproval: payout &gt; limit Assess --&gt; Payout: payout ≤ limit AwaitApproval --&gt; Payout: approved AwaitApproval --&gt; Rejected: rejected Payout --&gt; [*] Rejected --&gt; [*] The LLM handles judgement inside states (understanding documents, assessing evidence); code controls the transitions. This hybrid is common in regulated industries because it is auditable. Durable execution and checkpoints# Agents that run for minutes, hours or days — waiting for approvals, external systems or users — must survive restarts and deployments. Checkpointed agent execution flowchart LR S1[&#34;Step 1: retrieve data&#34;] --&gt; CP1[(&#34;Checkpoint&#34;)] CP1 --&gt; S2[&#34;Step 2: call LLM&#34;] --&gt; CP2[(&#34;Checkpoint&#34;)] CP2 --&gt; S3[&#34;Step 3: wait for approval&lt;br/&gt;hours&#34;] --&gt; CP3[(&#34;Checkpoint&#34;)] CP3 --&gt; S4[&#34;Step 4: execute payment&#34;] CRASH[&#34;Pod restarts during step 3&#34;] -.-&gt;|&#34;resume from CP2/CP3,&lt;br/&gt;no repeated LLM calls or payments&#34;| S3 Checkpointing — save state after each step (LangGraph checkpointers, Spring AI chat memory repositories, your own tables). Durable execution engines — Temporal, AWS Step Functions, Azure Durable Functions, Restate — persist every step and replay deterministically after failures. Idempotency — side-effecting tools must use idempotency keys, because a step may be retried. Time travel / replay — saved checkpoints let you inspect and debug what the agent saw at each step. Privacy and governance of memory# Memory is personal data when it is about people: apply purpose limitation, retention limits, access control and the right to erasure. Let users see and delete what the assistant remembers. Separate memories by tenant and user; never retrieve one user&rsquo;s memories for another. Memory poisoning — an

b: Simple definition# A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file: YAML frontmatter saying what it is and when to use it, followed by Markdown instructions. Claude sees every skill&rsquo;s description in each session and loads the body only when the skill is invoked — by you typing /skill-name, or by Claude deciding it fits the task. Skills hold procedures and team knowledge that would otherwise bloat CLAUDE.md. Version noteSource and date Condensed from Anthropic&rsquo;s Skills page, read on 7 November 2026. Skills follow the open Agent Skills format; Claude Code adds extra frontmatter fields on top. How skills and sub-agents load into context · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. &copy; 2026 Samir Kumar Sahoo, all rights reserved. Open full screen ↗ Your first skill# --- name: summarize-changes description: Summarize uncommitted changes and flag risks. Use when asked what changed. --- ## Current changes !`git diff HEAD` ## Instructions Summarize the changes above in two or three bullets, then list risks such as missing error handling, hardcoded values or tests that need updating. Save as .claude/skills/summarize-changes/SKILL.md. Then either ask &ldquo;What did I change?&rdquo; (Claude invokes it) or type /summarize-changes. Where skills load from# Location Path Loads in Enterprise .claude/skills/&lt;name&gt;/SKILL.md in the managed settings directory Every user on managed machines Personal ~/.claude/skills/&lt;name&gt;/SKILL.md All your projects (not cloud sessions) Project .claude/skills/&lt;name&gt;/SKILL.md This repository — commit it for the team Nested &lt;subdir&gt;/.claude/skills/&lt;name&gt;/SKILL.md Sessions in, or working on files under, &lt;subdir&gt; (monorepos) --add-dir .claude/skills/ in the added directory That session Plugin &lt;plugin&gt;/skills/&lt;name&gt;/SKILL.md Where enabled, as /plugin-name:skill-name claude.ai Skills enabled on your account Cowork, cloud, and terminal sessions signed in with that account .claude/commands/&lt;name&gt;.md is the older single-file format and still works; prefer skills for new work (they support supporting files). Edits on disk apply after /reload-skills. Frontmatter# All fields are optional; description is the one that matters. Unknown fields are silently ignored — check spelling. Field Does name Command name (defaults to the folder name) description What it does and when to use it — Claude matches requests against this. Put the key use first; description + when_to_use are truncated at 1,536 characters when_to_use Extra trigger phrases or example requests argument-hint Autocomplete hint, e.g. issue-number arguments Named positional arguments for $name substitution disable-model-invocation true: only you can run it (/name); its description leaves Claude&rsquo;s context user-invocable false: only Claude can use it; hidden from the / menu allowed-tools Tools pre-approved for the turn that invokes the skill disallowed-tools Tools removed while the skill is active model, effort Model and effort for the rest of the current turn (or for the fork) context: fork Run in a sub-agent with the skill as its prompt agent Which sub-agent type runs the fork (e.g. Explore) background With fork: false waits for the result instead of running in the background hooks Hooks registered when the skill runs, for the rest of the session paths Glob patterns — auto-load only when working on matching files shell bash (default) or powershell for ! commands metadata, license, compatibility Accepted, not acted on (for your tooling and the open spec) Who can invoke a skill# Frontmatter You (/name) Claude In context default Yes Yes Description always; body when invoked disable-model-invocation: true Yes No Nothing until you invoke it user-invocable: false No Yes Description always; body when invoked Key conceptSide effects need a human trigger Any skill that deploys, publishes, commits or messages people should set disable-model-invocation: true. If Claude tries anyway, Claude Code blocks the call and tells it not to reproduce the steps another way. /deploy staging at the start of a message runs the skill; go ahead and /deploy later in a sentence only permits Claude to run it. You can stack up to six inline skills at the start of one message in the terminal. Arguments# Placeholder Becomes $ARGUMENTS Everything after the skill name $0, $1… or $ARGUMENTS0… Positional arguments $name Named argument from arguments: --- name: migrate-component description: Migrate a component between languages argument-hint: component from-lang to-lang disable-model-invocation: true --- Migrate the $0 component from $1 to $2. Preserve all existing behaviour and tests. /migrate-component SearchBar JavaScript TypeScript. If no placeholder is used, Claude Code appends ARGUMENTS: &lt;input&gt; so nothing is lost. Supporting files and dynamic context# release/ ├── SKILL.md # overview and steps — keep under 500 lines ├── checklist.md # loaded only when SKILL.md points Claude to it └── scripts/bump.sh # executed, not loaded Reference supporting files from SKILL.md (&ldquo;for the full checklist, see checklist.md&rdquo;) so Claude knows when to read them. !`command` runs before Claude sees the skill and inlines the output — live git diff, gh pr view, environment facts. (disableSkillShellExecution turns this off.) Run a skill in a sub-agent# --- name: pr-summary description: Summarize the current pull request context: fork agent: Explore allowed-tools: Bash(gh *) --- ## Pull request !`gh pr view --json title,body,files` Summarize what changed and why, list risky files, and suggest reviewers. The sub-agent doesn&rsquo;t see your conversation — the skill must contain a complete task. A skill of pure guidelines under fork returns nothing useful. Forks run in the background by default (in -p and SDK runs they wait); set background: false to wait. A background fork&rsquo;s edits are outside your checkpoints — use Git to revert them. To hand over the whole conversation

b: Simple definition# Dataset engineering is the work of producing the data a model is trained or evaluated on: deciding what data you need, getting it, generating it when you cannot get it, and cleaning it into a usable format. As models become commodities, data becomes the differentiator. Two teams using the same base model are separated mostly by the quality of their instructions, examples, preferences and evaluation sets. Key conceptThe one idea to keep A small amount of high-quality, well-covered data beats a large amount of noisy data. Fine-tuning has been shown to work with only a few thousand carefully chosen examples. What data are we talking about?# Purpose Shape of the data Supervised fine-tuning (instruction, response) pairs; multi-turn conversations Preference fine-tuning (prompt, preferred response, rejected response) Reasoning Problems with step-by-step solutions (chain-of-thought) Tool use Conversations including tool calls, arguments and results — often hard to collect from humans, because people use tools differently from agents Evaluation Inputs with expected outputs, rubrics or reference answers — see evaluating AI systems Retrieval Queries with relevant documents, for embedding and reranker tuning Single-turn data teaches answering; multi-turn data teaches clarification, follow-up and correction. Most real applications need both. Data curation: quality, coverage, quantity# Quality# High-quality examples are: Property Meaning Relevant Match the task and domain you will serve Aligned with task requirements Follow the format, policy and style the product needs — a correct but off-format answer is a bad example Consistent Annotators agree; the same input gets the same label Correctly formatted No stray HTML, broken encodings, truncated responses Sufficiently unique Few duplicates, which distort training and contaminate evaluation Compliant Licensed for use, free of personal data you cannot keep Coverage# Data must span the range of inputs the product will see: topics, lengths, languages, user expertise, phrasing styles, edge cases and adversarial inputs. Missing a slice in training shows up as a failure for that slice in production. Mix matters too. If 80% of your traffic is billing questions, training on 80% technical questions skews behaviour. Experiment with mixes and measure per-slice quality. Quantity# How much you need depends on: Technique — full fine-tuning needs more data than LoRA; a strong base model needs less. Task complexity — classification needs less than open-ended generation or reasoning. Base-model fit — the closer the base model already is, the less you need. Run a data scaling experiment: train on 25%, 50% and 100% of your data and plot quality. If the curve is still rising, more data will help; if it has flattened, invest elsewhere. Acquisition and annotation# The best source is usually your own application — real user queries, corrections and feedback (see user feedback). Other sources: public datasets (check licences), purchased data, and annotation by experts or vendors. Annotation is mostly a guidelines problem. Write clear rubrics with examples of good and bad responses; the same guidelines later become your evaluation rubric. Measure inter-annotator agreement and resolve disagreements before scaling up. Data augmentation and synthesis# Synthetic data is used to increase quantity, increase coverage (rare cases, adversarial inputs), improve quality (better than average human writing for some tasks), protect privacy (realistic data without real customers) and distil models. Traditional techniques# Technique Example Rule-based / templates Generate transactions, forms or invoices from templates and value lists Perturbation Paraphrase, swap entities, add typos and noise to make models robust Simulation Simulate environments — robotics, game play, tool use — and record trajectories AI-powered synthesis# Models can generate inputs, outputs, or both: Instruction synthesis — generate diverse instructions from seed topics, then responses to them. Reverse instruction — start with high-quality human content (an article, code) and ask a model to write the instruction it answers; the response stays human-quality. Self-play and role-play — models simulate users, customers or opponents to create multi-turn data. Long-context data — split long documents and generate questions that require the whole document. An AI-powered synthetic data pipeline flowchart LR S[&#34;Seed topics,&lt;br/&gt;real examples,&lt;br/&gt;documents&#34;] --&gt; G[&#34;Generate&lt;br/&gt;instructions + responses&lt;br/&gt;with a strong model&#34;] G --&gt; V{&#34;Verify&#34;} V --&gt;|&#34;functional checks&lt;br/&gt;(code runs, math checks)&#34;| K[&#34;Keep&#34;] V --&gt;|&#34;AI judge scores&lt;br/&gt;above threshold&#34;| K V --&gt;|&#34;fails / duplicate /&lt;br/&gt;off-policy&#34;| X[&#34;Discard&#34;] K --&gt; D[&#34;Deduplicate&lt;br/&gt;and balance&#34;] D --&gt; H[&#34;Human spot-check&lt;br/&gt;sample&#34;] H --&gt; T[&#34;Training set&#34;] Verifying synthetic data# Generated data is only as useful as its verification: Functional correctness — run code, check math, validate JSON against a schema. AI judges — score quality, faithfulness and policy compliance; keep the top slice. Heuristics — remove repetitive examples, instructions that are too long or short, identical instructions with conflicting responses, outputs that just repeat the input. Human review of a sample — always. Limits of synthetic data# WarningSynthetic data has real failure modes Quality control — errors in generated data become errors in the model. Superficial imitation — a student can copy a teacher&rsquo;s style without its capability, and learn to hallucinate confidently. Model collapse — training repeatedly on model-generated data can lose rare cases and diversity over generations. Mix in real data. Obscure lineage — you may not know what the generating model was trained on, which complicates copyright,

b: Simple definition# A sub-agent is a separate Claude worker that the main conversation hands a task to. It has its own context window, its own system prompt, and optionally its own tools, model and permission mode. It does the work and returns a summary, so long searches, test logs or file dumps never enter your main conversation. Claude delegates on its own when a sub-agent&rsquo;s description fits; you can also ask for one by name. Version noteSource and date Condensed from Anthropic&rsquo;s Create custom subagents page, read on 7 November 2026. Built-in sub-agents# Agent Tools Model Used for Explore Read-only (no Write/Edit) Main conversation&rsquo;s model Fast codebase search; Claude picks quick, medium or very thorough Plan Read-only Inherits Research during plan mode general-purpose All sub-agent tools CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL if set, else inherits Multi-step tasks that explore and modify claude, statusline-setup, claude-code-guide Varies Varies Catch-all, /statusline, Claude Code questions Explore and Plan start without CLAUDE.md and git status to stay cheap. Define your own Explore with model: haiku to make exploration cheaper; deny Agent(Explore) to disable it; CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPLORE_PLAN_AGENTS=1 removes both. Where definitions live# Location Scope Priority Managed settings Organisation 1 (highest) --agents '&lt;json&gt;' This session 2 .claude/agents/ This project (commit it) 3 ~/.claude/agents/ All your projects 4 Plugin agents/ Where the plugin is enabled (plugin:name) 5 Same name in two places → the higher priority wins. Folders are scanned recursively, so agents/review/security.md is fine. Ask Claude to create one, or write the file. Definition format# --- name: reviewer description: Reviews changed files against the spec. Use after implementing a feature, before the PR. tools: Read, Grep, Glob model: sonnet effort: high maxTurns: 30 color: purple --- You are reviewing code you didn&#39;t write. Compare the changed files with the spec you are given. Check every requirement is implemented and edge cases have tests. Report only gaps that affect correctness, as a numbered list with file:line. Skip style. The body is the sub-agent&rsquo;s system prompt. The delegating Claude writes the task prompt from your request. Frontmatter# Field Required Does name Yes Identifier (no :); hooks see it as agent_type description Yes When Claude should delegate — add &ldquo;use proactively&rdquo; to encourage it tools No Allowlist, e.g. Read, Grep, Bash. Omit to inherit all sub-agent tools disallowedTools No Remove tools (a specifier like Bash(git push *) removes the whole tool) model No sonnet, opus, haiku, fable, a full ID, or inherit effort No low … max permissionMode No default, acceptEdits, auto, dontAsk, bypassPermissions, plan (ignored for plugin agents) maxTurns No Turn cap; output is returned marked partial skills No Skills preloaded in full at start mcpServers No Server names, or inline server configs, for this agent only hooks No Hooks active while this agent runs memory No user, project or local — persistent learning across sessions background No true keeps it in the background even when Claude asks to wait isolation No worktree — temporary git worktree, removed if unchanged omitClaudeMd No Start without user/project/local CLAUDE.md autoCompactWindow No Lower this agent&rsquo;s auto-compact threshold color No Display colour initialPrompt No First turn when run as the main agent (--agent) Which model runs it# The model Claude passes on that call (an alias). The definition&rsquo;s model (inherit = main model). CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL. The main conversation&rsquo;s model. A family alias that matches the main model&rsquo;s family resolves to the exact main model (including a 1M-context variant). Organisation availableModels still applies — a blocked model is substituted with a warning. TipThe cheapest lever model: haiku for mechanical jobs — collecting importers of a module, checking links, summarising logs — costs a fraction of the main model and is just as good at them. Invoking# How Guarantee Automatic Claude matches the task to a description &ldquo;Use the reviewer subagent to…&rdquo; Claude usually delegates @&quot;reviewer (agent)&quot; check the auth changes That sub-agent runs for this task claude --agent reviewer, or &quot;agent&quot; setting The whole session is that agent /subtask &lt;task&gt; A forked sub-agent that inherits your full conversation Foreground, background and forks# Sub-agents Claude spawns from your main conversation start in the background by default (fork mode on); permission prompts surface in your session, naming the agent. Ctrl+B backgrounds a running one; /tasks lists them; Ctrl+X Ctrl+K stops all. To let Claude wait for results, set CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=0. In -p and SDK runs, Claude can wait on its own judgment. A fork inherits the conversation instead of starting fresh — no re-gathering context, but it carries everything. Limits# Limit Default Change with Nesting depth below main 3 layers CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH (1 = no nesting) Concurrent sub-agents 20 CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS Combined descriptions Warning above 15,000 tokens Shorter descriptions Keep a reviewer from spawning more agents by omitting Agent from its tools. Controlling sub-agents# { &#34;permissions&#34;: { &#34;deny&#34;: [&#34;Agent(Explore)&#34;, &#34;Agent(general-purpose)&#34;] }, &#34;env&#34;: { &#34;CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL&#34;: &#34;haiku&#34; } } Deny Agent entirely to stop all delegation. Settings, managed and plugin hooks fire inside sub-agents too; SubagentStart / SubagentStop hooks see them start and finish. --append-subagent-system-prompt adds text to every sub-agent&rsquo;s prompt (useful in CI). Example agents# The first four follow Anthropic&rsquo;s published examples; the last two are common additions. Agent Tools Prompt essentials code-reviewer Read, Grep, Glob, Bash Review recent changes; report by severity; skip style

b: Simple definition# Agent reliability is the engineering that makes an agent do the right thing consistently, stop when it should, and fail safely when it cannot succeed. It combines guardrails (prevent bad actions), budgets (bound cost and time), evaluation (measure behaviour before and after release) and observability (see what happened). Why agents are hard to make reliable# Errors compound. If each step is 95% reliable, a 10-step task succeeds only 0.95¹⁰ ≈ 60% of the time. Agents also face non-deterministic outputs, changing tools and data, and adversarial inputs. So reliability comes from design, not just a better model: fewer steps, verification at each step, recovery from errors, and human checkpoints. Layered guardrails# Defence in depth for agents flowchart LR IN[&#34;User input /&lt;br/&gt;external content&#34;] --&gt; G1[&#34;Input guardrails&lt;br/&gt;topic, injection, PII,&lt;br/&gt;jailbreak classifiers&#34;] G1 --&gt; AG[&#34;Agent reasoning&#34;] AG --&gt; G2[&#34;Action guardrails&lt;br/&gt;tool allow-list, schema validation,&lt;br/&gt;authorisation, limits, approval&#34;] G2 --&gt; EXEC[&#34;Tool execution&lt;br/&gt;sandbox, scoped credentials&#34;] EXEC --&gt; AG AG --&gt; G3[&#34;Output guardrails&lt;br/&gt;grounding, PII, toxicity,&lt;br/&gt;policy, format&#34;] G3 --&gt; OUT[&#34;Response / action result&#34;] MON[&#34;Monitoring &amp; audit&lt;br/&gt;traces, alerts, kill switch&#34;] -.-&gt; AG Layer Examples Input Off-topic detection, prompt-injection classifiers, PII detection/masking, content moderation Action Allow-listed tools per agent, argument validation, per-user authorisation, amount limits, rate limits, human approval for irreversible actions Execution Sandboxed code execution (containers, no network by default), read-only credentials where possible, network egress allow-lists Output Groundedness check, PII leak detection, toxicity, brand/policy rules, schema validation Runtime Step, token, time and cost budgets; loop detection; kill switch Guardrail tools include NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails, Guardrails AI, Llama Guard / Prompt Guard models, cloud provider guardrail services (Bedrock Guardrails, Azure AI Content Safety), and custom rules. Budgets and stop conditions# Every agent run needs explicit limits: Max steps / tool calls (for example 15). Max tokens and cost per run and per user per day. Wall-clock timeout. Loop detection — same tool with same arguments repeated. Stop conditions in the prompt — what &ldquo;done&rdquo; means, when to ask the user, when to escalate. When a limit is hit, the agent should fail gracefully: summarise progress, explain what is blocking, and hand over to a human. Designing for recovery# Return informative tool errors so the model can self-correct. Verify after important steps (re-read the record you updated; run the tests). Checkpoint so retries do not repeat side effects; make writes idempotent. Prefer reversible actions (drafts, pending states) followed by confirmation. Evaluating agents# Agents need more than input → output checks, because how they got there matters too. For a taxonomy of planning, tool and efficiency failures and the metrics for each, see agent planning and failure modes. What to evaluate flowchart TB E[&#34;Agent evaluation&#34;] --&gt; O[&#34;Outcome&lt;br/&gt;was the task completed correctly?&lt;br/&gt;final state of systems&#34;] E --&gt; T[&#34;Trajectory&lt;br/&gt;right tools, right order,&lt;br/&gt;no unnecessary or unsafe steps&#34;] E --&gt; S[&#34;Single steps&lt;br/&gt;tool selection accuracy,&lt;br/&gt;argument correctness&#34;] E --&gt; Q[&#34;Quality &amp; safety&lt;br/&gt;tone, policy, refusals,&lt;br/&gt;injection resistance&#34;] E --&gt; C[&#34;Efficiency&lt;br/&gt;steps, tokens, latency, cost&#34;] Level Metric examples How Outcome Task success rate; final database state matches expected Compare end state with ground truth; LLM judge for open tasks Trajectory Tool-call precision/recall vs reference path; forbidden actions taken Compare the sequence of calls with expected; rules for forbidden actions Step Correct tool chosen; arguments valid and correct Unit-style tests on single decisions Safety Injection success rate; policy violations; unauthorised actions Red-team datasets, adversarial simulations Efficiency Mean steps, tokens, cost, latency per task From traces Consistency pass^k — succeeds in all k repeated runs Run each case several times Key conceptpass@k vs pass^k pass@k — at least one of k attempts succeeds (useful when a human picks the best). pass^k — all k attempts succeed. For an agent that runs unattended, pass^k is the honest measure: users experience every run, not the best one. Testing with simulations# Simulated end-to-end agent test sequenceDiagram participant H as Test harness participant SU as Simulated user (LLM with persona + goal) participant AG as Agent under test participant MT as Mock tools / sandbox systems participant J as Judge H-&gt;&gt;SU: scenario: &#34;angry customer wants refund for late order A-10293&#34; loop conversation SU-&gt;&gt;AG: message AG-&gt;&gt;MT: tool calls MT--&gt;&gt;AG: deterministic results AG--&gt;&gt;SU: reply end H-&gt;&gt;MT: read final state (refund issued? amount?) H-&gt;&gt;J: transcript + final state + rubric J--&gt;&gt;H: success, policy compliance, tone scores Mock or sandboxed tools make runs repeatable and safe. Simulated users (an LLM with a persona and a goal) exercise multi-turn behaviour. Benchmarks such as τ-bench follow this approach for customer-service agents. Observability for agents# Trace every run as a tree: user turn → LLM calls → tool calls → sub-agents, with inputs, outputs, tokens, latency and decisions. Needed for debugging, audit (&ldquo;why did the agent refund this?&rdquo;), cost control and building evaluation sets from real failures. Tools: OpenTelemetry with GenAI conventions, Langfuse, LangSmith, Arize Phoenix, cloud-native tracing. Rolling out an agent safely# Progressive autonomy rollout flowchart

b: Simple definition# Agents need to talk to three kinds of counterpart: tools and data, other agents, and people through a user interface. Since 2024 an open standard has emerged for each, plus two lightweight file conventions for giving agents know-how and instructions: Standard Connects One-line purpose MCP — Model Context Protocol Agent ↔ tools &amp; data Discover and call tools, read resources, use prompts A2A — Agent2Agent Agent ↔ agent Discover remote agents and delegate tasks with a lifecycle AG-UI — Agent–User Interaction Agent ↔ user interface Stream typed events (text, tool calls, state) to front ends Agent Skills (SKILL.md) Agent ↔ packaged know-how Folders of instructions, scripts and resources loaded on demand AGENTS.md Agent ↔ repository A README for agents: build, test and style instructions The stack in one picture# Agent protocol stack flowchart TB UI[&#34;User interface&lt;br/&gt;web, IDE, chat&#34;] &lt;--&gt;|&#34;AG-UI events&#34;| AG[&#34;Agent&lt;br/&gt;any framework&#34;] AG &lt;--&gt;|&#34;A2A tasks&#34;| RA[&#34;Remote agents&lt;br/&gt;other teams, vendors&#34;] AG &lt;--&gt;|&#34;MCP&#34;| T[&#34;MCP servers&lt;br/&gt;tools, resources, prompts&#34;] SK[&#34;Agent Skills&lt;br/&gt;SKILL.md folders&#34;] -.-&gt;|&#34;loaded on demand&#34;| AG MD[&#34;AGENTS.md&lt;br/&gt;repo instructions&#34;] -.-&gt;|&#34;read at start&#34;| AG T --- SYS[&#34;Enterprise systems&#34;] One task across the stack# One agent task across AG-UI, MCP and A2A · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. &copy; 2026 Samir Kumar Sahoo, all rights reserved. Open full screen ↗ The UI sends the user&rsquo;s request to the agent as an AG-UI run and listens to the event stream. The agent asks the LLM, which requests a tool; the agent calls it on an MCP server (tools/call) and streams TOOL_CALL_* events to the UI so the user sees progress. A policy check belongs to the finance team&rsquo;s expense agent, so the agent delegates it as an A2A task and receives the result as an artifact. The final answer streams to the UI as TEXT_MESSAGE_* events; the UI renders options and an approval button. MCP (recap)# Agent-to-tool standard: hosts, clients and servers; tools, resources and prompts; stdio and Streamable HTTP; OAuth for remote servers. Full article: MCP. A2A in more depth# A2A task lifecycle stateDiagram-v2 [*] --&gt; submitted submitted --&gt; working working --&gt; input_required: needs more info input_required --&gt; working: client replies working --&gt; auth_required: needs credentials auth_required --&gt; working working --&gt; completed working --&gt; failed working --&gt; canceled submitted --&gt; rejected completed --&gt; [*] failed --&gt; [*] canceled --&gt; [*] rejected --&gt; [*] Agent Card — JSON published at a well-known URL describing the agent&rsquo;s name, skills, endpoint, supported modalities and authentication. Task — the unit of work with the lifecycle above; long tasks report progress by streaming (server-sent events) or push notifications to a webhook. Messages and parts — text, files and structured data; results come back as artifacts. Opaque agents — the client does not see the remote agent&rsquo;s tools, prompts or memory: it is a black-box collaborator, which suits cross-team and cross-company work. Security — standard HTTP auth schemes declared in the Agent Card (OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, API keys, mTLS); signed Agent Cards for authenticity. A2A reached its 1.0 specification in 2026 and, like MCP, is governed under the Linux Foundation. AG-UI# AG-UI standardises the stream between an agent back end and an interactive front end, so any compliant UI can render any compliant agent: Event family Examples UI behaviour Lifecycle RUN_STARTED, RUN_FINISHED, RUN_ERROR Spinners, errors Text TEXT_MESSAGE_START/CONTENT/END Streamed answer Tool calls TOOL_CALL_START/ARGS/END Show &ldquo;searching flights…&rdquo;, render tool UIs State STATE_SNAPSHOT, STATE_DELTA Shared state between agent and app (forms, canvases) Human-in-the-loop Interrupt / resume patterns Approval buttons, edits It is transport-agnostic (SSE, WebSockets, webhooks) and supported by several frameworks (LangGraph, CrewAI, Mastra, ADK, Microsoft Agent Framework, Pydantic AI and others). Related efforts define declarative, generated UI components that agents can send for rendering. Agent Skills# A skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file — YAML front matter (name, description) plus instructions — and optional scripts, templates and reference files. The agent sees only each skill&rsquo;s short description at start-up and loads the full skill when relevant (progressive disclosure), so hundreds of skills cost almost no context until used. skills/ └── credit-memo/ ├── SKILL.md # name, description, step-by-step instructions ├── template.docx # resources the instructions refer to └── scripts/ └── ratios.py # deterministic helpers the agent can run Anthropic published Agent Skills as an open standard in December 2025; many agent products and coding tools now read the same format. Skills package procedural knowledge; MCP provides capabilities. They complement each other. See agent harnesses and skills. AGENTS.md# A Markdown file at the root of a repository with instructions for coding agents: how to build, test, lint, conventions and boundaries. Many coding agents read it automatically — a simple, tool-neutral way to give agents project context. Governance of the standards# In December 2025 the Linux Foundation launched the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) as a neutral home for open agent standards, starting with MCP, AGENTS.md and goose; other projects such as A2A have since been brought under Linux Foundation governance. Neutral governance reduces vendor-lock-in risk for enterprises adopting these protocols. Adoption guidance# Need Adopt Agents use internal systems MCP servers per domain, behind an MCP gateway Agents from different teams or vendors cooperate A2A with Agent Cards in a registry Rich

b: Simple definition# Evaluation methodology is the toolbox of ways to score a model&rsquo;s output. There are four families: language-modelling metrics (how well the model predicts text), exact evaluation (checks with an unambiguous answer), AI as a judge (another model scores the output) and comparative evaluation (rank models by which output people or judges prefer). No single method is enough. Production evaluation combines them — see evaluating AI systems for how to build the pipeline. Why evaluating foundation models is hard# Challenge Why it matters Open-ended outputs A question can have many good answers; you cannot compare to one reference Stronger models are harder to judge Checking a PhD-level proof or a long research report takes an expert Black boxes You often do not know the training data, architecture or post-training Benchmarks saturate Public benchmarks are solved, or leaked into training data, within months The scope widened General-purpose models must be checked for capabilities nobody asked for — and for harms Key conceptThe one idea to keep Evaluation is about detecting failures before users do. The best metric is one that fails when your product fails — tied to your task, your data and your users. Language-modelling metrics# These measure how well a model predicts text. They matter most to model builders, but are useful to application teams for data checks and confidence. Metric Meaning Lower is better? Entropy How much information a token carries on average — how unpredictable the data is — (property of data) Cross-entropy How hard it is for the model to predict the next token in a dataset Yes Bits-per-character / bits-per-byte (BPB) Cross-entropy normalised per character or byte, so models with different tokenizers can be compared Yes Perplexity The exponential of cross-entropy — roughly &ldquo;how many tokens the model is choosing between&rdquo; Yes How to read perplexity: More structured data → lower perplexity. Code and HTML are more predictable than poetry. Bigger vocabulary → higher perplexity, because there are more options per token. Longer context → lower perplexity, because the model has more to condition on. Post-training (SFT, RLHF) usually raises perplexity even as the model becomes more useful, so perplexity is a poor guide to assistant quality. Practical uses: detecting data contamination (unusually low perplexity on a benchmark suggests the model saw it), filtering training data, flagging unusual inputs, and as a confidence signal. Exact evaluation# Exact methods produce a verdict without ambiguity. Functional correctness# Does the output do what it should? This is the gold standard wherever you can run it. Task Check Code generation Run unit tests; pass@k — the probability that at least one of k samples passes Text-to-SQL Execute the query and compare result sets Structured extraction Validate against a schema and compare field values Agents and games Did the task complete? Did the score improve? Optimisation tasks Is the schedule feasible, is the cost lower? Similarity against reference data# When you have reference answers, compare the output to them: Method How it works Strength Weakness Exact match Output equals the reference (or contains it) Simple, strict Fails on valid paraphrases Lexical similarity Overlap of tokens or n-grams: BLEU, ROUGE, edit distance Cheap, established in translation and summarisation Rewards wording, not meaning; needs many references Semantic similarity Cosine similarity of embeddings; BERTScore Captures paraphrases Depends on the embedding model; a fluent wrong answer can still look similar TipReferences are expensive Reference answers take time to write and age as products change. Use them for stable, closed tasks; use rubrics and judges for open-ended ones. Embeddings turn text into vectors where semantically similar text sits close together — the same building block used for retrieval. Their quality is measured on benchmarks such as MTEB, but test on your domain. AI as a judge# An AI judge is a model prompted (or fine-tuned) to evaluate outputs. It is fast, cheap compared with humans, works without reference data and can explain its verdict, so it has become the default for open-ended evaluation. Three ways to use a judge# Mode Prompt shape Use Score a single output &ldquo;Rate this answer&rsquo;s helpfulness from 1 to 5&rdquo; Absolute quality monitoring Compare to a reference &ldquo;Is this answer consistent with the reference?&rdquo; Correctness when references exist Compare two outputs &ldquo;Which response better answers the question?&rdquo; Model comparisons, preference data A good judge prompt contains: the task, the criteria (with definitions), a scoring system (binary or a short scale, which judges handle better than 1–100), and examples of each score with explanations. Ask for the reasoning before the score. Limits and biases# Problem What it looks like Mitigation Inconsistency The same input scored differently across runs Low temperature, multiple samples, examples in the prompt Criteria ambiguity Different judge tools define &ldquo;faithfulness&rdquo; differently, so scores are not comparable Fix your own definitions and rubric; version the judge prompt and model Cost and latency A judge call per output doubles the bill Sample in production; use small specialised judges; judge offline Self-bias A model favours outputs from itself or its family Use a different model family as the judge Position bias Prefers the first (or second) option in pairwise comparison Evaluate both orders; average Verbosity bias Prefers longer answers Instruct against it; control for length Shared blind spots The judge misses the same errors the model makes Validate the judge against human labels WarningA judge is a model — evaluate it Treat the judge like any other component: measure its agreement with human ratings on a labelled sample, and re-check whenever you change the judge model or prompt. Never compare scores produced by

b: Simple definition# The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data. Claude Code is an MCP client: each MCP server you add — a local process or a remote URL — contributes tools (and optionally resources and prompts) that Claude can call, such as &ldquo;query the database&rdquo;, &ldquo;read the Jira ticket&rdquo; or &ldquo;fetch the Sentry error&rdquo;. For the protocol itself, see Model Context Protocol. Version noteSource and date Condensed from Anthropic&rsquo;s Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP and Control MCP server access, read on 7 November 2026. Claude Code and MCP: where servers come from and how they connect · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. &copy; 2026 Samir Kumar Sahoo, all rights reserved. Open full screen ↗ Key conceptPrefer a CLI when one exists If a system has a CLI Claude can use — gh, kubectl, aws — Claude will use it with no MCP server and no context cost. Add MCP for systems without a CLI, or when you need OAuth, structured tools or resources. Adding servers# Transport Use for Command HTTP (recommended remote) Cloud services claude mcp add --transport http notion https://mcp.notion.com/mcp HTTP with a token Private APIs … --header &quot;Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN&quot; stdio Local processes, scripts, direct system access claude mcp add --transport stdio --env KEY=v db -- npx -y @bytebase/dbhub --dsn &quot;$DSN&quot; SSE (deprecated) Services with only an SSE endpoint --transport sse (HTTP falls back to SSE automatically) WebSocket Servers that push events claude mcp add-json events '{&quot;type&quot;:&quot;ws&quot;,&quot;url&quot;:&quot;wss://…&quot;}' For stdio, -- separates Claude&rsquo;s options from the server command; everything after it is passed untouched. A JSON entry with a url but no type is an error (no type means stdio). Stdio servers get CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR in their environment. Managing servers# claude mcp list # all servers with health: ✔ Connected, ! Needs authentication, ✘ Failed claude mcp get notion # details for one claude mcp remove notion # also deletes stored OAuth tokens (doesn&#39;t revoke them) claude mcp add-json name &#39;&lt;json&gt;&#39; # add from a JSON config claude mcp add-from-claude-desktop # import servers from Claude Desktop claude mcp login sentry # run OAuth without the /mcp panel (--no-browser over SSH) claude mcp reset-project-choices # forget .mcp.json approvals Inside a session: /mcp shows status, authenticates, and enables or disables servers (/mcp disable &lt;server&gt; keeps it configured but off). Scopes# Scope Loads in Shared Stored in local (default) This project, only you No ~/.claude.json under the project path project This project Yes, via Git .mcp.json at the repo root user All your projects No ~/.claude.json When the same server appears in several places, Claude Code connects once, using the whole entry from the highest source: local → project → user → plugin → claude.ai connectors. An organisation&rsquo;s managedMcpServers outranks all of them. Plugins and connectors are matched by endpoint, so a duplicate URL counts as the same server. WarningProject servers and approval Interactive sessions ask each developer to approve servers in .mcp.json. claude -p, SDK and some cloud sessions load them without asking. Before scripting over a repository you didn&rsquo;t write, review .mcp.json, use --strict-mcp-config with --mcp-config, or block servers with disabledMcpjsonServers. .mcp.json with environment variables# { &#34;mcpServers&#34;: { &#34;api&#34;: { &#34;type&#34;: &#34;http&#34;, &#34;url&#34;: &#34;${API_BASE_URL:-https://api.example.com}/mcp&#34;, &#34;headers&#34;: { &#34;Authorization&#34;: &#34;Bearer ${API_KEY}&#34; } }, &#34;db&#34;: { &#34;type&#34;: &#34;stdio&#34;, &#34;command&#34;: &#34;npx&#34;, &#34;args&#34;: [&#34;-y&#34;, &#34;@bytebase/dbhub&#34;, &#34;--dsn&#34;, &#34;${DATABASE_URL}&#34;], &#34;env&#34;: { &#34;READ_ONLY&#34;: &#34;true&#34; } } } } ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} expand in command, args, env, url and headers. Unset variables without defaults stay literal and produce a warning in claude mcp list. Credential variables read as empty in remote url and headers — ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, cloud provider tokens, NPM_TOKEN and similar — so a committed .mcp.json or plugin can&rsquo;t exfiltrate them. Copy a credential into a variable with your own name if a server truly needs it. streamable-http is accepted as an alias for http. Authentication# Remote servers that answer 401/403 are flagged in /mcp; select Authenticate to run OAuth 2.0 in the browser. Tokens refresh automatically; if the refresh token is rejected, Claude Code tells you to re-authenticate. Options for awkward setups: a fixed callback port, pre-configured OAuth client credentials (--client-id, --client-secret), restricted scopes, metadata-discovery overrides, and headersHelper for dynamic headers from your own command. A server whose Authorization header you configured isn&rsquo;t flagged for OAuth on 401 — fix the credential you set. What Claude sees: tool search# Tool search is on by default: only tool names and server instructions load at start; full schemas load when Claude searches for a tool. Adding servers therefore costs little context — but names still sit there every turn, so disable servers you don&rsquo;t use. ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH Behaviour unset / true Defer all MCP tools (loaded up front on older models and some providers) auto Load up front while definitions total under 10% of the window; defer beyond that auto:N Same with an N% threshold Server authors can exempt a server from deferral (always-loaded tools) or mark tools for deferral. Output limits# Limit Default Warning threshold 10,000 tokens per tool result Maximum 25,000 tokens (MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS); larger results are saved to a file Claude can read Text without a declared limit Saved to file above 50,000 characters HTTP/SSE response, WebSocket message Fails above 16

b: Simple definition# Evaluating an AI system means checking whether the whole application — prompts, retrieval, model, tools and guardrails — does its job well enough, safely enough and cheaply enough. It turns the methods in evaluation methodology into a repeatable pipeline that runs before every change and continuously in production. Key conceptEvaluation-driven development Define how you will evaluate the application before you build it, the same way test-driven development writes tests first. The use cases that succeed in production are mostly the ones with clear, measurable outcomes — so make yours measurable from day one. Evaluation criteria# Group criteria into four buckets. 1. Domain-specific capability# Can the model do the work at all — write code in your language, understand your legal domain, reason over your tables? Measure with functional checks (code runs, SQL returns the right rows) or multiple-choice and closed-form questions from your domain. 2. Generation capability# The quality of open-ended text: Criterion Question Fluency and coherence Is it readable and logically organised? (Rarely a problem with modern models) Factual consistency Is it supported by the facts? Relevance Does it answer the question asked? Safety Is it free of harmful content? Factual consistency# Two settings: Local — consistent with the context given (a document, retrieved passages). Central to RAG and summarisation. Global — consistent with facts about the world. Harder: you need a source of truth. Ways to check it: Technique How AI judge Ask a model whether each claim is supported by the context Self-verification Sample several answers; if they disagree, the answer is probably made up Knowledge-augmented verification Split the answer into atomic claims, search for evidence for each, judge each claim (as in SAFE) Entailment classifiers A small model predicts whether the context entails, contradicts or is neutral to each claim Safety# Check for harmful or inappropriate content (violence, self-harm, illegal advice), toxicity and bias, privacy leaks, and policy violations specific to your organisation. Use moderation models and red-team prompt sets; see AI security. 3. Instruction-following capability# Does the model follow the format, length, language and constraints you asked for? This matters most for structured outputs that downstream code parses. Instruction type Example check Format Valid JSON matching the schema; no preamble Content Includes / excludes given keywords; stays on topic Length Under n words, exactly three bullet points Language and style Responds in French; formal tone Roleplay Stays in character and persona; consistent style Build a small set of verifiable instructions (like the IFEval benchmark) for your product&rsquo;s actual constraints, and test them on every model or prompt change. 4. Cost and latency# A perfect answer that takes 40 seconds or costs €2 may be useless. Track cost per request, TTFT, TPOT and total latency alongside quality, and decide what you would trade: a slightly worse but much cheaper model is often the right choice. See inference and serving. TipMake a criteria table For each criterion, write the metric, the benchmark or dataset, the hard requirement and the ideal target. It becomes the contract for model selection and the agenda for review meetings. Criterion Metric Dataset Hard requirement Ideal Factual consistency Judge-scored grounding 300 internal Q&amp;A ≥ 0.90 ≥ 0.97 Safety Policy-violation rate Red-team set 0 critical 0 Format Valid JSON rate 500 extraction samples ≥ 99% 100% Latency p95 TTFT Load test &lt; 1.5 s &lt; 0.5 s Cost € per 1k requests Production mix &lt; €5 &lt; €2 Public benchmarks: useful, not sufficient# Public benchmarks and leaderboards narrow the candidate list. Three problems limit them: Selection and aggregation. Leaderboards average benchmarks that may be irrelevant to you, and the weights are arbitrary. Saturation. Top models cluster near the ceiling, so differences are noise. Data contamination. Benchmark questions leak into training data — through web crawls, deliberate inclusion or synthetic data — inflating scores. Detecting contamination: n-gram overlap between benchmark and training data (if you have it), and unusually low perplexity on benchmark items. Handling it: report results on a held-out, private set; prefer benchmarks with fresh or private questions. Build a custom leaderboard: pick the public benchmarks that match your criteria, weight them by importance, and add your own private evaluation set. See model selection. Designing the evaluation pipeline# An evaluation pipeline, from components to iteration flowchart TD C[&#34;1 · Evaluate every component&lt;br/&gt;retrieval, prompt steps, tools, final answer&#34;] --&gt; G[&#34;2 · Write guidelines and rubrics&lt;br/&gt;with scored examples&#34;] G --&gt; B[&#34;3 · Tie metrics to business metrics&#34;] B --&gt; M[&#34;4 · Select methods per criterion&lt;br/&gt;functional, judge, human&#34;] M --&gt; D[&#34;5 · Annotate evaluation data&lt;br/&gt;by slice, enough samples&#34;] D --&gt; E[&#34;6 · Evaluate the evaluator&lt;br/&gt;signal, reliability, cost&#34;] E --&gt; I[&#34;7 · Iterate&lt;br/&gt;version everything&#34;] I --&gt; C Step 1 — Evaluate every component# A system with several steps can fail at each one. Evaluate per step (was the right document retrieved? was the right tool chosen?) and end to end (was the final answer right?). Evaluate per turn and per task: a multi-turn conversation can have good turns and still fail the task. Step 2 — Create guidelines and scoring rubrics# Write down what good means, with examples of each score. A rubric such as &ldquo;1 = wrong or ungrounded, 2 = partly correct, 3 = correct and grounded, with citations&rdquo; makes humans and judges consistent. Include what a correct but unhelpful answer looks like — it is common. Step 3 — Tie evaluation metrics to business metrics# Map model quality to outcomes: &ldquo;at 80%

b: Simple definition# An agent harness is everything around the model that turns it into a working agent: the loop, tools, permissions, context management, memory files, sub-agents, skills, checkpoints and verification. Two agents using the same model can perform very differently because of their harnesses — which is why &ldquo;harness engineering&rdquo; became a discipline of its own in 2025–2026. Why harnesses matter for long tasks# A single context window cannot hold a multi-hour task: history grows, old tool results crowd out instructions, and quality decays (&ldquo;context rot&rdquo;). Long-running agents need a harness that keeps the window small, relevant and recoverable. Harness = model &#43; everything that makes it reliable flowchart LR M((&#34;Model&#34;)) --- H[&#34;Harness&#34;] H --- L[&#34;Agent loop&lt;br/&gt;+ step budgets&#34;] H --- T[&#34;Tools&lt;br/&gt;files, shell, browser, MCP&#34;] H --- P[&#34;Permissions &amp; hooks&#34;] H --- C[&#34;Context management&lt;br/&gt;compaction, clearing&#34;] H --- S[&#34;Skills&lt;br/&gt;loaded on demand&#34;] H --- SA[&#34;Sub-agents&lt;br/&gt;isolated contexts&#34;] H --- F[&#34;File-based memory&lt;br/&gt;progress notes, plans&#34;] H --- V[&#34;Verification&lt;br/&gt;tests, linters, evals&#34;] Inside one working session# Inside an agent harness: one working session · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. &copy; 2026 Samir Kumar Sahoo, all rights reserved. Open full screen ↗ Start session with a task and budget. Build context: instructions (system prompt, AGENTS.md), the progress notes from previous sessions, and only the skills relevant to the step. Compact when the window gets long: summarise older turns, clear stale tool output. The model decides the next step and proposes a tool call. The permission check allows, asks a human, or denies. Run the tool in a sandbox (shell, browser, MCP server). Verify the result with real signals — tests, linters, schema checks, evaluations. Save progress — commit work, update the progress file, checkpoint state — so a fresh session can resume. Context engineering techniques# Technique What it does Compaction Summarise the conversation when nearing the limit; continue with the summary plus recent turns Tool-result clearing Drop or shorten bulky outputs once they have been used Just-in-time retrieval Give the agent search/read tools rather than preloading files Structured notes The agent writes plans, decisions and progress to files it can re-read later Sub-agents Delegate exploration to a sub-agent with a fresh window; receive a short summary back Progressive disclosure Show only short descriptions of skills/tools; load details when needed Stable prefix Keep system prompt and tool definitions stable for prompt caching Patterns for long-running work# Published guidance on long-running agents converges on a few patterns: Initializer + worker sessions. A first session sets up the environment: task list, progress file, test harness. Every later session reads the state from disk, picks one task, works, verifies, commits and updates the notes. State lives in files, not in the window. A fresh session must be able to resume from the repository and progress notes alone. Small, verifiable increments. One feature or fix per step, each with a test that proves it. Explicit definition of done. Acceptance tests written before work begins; the agent may not mark a task complete until they pass. Budgets and escalation. Step, token and time limits; escalate to a human when stuck. Durable progress# Long-running agent task with durable checkpoints · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. &copy; 2026 Samir Kumar Sahoo, all rights reserved. Open full screen ↗ Checkpoints after every step make restarts cheap: a crashed pod, a deployment or a multi-day approval wait resumes from the last saved state instead of repeating work or side effects. Combine with idempotent tools (see memory and state). Agent Skills in practice# Skills package how your organisation does things so agents can do it the same way: --- name: credit-memo description: Write a credit memo for an SME loan application in the bank&#39;s standard format. Use when asked to prepare, draft or review a credit memo. --- # Credit memo 1. Collect: applicant, facility requested, financials (3 years), collateral. 2. Run `scripts/ratios.py` on the financials; never compute ratios by hand. 3. Fill `template.md` section by section. Keep the risk summary under 150 words. 4. Flag any covenant breach or ratio outside policy limits in **bold**. 5. Finish with the checklist in `checklist.md`. Progressive disclosure: only name and description sit in context until the skill is needed. Deterministic helpers: scripts do calculations and transformations reliably. Governance: store skills in Git, review them like code, sign and version them, and install only trusted skills — a malicious skill is a supply-chain attack. Coding agents in the enterprise# Coding agents (CLI and IDE agents, cloud agents that open pull requests) are the most mature agentic use case. Architecture guidance: Concern Practice Sandbox Containerised workspace; no production credentials; network egress allow-list Permissions Read freely; ask before shell commands outside an allow-list; never push to protected branches Context AGENTS.md per repo; skills for internal frameworks; MCP servers for issue trackers and docs Verification CI must pass; agent-written code reviewed by humans; security scanning Audit Agent identity on commits; traces of sessions Metrics Lead time, change failure rate, review load — not lines of code Common mistakes# Common mistakeOne giant session Letting one session run until the window overflows. Split work into sessions that resume from files. Common mistakeTrusting &ldquo;done&rdquo; without verification Agents can declare success prematurely. Require passing tests or checks before a task is marked complete. Common

b: Simple definition# A plugin is a directory that bundles Claude Code extensions — skills, sub-agents, hooks, MCP servers, language servers, output styles and more — so they install, update and enable as one unit. A marketplace is a catalogue (usually a Git repository with a marketplace.json) that lists plugins and where to fetch them. Plugins are how a team or organisation shares one Claude Code setup across many repositories and machines. Version noteSource and date Condensed from Anthropic&rsquo;s Plugins overview, Plugin components, Manifest reference, Plugin marketplaces and Plugin CLI reference, read on 7 November 2026. Do you need a plugin?# You want… Use One skill, agent, hook or server for yourself or one repo The standalone file (.claude/skills/, .claude/agents/, settings, .mcp.json) The same setup in many repos, or for a whole team A plugin in a marketplace Someone else&rsquo;s tooling with one command and updates Install their plugin Policy that users can&rsquo;t remove Managed settings (which can force-install plugins) Directory layout# my-plugin/ ├── .claude-plugin/ │ └── plugin.json # manifest (only &#34;name&#34; is required; optional altogether) ├── skills/ │ └── review/SKILL.md # → /my-plugin:review ├── commands/about.md # older single-file commands ├── agents/security-reviewer.md ├── hooks/hooks.json # same format as settings &#34;hooks&#34; ├── .mcp.json # MCP servers started while enabled ├── .lsp.json # language servers (code intelligence) ├── monitors/monitors.json # background commands whose output reaches Claude ├── output-styles/terse.md ├── themes/dracula.json ├── workflows/ # dynamic workflow scripts ├── scripts/format.sh # called by hooks via ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} └── evals/ # cases for claude plugin eval Component Appears as Skill / command /my-plugin:name Agent my-plugin:security-reviewer Hook Runs at its event while enabled MCP server mcp__plugin_my-plugin_&lt;server&gt;__&lt;tool&gt; LSP server Go-to-definition and diagnostics for its language Output style /output-style my-plugin:terse Theme In /theme Monitor Notifications from a background command Hooks module (JavaScript) A mod — can also draw panes and add commands Every component is namespaced under the plugin name, so two plugins can both have a review skill. plugin.json# { &#34;name&#34;: &#34;acme-dev&#34;, &#34;displayName&#34;: &#34;Acme developer toolkit&#34;, &#34;version&#34;: &#34;1.4.0&#34;, &#34;description&#34;: &#34;Review, release and database tools for Acme services&#34;, &#34;author&#34;: { &#34;name&#34;: &#34;Platform Team&#34;, &#34;email&#34;: &#34;platform@acme.example&#34; }, &#34;license&#34;: &#34;MIT&#34;, &#34;keywords&#34;: [&#34;review&#34;, &#34;release&#34;], &#34;dependencies&#34;: [&#34;acme-security&#34;], &#34;userConfig&#34;: { &#34;webhook_url&#34;: { &#34;type&#34;: &#34;string&#34;, &#34;title&#34;: &#34;Slack webhook&#34;, &#34;description&#34;: &#34;Team channel webhook&#34;, &#34;sensitive&#34;: true } } } Field Notes name Required; kebab-case; the namespace for every component version Pins users to that version until you change it description, displayName, author, homepage, repository, license, keywords Metadata (homepage must be a valid URL) defaultEnabled Start enabled unless the user says otherwise (default true) dependencies Other plugins that must be enabled userConfig Values Claude Code prompts for at enable time (available to hooks and servers as CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_*) settings Settings applied while enabled — only agent and subagentStatusLine take effect skills, commands, agents, hooks, mcpServers, lspServers, outputStyles, workflows Custom paths or inline config; most replace the default folder scan (skills adds to it; hooks and mcpServers load alongside the defaults) experimental.themes, .monitors, .evals Shapes may change Use ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} for paths inside the plugin and ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA} for persistent data. Installing and managing# In a session: /plugin opens Discover, Installed and Marketplaces tabs. /reload-plugins applies changes without restarting. /plugin marketplace add acme/claude-plugins # GitHub repo, git URL, local path or URL /plugin install acme-dev@acme-tools From the shell: claude plugin install acme-dev@acme-tools --scope project claude plugin enable|disable|uninstall acme-dev claude plugin update acme-dev@acme-tools claude plugin list · claude plugin details acme-dev claude plugin configure acme-dev@acme-tools # set userConfig values claude plugin marketplace list|add|remove claude plugin prune --dry-run # remove unused installs Install scope Enabled for Recorded in user You, every project ~/.claude/settings.json project Everyone in the repo (each still installs locally) .claude/settings.json local You, this repo .claude/settings.local.json Anthropic&rsquo;s official marketplace is added automatically on first interactive start (unless policy blocks it). Cloud sessions don&rsquo;t load plugins from your local settings. Creating a marketplace# { &#34;name&#34;: &#34;acme-tools&#34;, &#34;description&#34;: &#34;Acme&#39;s internal Claude Code plugins&#34;, &#34;owner&#34;: { &#34;name&#34;: &#34;Platform Team&#34; }, &#34;plugins&#34;: [ { &#34;name&#34;: &#34;acme-dev&#34;, &#34;source&#34;: &#34;./plugins/acme-dev&#34;, &#34;description&#34;: &#34;Review and release tools&#34; }, { &#34;name&#34;: &#34;acme-security&#34;, &#34;source&#34;: { &#34;source&#34;: &#34;github&#34;, &#34;repo&#34;: &#34;acme/security-plugin&#34; } } ] } Save as .claude-plugin/marketplace.json at the repository root. Then make it automatic for a repo: { &#34;extraKnownMarketplaces&#34;: { &#34;acme-tools&#34;: { &#34;source&#34;: { &#34;source&#34;: &#34;github&#34;, &#34;repo&#34;: &#34;acme/claude-plugins&#34; } } }, &#34;enabledPlugins&#34;: { &#34;acme-dev@acme-tools&#34;: true } } Committed in .claude/settings.json, this offers the marketplace and plugin to each developer once they trust the folder. Developing a plugin# claude plugin init
