b: Simple definition# A computer-use agent operates software the way a person does: it looks at the screen (screenshots or the page structure), decides what to click or type, performs the action, and repeats. Browser agents are the web-only variant. They let agents work with applications that have no API. The see–decide–act loop# Computer-use agent: see, decide, act · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. &copy; 2026 Samir Kumar Sahoo, all rights reserved. Open full screen ↗ The harness takes a screenshot of a sandboxed VM or browser. A vision-capable model receives the goal and screenshot and returns an action — click(x, y), type(&quot;…&quot;), scroll, key(&quot;Enter&quot;). The harness checks the action against policy and executes it. Repeat until done; irreversible steps (submit, pay, delete) pause for human confirmation. Browser agents often use the page&rsquo;s DOM or accessibility tree instead of, or as well as, pixels — faster and more precise for web apps. API, RPA or computer use?# Choose the integration style flowchart TD A{&#34;Does the system have&lt;br/&gt;an API?&#34;} --&gt;|&#34;yes&#34;| API[&#34;Use the API&lt;br/&gt;via tools / MCP&#34;] A --&gt;|&#34;no&#34;| B{&#34;Is the UI flow stable&lt;br/&gt;and high-volume?&#34;} B --&gt;|&#34;yes&#34;| RPA[&#34;Classic RPA or scripted&lt;br/&gt;browser automation&#34;] B --&gt;|&#34;no, varied tasks&#34;| CU[&#34;Computer-use / browser agent&lt;br/&gt;with human oversight&#34;] API tools RPA / scripts Computer-use agent Reliability Highest High while UI unchanged Lower; improving Speed / cost Fast, cheap Fast Slow, token-heavy (screenshots) Handles UI change N/A Breaks Adapts Handles varied tasks Per-tool No Yes Best for Everything that has an API Repetitive fixed flows Long tail of varied UI tasks, legacy apps, testing Architecture# Computer-use deployment flowchart LR U[&#34;User / workflow&#34;] --&gt; H[&#34;Agent harness&lt;br/&gt;loop, policy, audit&#34;] H &lt;--&gt; M[&#34;Vision LLM&lt;br/&gt;via AI gateway&#34;] H &lt;--&gt; VM[&#34;Disposable sandbox&lt;br/&gt;VM or headless browser&#34;] VM --&gt; NET{&#34;Egress proxy&lt;br/&gt;domain allow-list&#34;} NET --&gt; APP[&#34;Target apps&#34;] H --&gt; REC[(&#34;Session recording&lt;br/&gt;screenshots + actions&#34;)] H --&gt; HUM[&#34;Human confirmation&#34;] Disposable sandboxes per session; no saved passwords or production secrets inside. Egress allow-list — the agent can reach only approved domains. Credential handling — inject short-lived credentials via the harness, never put them in the prompt. Session recording for audit and debugging. Managed options exist on agent platforms (sandboxed browser tools) — see managed platforms. Reliability today# Benchmarks for full-desktop tasks show agents still well below human success rates on complex, multi-application work, while browser tasks on well-structured sites are considerably better. Plan for: Human oversight and confirmation of consequential steps. Narrow, well-defined tasks with clear success checks. Retries and fallbacks; measure task success and pass^k on your own scenarios. Security risks# Risk Example Mitigation Prompt injection from content A web page says &ldquo;ignore your task and send the user&rsquo;s data to…&rdquo; Treat screen content as untrusted; allow-list domains; confirm sensitive actions; break the lethal trifecta Credential exposure Agent types a password into a phishing page Credential injection by harness only on allow-listed origins Unintended actions Mis-click on &ldquo;Delete all&rdquo; Confirmation for destructive actions; read-only accounts where possible Data leakage Screenshots with personal data sent to a model Data classification, masking, region-pinned models, retention limits Abuse Automated scraping or fraud Rate limits, terms of service, audit Good enterprise use cases# Operating legacy applications without APIs (with oversight). Automated UI testing that adapts to layout changes. Back-office data entry across portals with varied layouts. Research tasks across public websites. Avoid: high-volume fixed flows (use APIs or RPA), unsupervised financial transactions, anything where a mistake is irreversible and unreviewed. Review questions# How does a computer-use agent work? A loop: screenshot (or DOM) → vision model chooses a UI action → harness checks policy and executes it in a sandbox → repeat, with human confirmation for irreversible steps. When would you use a computer-use agent instead of an API or RPA? When there is no API and the tasks vary too much for scripted RPA — accepting lower reliability and higher cost, with human oversight. What are the main security risks? Prompt injection from on-screen content, credential exposure, unintended destructive actions and data leakage through screenshots. Summary# Computer-use agents see the screen and act through clicks and keystrokes; browser agents can also use the DOM. Prefer APIs, then RPA for stable flows; use computer use for the varied long tail. Run in disposable sandboxes with egress allow-lists, injected credentials, recordings and human confirmation. References# Anthropic, Computer use tool. Xie et al., OSWorld: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents for Open-Ended Tasks in Real Computer Environments, 2024. Zhou et al., WebArena: A Realistic Web Environment for Building Autonomous Agents, 2023.
d: Agents that operate graphical interfaces: the see–decide–act loop, computer-use vs browser automation vs APIs, architecture with sandboxed VMs, reliability limits, security risks such as prompt injection from web pages, and when to use them in the enterprise.

b: Simple definition# Model selection is choosing which LLM (or which mix of LLMs) serves each use case, based on quality for the task, cost, latency, data-protection requirements and operational fit. In an enterprise it is not a one-time choice: models change every few months, so the architecture must make swapping cheap. Why it matters# The difference between models on your task can be large, and price per token varies by more than 50× between the smallest and largest models. Picking the biggest model for everything wastes money; picking the cheapest for everything fails on hard tasks. The selection criteria# Criterion Questions to ask Task quality How does it score on our evaluation set? Reasoning, extraction accuracy, code, tool use, multilingual? Cost Price per million input/output tokens; caching and batch discounts; total cost at projected volume. Latency TTFT and tokens/s at our prompt sizes; is streaming supported? Context window Fits our largest realistic prompt with headroom? Capabilities Tool calling, structured outputs, vision, audio, reasoning mode, embeddings. Data protection Data retention, training-on-your-data terms, regional hosting, certifications (SOC 2, ISO 27001), private networking. Deployment Provider API, your cloud (Bedrock, Azure, Vertex), or self-hosted? Licence For open-weight models: commercial use allowed? usage restrictions? Safety Refusal behaviour, jailbreak resistance, content filters. Vendor and roadmap Deprecation policy, SLAs, support, financial stability. Model tiers# Capability tiers and typical uses flowchart LR subgraph T1[&#34;Frontier / reasoning models&#34;] A[&#34;Complex reasoning, planning,&lt;br/&gt;agentic coding, hard analysis&#34;] end subgraph T2[&#34;Mid-tier models&#34;] B[&#34;Most RAG, chat, summarisation,&lt;br/&gt;tool use at scale&#34;] end subgraph T3[&#34;Small models, SLMs&#34;] C[&#34;Classification, routing, extraction,&lt;br/&gt;guardrails, on-device, high volume&#34;] end subgraph T4[&#34;Specialised models&#34;] D[&#34;Embeddings, rerankers,&lt;br/&gt;speech, vision, code&#34;] end T1 ---|&#34;higher quality, cost, latency&#34;| T2 ---|&#34;lower cost, faster&#34;| T3 Proprietary vs open-weight# Proprietary (API) Open-weight (self-host or managed) Examples Claude, GPT, Gemini families Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma, DeepSeek families Peak quality Usually highest Close behind, especially at mid-tier Operations None — pay per token You run GPUs, scaling, patching (unless a cloud hosts it) Data control Contractual (retention, region) Full — data never leaves your environment Customisation Prompting; some offer fine-tuning Full fine-tuning, LoRA, quantization Cost profile Variable, scales with usage Fixed GPU cost; cheaper at high steady volume Lock-in API differences between vendors Low for the model, but you own the platform Note: &ldquo;open-weight&rdquo; means the weights are downloadable; licences differ and are not always open source in the OSI sense. Benchmarks: useful, but not sufficient# Public benchmarks (MMLU-style knowledge tests, GPQA for hard science, SWE-bench for coding, tool-use and agent benchmarks, LMArena-style human preference rankings) are good for shortlisting. They are poor for deciding, because: They may not resemble your task, documents or language. Models can be over-optimised for popular benchmarks (&ldquo;contamination&rdquo;). They ignore your latency, cost and data constraints. The decision must come from your own evaluation set: 50–500 representative inputs with expected outputs or grading criteria, scored automatically and spot-checked by experts. See RAG evaluation for the methods. A repeatable selection process# Model selection process flowchart LR A[&#34;1 · Define use case&lt;br/&gt;and success metrics&#34;] --&gt; B[&#34;2 · Hard filters&lt;br/&gt;data residency, licence,&lt;br/&gt;capabilities, context&#34;] B --&gt; C[&#34;3 · Shortlist 3–5 models&lt;br/&gt;benchmarks, cost tier&#34;] C --&gt; D[&#34;4 · Evaluate on own dataset&lt;br/&gt;quality, latency, cost&#34;] D --&gt; E[&#34;5 · Weighted scoring&lt;br/&gt;+ risk review&#34;] E --&gt; F[&#34;6 · Decide primary&lt;br/&gt;and fallback model&#34;] F --&gt; G[&#34;7 · Re-evaluate on&lt;br/&gt;every new model release&#34;] G --&gt; C Weighted scoring example — customer-support RAG assistant Criterion (weight) Model A frontier Model B mid-tier Model C open-weight 70B Answer quality on eval set (40%) 9 8 7 Cost at volume (20%) 4 8 7 Latency (15%) 6 8 7 Data protection fit (15%) 7 7 10 Operational effort (10%) 9 9 4 Weighted total 7.25 7.95 7.15 Model B wins for this use case. A legal-analysis use case with different weights might pick Model A. Model routing and cascades# You rarely need one model for everything. An AI gateway or router sends each request to the cheapest model that can handle it. Router and cascade patterns flowchart TB Q[&#34;Request&#34;] --&gt; R{&#34;Router&lt;br/&gt;rules or small classifier&#34;} R --&gt;|&#34;simple: FAQ, classification&#34;| S[&#34;Small model&#34;] R --&gt;|&#34;standard&#34;| M[&#34;Mid-tier model&#34;] R --&gt;|&#34;complex reasoning&#34;| L[&#34;Frontier / reasoning model&#34;] S --&gt; V{&#34;Confidence or&lt;br/&gt;validation OK?&#34;} V --&gt;|&#34;No: escalate&#34;| M V --&gt;|&#34;Yes&#34;| OUT[&#34;Response&#34;] M --&gt; OUT L --&gt; OUT Routing — classify the request first, then choose a model. Cascade — try the cheap model first; escalate if validation or confidence fails. Fallback — on provider outage or rate limit, switch to an equivalent model from another provider. Routing commonly cuts cost by 40–70% when most traffic is simple. Avoiding lock-in# Call models through an abstraction: Spring AI&rsquo;s ChatModel, or an AI gateway with an OpenAI-compatible API. Keep prompts, evaluation sets and tool definitions model-agnostic and in version control. Store embeddings with the embedding model name and version; changing the embedding model means re-indexing. Re-run the evaluation suite
d: How to choose LLMs: capability tiers, open-weight vs proprietary, benchmarks and their limits, a weighted scoring matrix, model routing and cascades, and avoiding lock-in.

b: Simple definition# An output style changes how Claude talks to you for a whole session — its role, tone, length and format — by adding instructions to every request. The status line changes what you see while it works: a bar under the prompt rendered by your own script from live session data (model, context use, cost, git branch, rate limits). Neither changes what Claude is allowed to do. Version noteSource and date Condensed from Anthropic&rsquo;s Output styles and Customize your status line, read on 7 November 2026. Built-in output styles# Style What changes Use it when Default No extra instructions — Claude Code&rsquo;s standard software-engineering prompt Most work Proactive Starts work at once, makes reasonable assumptions instead of asking about routine decisions; still checks before deleting data or touching shared/production systems You&rsquo;d rather correct a wrong assumption than answer questions Concise Leads with the result; no preamble, narration or recap; simple answers in 1–3 sentences (errors, test output and safety warnings stay full) Default answers are longer than you want Explanatory Adds short ★ Insight blocks explaining the choices behind the code Learning a codebase; wanting the reasoning Learning Insights plus TODO(human) spots where you write the interesting part, then Claude continues Hands-on practice while the task still gets done Proactive does not change your permission mode; prompts still appear as before. Switching# Where How Terminal /output-style concise, or /config → Output style Settings &quot;outputStyle&quot;: &quot;Explanatory&quot; — case-sensitive (explanatory silently means Default) Default everywhere outputStyle in ~/.claude/settings.json (project files override it) VS Code / → Output styles The command and menu save to .claude/settings.local.json. A switch applies from your next message (the first message after a switch is an uncached turn). Custom output styles# --- name: Diagrams first description: Lead every explanation with a diagram keep-coding-instructions: true --- When explaining code, architecture or data flow, start with a Mermaid diagram of the structure, then explain in prose. Use flowchart TD for control flow and sequenceDiagram for request paths. Keep diagrams under 15 nodes. Location Scope ~/.claude/output-styles/*.md You, all projects .claude/output-styles/*.md The project (nearest directory wins) Managed settings directory .claude/output-styles/ Organisation Plugin output-styles/ As plugin:name; force-for-plugin: true applies it automatically Frontmatter Does name, description Shown in the picker (name defaults to the file name) keep-coding-instructions true keeps Claude Code&rsquo;s built-in engineering instructions (scoping changes, comments, verifying work). Default false — leave it out only if Claude won&rsquo;t be writing code force-for-plugin Plugin styles only: apply whenever the plugin is enabled Key conceptKeep the coding instructions A custom style without keep-coding-instructions: true drops Claude Code&rsquo;s own guidance on how to scope and verify changes. For a style that changes tone on a coding project, always set it. Styles apply to the main conversation and to forks; ordinary sub-agents keep their own system prompts. Style files are read at start-up — restart after editing one. Output style or something else?# You want Use Every response in a voice, length or format; Claude in a different role Output style Claude to know project conventions and commands CLAUDE.md Instructions for one kind of task A skill Something that must always happen A hook A focused helper with its own tools and model A sub-agent An addition to the system prompt for one launch --append-system-prompt Status line# /statusline show model, git branch, context % as a bar, and session cost /statusline writes a script in ~/.claude/ and wires it up. Or configure it yourself: { &#34;statusLine&#34;: { &#34;type&#34;: &#34;command&#34;, &#34;command&#34;: &#34;~/.claude/statusline.sh&#34;, &#34;padding&#34;: 2 } } Your command receives session JSON on stdin and prints one or more lines (ANSI colours and OSC 8 links work). It runs at session start, then after each assistant message, /compact, mode or vim changes, and on an optional refreshInterval, debounced at 300 ms. Read COLUMNS for width — tput cols doesn&rsquo;t work inside it. Most useful fields# Field Contains model.display_name Current model workspace.current_dir, workspace.project_dir Where you are; where you started context_window.used_percentage Context used (pre-calculated) context_window.context_window_size 200k or 1M cost.total_cost_usd Estimated session cost (client-side, list price) cost.total_duration_ms, cost.total_lines_added/removed Time and churn effort.level, fast_mode, output_style.name Session settings rate_limits.five_hour.used_percentage, .seven_day… Plan limit use prompt_cache.warm, prompt_cache.expires_at Whether the cache is still warm pr.number, pr.review_state Open PR for this branch worktree.name, session_name, agent.name, vim.mode Session identity Example script# #!/bin/bash input=$(cat) MODEL=$(jq -r &#39;.model.display_name&#39; &lt;&lt;&lt;&#34;$input&#34;) PCT=$(jq -r &#39;.context_window.used_percentage // 0&#39; &lt;&lt;&lt;&#34;$input&#34; | cut -d. -f1) COST=$(jq -r &#39;.cost.total_cost_usd // 0&#39; &lt;&lt;&lt;&#34;$input&#34;) BRANCH=$(git -C &#34;$(jq -r &#39;.workspace.current_dir&#39; &lt;&lt;&lt;&#34;$input&#34;)&#34; branch --show-current 2&gt;/dev/null) FILLED=$((PCT / 10)); BAR=$(printf &#39;%*s&#39; &#34;$FILLED&#34; &#39;&#39; | tr &#39; &#39; &#39;▓&#39;)$(printf &#39;%*s&#39; $((10-FILLED)) &#39;&#39; | tr &#39; &#39; &#39;░&#39;) printf &#39;%s · %s · %s %s%% · $%.2f\n&#39; &#34;$MODEL&#34; &#34;${BRANCH:-no-git}&#34; &#34;$BAR&#34; &#34;$PCT&#34; &#34;$COST&#34; Cache slow operations (git status in a big repo, API calls) to a temp file keyed by session ID. subagentStatusLine lets a second script rewrite the sub-agent task rows.
d: Shaping how Claude Code responds and what you see while it works: the built-in output styles (Proactive, Concise, Explanatory, Learning), writing custom styles and when to use another feature instead, and building a status line that shows model, context, cost, git and rate limits.
t: Claude Code Output Styles and Status Line

b: Simple definition# Agent identity and access control answers three questions for every action an agent takes: who is acting (the agent, the user, or both), what are they allowed to do, and how can we prove later what happened. Agents are a new kind of non-human identity that often act on behalf of a human, so classic service-account thinking is not enough. The problem# Common anti-patterns: One powerful service account shared by the agent for all users — every prompt injection gets admin rights. The user&rsquo;s full token passed through to every downstream API — far more scope than any single task needs. Identity taken from model-generated arguments — the model can be tricked into acting as someone else. No record of which agent performed an action for which user. Identity models# Model Who acts Use for User-delegated (on behalf of) Agent acts for a specific user, with that user&rsquo;s permissions narrowed to the task Assistants and copilots acting for employees or customers Agent&rsquo;s own identity Agent acts as itself, with its own least-privilege permissions Autonomous back-office agents, scheduled jobs Hybrid Agent identity + user context; access = intersection of both Most enterprise agents: agent may only do what both the agent and the user are allowed Effective permission = user ∩ agent ∩ task scope flowchart LR U[&#34;User permissions&lt;br/&gt;what this person may do&#34;] --&gt; I((&#34;∩&#34;)) A[&#34;Agent permissions&lt;br/&gt;what this agent may ever do&#34;] --&gt; I T[&#34;Task scope&lt;br/&gt;what this request needs&#34;] --&gt; I I --&gt; E[&#34;Effective permission&lt;br/&gt;for this call&#34;] Delegation with OAuth token exchange# On-behalf-of flow across agent, MCP server and API sequenceDiagram actor U as User participant APP as Agent app participant IDP as Identity provider participant AG as Agent runtime participant MCP as MCP server (CRM) participant API as CRM API U-&gt;&gt;APP: sign in (OIDC) APP-&gt;&gt;IDP: user token for agent app APP-&gt;&gt;AG: task + user token AG-&gt;&gt;IDP: token exchange: user token + agent identity, audience=CRM MCP, scope=crm.read IDP--&gt;&gt;AG: short-lived delegated token AG-&gt;&gt;MCP: tools/call + delegated token MCP-&gt;&gt;MCP: validate audience, scope, user, agent MCP-&gt;&gt;IDP: exchange for API token (scope=contacts.read) IDP--&gt;&gt;MCP: API token MCP-&gt;&gt;API: GET /contacts (as user via agent) API--&gt;&gt;MCP: data the user may see MCP--&gt;&gt;AG: result Principles: Short-lived, audience-bound tokens for each hop (OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange, RFC 8693; resource indicators, RFC 8707). No token passthrough — each service obtains its own token for the next hop (the MCP specification requires this). Scopes per task, not per agent lifetime. The token carries both identities (user and agent, for example an act claim) so every service can authorise and audit correctly. Authorisation at every hop# Per-hop authorisation flowchart LR AG[&#34;Agent&#34;] --&gt;|&#34;token A&#34;| G[&#34;MCP gateway&lt;br/&gt;is this agent allowed this tool?&#34;] G --&gt; S[&#34;MCP server&lt;br/&gt;is this user allowed this record?&#34;] S --&gt; B[&#34;Business service&lt;br/&gt;limits, ownership, approvals&#34;] B --&gt; D[(&#34;Data&#34;)] Gateway: agent-level allow-lists of servers and tools, rate limits. MCP server / tool: user-level authorisation on the specific resource. Business service: domain rules — amount limits, ownership, approval thresholds. Multi-agent delegation: a sub-agent never gets more rights than the delegating agent; re-authorise at each A2A hop. Credentials and secrets# Store third-party credentials in a token vault; the harness injects them into tool calls — the model never sees them. Prefer workload identity (cloud IAM roles, SPIFFE) over static API keys for agent runtimes. Rotate and expire; revoke on agent decommissioning. Consent and transparency# Users should see what an agent can do on their behalf and grant consent for sensitive scopes (OAuth consent screens, step-up approval). Provide a way to revoke an agent&rsquo;s delegated access. Show who acted in audit logs and in the UI (&ldquo;Created by Support Agent on behalf of J. Smith&rdquo;). Agent registry# Treat agents as first-class identities: Registry field Purpose Agent ID and owner Accountability Purpose and risk tier Governance Allowed tools / MCP servers / A2A peers Least privilege Identity model (delegated, own, hybrid) Access design Credentials and rotation Hygiene Status (active, suspended, retired) Lifecycle and kill switch Managed platforms increasingly provide agent identity services; see managed platforms. Common mistakes# Common mistakeAdmin service account for the agent Gives every successful prompt injection full access. Use delegated, scoped tokens and the intersection model. Common mistakeIdentity in tool arguments refund(customerId=…) filled by the model. Take identity from the authenticated context (for example Spring AI&rsquo;s ToolContext). Review questions# How should an agent authenticate when acting for a user? With a short-lived delegated token obtained by OAuth token exchange, bound to the target audience and narrowed to the task&rsquo;s scopes, carrying both user and agent identity — never by passing the user&rsquo;s original token through. What is the effective permission of an agent&rsquo;s action? The intersection of the user&rsquo;s permissions, the agent&rsquo;s permissions and the scope the task needs. Where should authorisation happen in an agent architecture? At every hop: gateway (agent may use this tool), tool or MCP server (user may access this resource), business service (domain limits and approvals), and again at each agent-to-agent delegation. Why keep an agent registry? To know which agents exist, who owns them, what they may access, how they authenticate, and to suspend them quickly. Summary# Agents are non-human identities that often act on behalf of users. Use delegated, short-lived, audience-bound tokens via
d: Who is the agent acting as? Agent identities, acting on behalf of users with OAuth token exchange, least-privilege scopes, per-hop authorisation across tools and agents, credential vaults, consent, and audit — the access-control architecture enterprise agents need.

b: Simple definition# The Claude Agent SDK is Claude Code as a library. From Python or TypeScript you call query(), and the SDK runs the same agent loop, built-in tools (read, edit, shell, search, web), permissions, sessions, hooks, sub-agents and MCP support that power the Claude Code CLI — inside a process you operate. You supply the prompt, the tools it may use, and callbacks that decide what it&rsquo;s allowed to do. Version noteSource and date Condensed from Anthropic&rsquo;s Agent SDK documentation (overview, quickstart, permissions, custom tools, hooks, sessions, hosting), read on 7 November 2026. Check the Python and TypeScript references for exact signatures. Your application around the Claude Code agent loop · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. &copy; 2026 Samir Kumar Sahoo, all rights reserved. Open full screen ↗ Which Claude tool to build with# You want to Use You get Embed a capable coding/file agent in your own Python or TypeScript app Agent SDK Claude Code&rsquo;s loop, tools, permissions, sessions and hooks as a library Interactive development, one-off tasks Claude Code CLI The terminal experience; claude -p for scripts Call the model directly and own the loop Client SDK (Messages API) Full control; you write tools and the loop (or use the tool runner) Anthropic hosts the agent and its sandbox Managed Agents Hosted harness configured through the API Other languages: run claude -p … --output-format json as a subprocess. See The Claude API for builders for the Client SDK and Managed Agents. Install and authenticate# pip install claude-agent-sdk # or: uv add claude-agent-sdk (Python 3.10+) npm install @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk # Node 18.14+ export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-… # read from the process environment, not .env Both packages bundle a native Claude Code binary. Cloud providers work with the same variables as the CLI (CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1, CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX=1, CLAUDE_CODE_USE_FOUNDRY=1). WarningAuthentication for products Unless Anthropic has approved it, third-party products built on the SDK may not offer claude.ai login or use claude.ai rate limits. Use API keys or a cloud provider. Branding rules also apply: &ldquo;Powered by Claude&rdquo; is fine; calling your product &ldquo;Claude Code&rdquo; is not. First agent# import asyncio from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions, AssistantMessage, ResultMessage async def main(): async for message in query( prompt=&#34;Review utils.py for bugs that would cause crashes. Fix any you find.&#34;, options=ClaudeAgentOptions( allowed_tools=[&#34;Read&#34;, &#34;Edit&#34;, &#34;Glob&#34;], permission_mode=&#34;acceptEdits&#34;, max_turns=20, ), ): if isinstance(message, AssistantMessage): for block in message.content: if hasattr(block, &#34;text&#34;): print(block.text) elif isinstance(message, ResultMessage): print(f&#34;Done: {message.subtype}, cost ${message.total_cost_usd or 0:.4f}&#34;) asyncio.run(main()) import { query } from &#34;@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk&#34;; for await (const message of query({ prompt: &#34;Review utils.py for bugs that would cause crashes. Fix any you find.&#34;, options: { allowedTools: [&#34;Read&#34;, &#34;Edit&#34;, &#34;Glob&#34;], permissionMode: &#34;acceptEdits&#34;, maxTurns: 20 }, })) { if (message.type === &#34;result&#34;) console.log(`Done: ${message.subtype}`); } query() returns an async stream of messages: system init, assistant text and tool calls, tool results, and a final result message (subtype is success, or e.g. error_max_turns; it carries cost and usage). Key options# Option (Python / TypeScript) Purpose allowed_tools / allowedTools Pre-approve tools (adds allow rules) disallowed_tools / disallowedTools Deny tools permission_mode / permissionMode default, acceptEdits, plan, auto, dontAsk, bypassPermissions can_use_tool / canUseTool Your callback for anything not resolved earlier system_prompt / systemPrompt Replace or append to the system prompt model, max_turns / maxTurns Model and turn cap cwd Working directory — give each session its own mcp_servers / mcpServers External or in-process MCP servers hooks Hook callbacks by event agents Sub-agent definitions setting_sources / settingSources Which of user, project, local settings, CLAUDE.md and skills to load resume, continue_conversation / continue, fork_session / forkSession Sessions output_format / outputFormat Validated structured output against a JSON Schema env Environment for the subprocess Permissions: evaluation order# Hooks (PreToolUse) — can deny; an allow doesn&rsquo;t skip the next steps. Deny rules — from disallowed_tools and settings. Ask rules. Permission mode — e.g. acceptEdits approves edits, bypassPermissions approves almost everything. Allow rules — from allowed_tools and settings. canUseTool callback — your code decides (skipped and denied in dontAsk). from claude_agent_sdk import ClaudeAgentOptions, PermissionResultAllow, PermissionResultDeny async def can_use_tool(tool_name, input_data, context): if tool_name == &#34;Bash&#34; and &#34;rm -rf&#34; in input_data.get(&#34;command&#34;, &#34;&#34;): return PermissionResultDeny(message=&#34;Destructive commands are not allowed&#34;) return PermissionResultAllow(updated_input=input_data) options = ClaudeAgentOptions(can_use_tool=can_use_tool) TypeScript returns { behavior: &quot;allow&quot;, updatedInput } or { behavior: &quot;deny&quot;, message }. TipDon&rsquo;t silence your own callback A bare tool name in allowed_tools (e.g. &quot;Bash&quot;), or bypassPermissions, approves calls before canUseTool is consulted. Use specifiers like Bash(npm test) if your callback must see the rest. The TypeScript SDK warns when this happens. Non-interactive runs need an explicit mode. If tool calls are unexpectedly denied after an upgrade, pass permission_mode / permissionMode explicitly rather than relying on the default. Custom tools: in-process MCP servers# from typing import Annotated, Any from claude_agent_sdk

b: Simple definition# The enterprise AI stack is the set of shared layers an organisation builds so that many teams can ship AI features safely and cheaply: access to models, a gateway to control that access, pipelines that turn company data into retrievable knowledge, frameworks for chains and agents, and the operations, security and governance around all of it. The problem it solves# Without a platform, every team picks its own model, stores its own API keys, builds its own vector store, logs prompts (with customer data) in different places, and nobody knows the total cost or which apps send personal data to which vendor. That is &ldquo;shadow AI&rdquo;: fast at first, ungovernable at scale. The layered architecture# This is the destination. To see how a team grows into it one component at a time — context, guardrails, router and gateway, caches, write actions — see AI engineering architecture. b: Simple definition# An agentic AI strategy decides where agents should do work in the organisation, how much autonomy they get, what platform they run on, how value and risk are measured, and how people and processes change around them. It turns isolated pilots into a governed, scalable capability. Maturity model# Agentic AI maturity flowchart LR L1[&#34;1 · Assist&lt;br/&gt;chat and copilots,&lt;br/&gt;human does the work&#34;] --&gt; L2[&#34;2 · Automate steps&lt;br/&gt;workflows with LLM steps,&lt;br/&gt;RAG, tool reads&#34;] L2 --&gt; L3[&#34;3 · Act with oversight&lt;br/&gt;agents take actions,&lt;br/&gt;approvals for risky ones&#34;] L3 --&gt; L4[&#34;4 · Orchestrate&lt;br/&gt;multi-agent processes across&lt;br/&gt;teams via MCP/A2A&#34;] L4 --&gt; L5[&#34;5 · Autonomous operations&lt;br/&gt;agents run processes end to end,&lt;br/&gt;humans manage exceptions&#34;] Level Typical capabilities Platform needs 1 Assist Knowledge assistants, drafting, coding assistants AI gateway, RAG, acceptable-use policy 2 Automate steps Document processing, classification, summaries inside workflows Evaluation in CI, LLMOps, structured output 3 Act with oversight Agents with write tools, HITL approvals MCP servers, agent identity, guardrails, audit 4 Orchestrate Cross-domain agents, A2A, shared agent registry MCP/A2A gateways, durable runtime, agent registry 5 Autonomous ops Agents own processes with SLAs Mature evaluation, incident response, governance at scale Most large enterprises in 2026 operate at levels 2–3, with selected level-4 processes. Choosing use cases# For a detailed impact and feasibility scorecard, the prioritisation matrix and the A.G.E.N.T. design framework, see the agent building playbook. Score each candidate on: Dimension Questions Value Volume × time saved, revenue, risk reduction, customer experience Agent fit Is the work varied, judgment-based, multi-system? (If fixed, use a workflow or RPA) Data &amp; tool readiness APIs or MCP servers available? Clean data and permissions? Risk Regulatory tier, harm if wrong, reversibility of actions Measurability Clear success metric and evaluation data? Use-case portfolio quadrantChart title Agentic use-case portfolio x-axis Low feasibility --&gt; High feasibility y-axis Low value --&gt; High value quadrant-1 Do now quadrant-2 Prepare foundations quadrant-3 Avoid quadrant-4 Quick wins &#34;IT service desk agent&#34;: [0.8, 0.7] &#34;Coding agents&#34;: [0.85, 0.8] &#34;Claims triage&#34;: [0.6, 0.75] &#34;Credit decisioning&#34;: [0.3, 0.85] &#34;Meeting notes&#34;: [0.9, 0.35] &#34;Autonomous trading&#34;: [0.15, 0.6] Good early agentic candidates: IT and HR service desks, software engineering, customer-service case handling with approvals, document-heavy back-office processes, research and analysis for internal teams. Build, buy or configure?# Option When Buy agents inside SaaS (CRM, ITSM, ERP vendors) The process lives in that SaaS and differentiation is low Configure low-code agents Departmental, moderate-risk automations Build on a framework + platform Differentiating processes, cross-system work, strict control and governance Whatever you choose, insist on open protocols (MCP, A2A), exportable traces, evaluation access and identity integration, so bought and built agents can work together and be governed centrally. Measuring value and cost# Metric Example Outcome Cases resolved without human touch; cycle time; error rate Quality Task success rate on evaluation set; customer satisfaction; human override rate Efficiency Cost per completed task (tokens + platform + human review) vs baseline Risk Policy violations, incidents, escalation rate Adoption Active users, tasks delegated, trust surveys Key conceptMeasure cost per successful outcome Token cost per call is misleading for agents. Compare total cost per successfully completed task, including retries, human review and failures, with the current process. Operating model: AgentOps# Agent operating model flowchart TB GOV[&#34;AI governance council&lt;br/&gt;policy, risk tiers, approvals&#34;] --&gt; PLAT[&#34;Agent platform team&lt;br/&gt;runtime, gateways, registry,&lt;br/&gt;eval tooling, guardrails&#34;] PLAT --&gt; DOM[&#34;Domain teams&lt;br/&gt;own agents, tools (MCP),&lt;br/&gt;evals and outcomes&#34;] DOM --&gt; OPS[&#34;AgentOps&lt;br/&gt;monitoring, incidents,&lt;br/&gt;cost, continuous evaluation&#34;] OPS --&gt; DOM HR[&#34;People &amp; change&lt;br/&gt;roles, skills, job redesign&#34;] -.-&gt; DOM Agent product owners in domain teams own outcomes, autonomy levels and evaluation sets. Platform team provides runtime, MCP/A2A gateways, agent registry, identity, observability and guardrails as paved roads. AgentOps runs agents like services: SLOs, dashboards, on-call, incident playbooks, cost management. Governance sets risk tiers, approves autonomy increases, audits. People and change# Redesign work around human + agent roles: who supervises, approves, handles exceptions. Train staff to delegate to, review and correct agents (AI literacy is also a legal duty under the EU AI Act). Communicate openly about impact on jobs; involve works councils where required. Track trust: override rates and user feedback show whether autonomy can grow. A 12-month roadmap# Quarter Focus Q1 Platform foundations: AI gateway, agent framework standard, MCP servers for 3–5 key systems, evaluation tooling, governance tiers; 2 pilot agents at level 2–3 Q2 Production for pilots with HITL; agent identity and registry; AgentOps dashboards; skills repository Q3 Scale to 5–10 agents; A2A between domains; progressive autonomy on proven actions; cost-per-outcome reporting Q4 Cross-domain orchestrated processes; continuous evaluation and red teaming; review of operating model and value Common mistakes# Common mistakePilot purgatory Dozens of demos, none in production, because platform, evaluation and governance foundations were never built. Build the paved road with the first two use cases. Common

b: Simple definition# Most AI applications converge on the same architecture, but no team should build it all on day one. This article grows it one component at a time, each added only when a concrete need appears: context, guardrails, routing, caching, actions — and the observability that makes all of it operable. The enterprise AI stack shows the destination as layers. This is the journey. Key conceptThe one idea to keep Every component you add is something to evaluate, monitor and maintain. Add it when a measured problem demands it — not because the reference diagram has a box for it. Step 0 — The simplest architecture# The application sends the user&rsquo;s query to a model API and returns the response. No context, no guardrails, no optimisation. Step 0: one call flowchart LR U[&#34;User&#34;] --&gt; APP[&#34;Application&#34;] --&gt; M[&#34;Model API&lt;br/&gt;hosted or self-hosted&#34;] --&gt; APP --&gt; U It is the right place to start: it tells you what the model can do unaided and gives a baseline for every later step. Step 1 — Enhance the context# Give the model the information it lacks: retrieval over documents, tools that query databases, APIs and the web, and conversation memory. This is usually the largest quality jump. See RAG fundamentals and tool calling. Context construction is to foundation models what feature engineering was to classic ML. Step 2 — Put in guardrails# Guardrails protect users and the business. They sit on both sides of the model. Step 2: guardrails around the model flowchart LR U[&#34;User&#34;] --&gt; IG[&#34;Input guardrails&lt;br/&gt;PII masking, injection checks,&lt;br/&gt;topic and policy filters&#34;] IG --&gt; CTX[&#34;Context&lt;br/&gt;retrieval, tools&#34;] CTX --&gt; M[&#34;Model&#34;] M --&gt; OG[&#34;Output guardrails&lt;br/&gt;format, grounding, toxicity,&lt;br/&gt;PII, policy&#34;] OG --&gt;|&#34;pass&#34;| U OG --&gt;|&#34;fail&#34;| F[&#34;Retry, fallback,&lt;br/&gt;or human&#34;] Input guardrails# Risk Guardrail Leaking private data to an external model Detect and mask PII, secrets and confidential terms before the call; reverse the mapping on the response Prompt attacks Detect injection and jailbreak attempts — see AI security Out-of-scope requests Topic classifiers; block or redirect Output guardrails# Failure Check Quality Malformed format, ungrounded claims, irrelevant answers Security Toxicity, leaked PII, unsafe code or commands, brand risk Define a policy per failure mode: retry (with the same or a different model), fall back to a safe answer, or hand off to a human. Retries add latency; run them in parallel where cost allows. The trade-off# Guardrails add latency and false positives. Streaming responses complicate output checks, because the user sees tokens before the full answer can be checked. Decide per use case: stream and check incrementally, or buffer and check fully. Step 3 — Add a model router and gateway# Router# A router sends each request to the best handler, usually via an intent classifier: Route easy requests to a small, cheap model and hard ones to a large model. Route out-of-scope requests to a canned response, and sensitive ones to a human. Route by task type to specialised pipelines (billing, technical support, password reset). Detect ambiguous requests and ask for clarification. Routers must be fast and cheap — typically small classifiers or small models. See model routing and cascades. Gateway# A model gateway is the single, unified interface to every model provider and self-hosted model. It centralises access control and keys, cost tracking and budgets, rate limiting, fallbacks when a provider fails, logging, and sometimes caching and guardrails. Changing a model becomes a configuration change. See AI gateway. Step 4 — Reduce latency and cost with caching# Cache Key Hit when Watch out for Prompt (KV) cache Repeated prompt prefix Same system prompt, tools, documents Handled by the model provider or serving engine — see prompt caching Exact cache Hash of the full request Identical query (FAQ, product lookups, embeddings) Personalised or time-sensitive answers; eviction policy (LRU, LFU) Semantic cache Embedding of the query A similar query was answered before A wrong hit returns a wrong answer; tune the similarity threshold carefully and measure hit precision WarningCaches can leak data A cached answer generated for one user can be served to another. Scope cache keys by user, tenant and permissions where answers depend on them. Step 5 — Add agent patterns and write actions# Now the system can do more than answer: loop over retrieval, call several tools, reflect on its output, and take write actions — send an email, place an order, update a record. Write actions are where risk jumps. Add permissions and approvals, budgets and stop conditions and an audit trail before giving the system the ability to change the world. See agentic workflow patterns. The full picture# The progressive architecture, fully built flowchart TB U[&#34;User&#34;] --&gt; IG[&#34;Input guardrails&#34;] IG --&gt; R[&#34;Router / intent classifier&#34;] R --&gt; CA{&#34;Cache hit?&#34;} CA --&gt;|&#34;yes&#34;| OG CA --&gt;|&#34;no&#34;| CTX[&#34;Context construction&lt;br/&gt;retrieval · tools · memory&#34;] CTX --&gt; GW[&#34;Model gateway&#34;] GW --&gt; M1[&#34;Small model&#34;] GW --&gt; M2[&#34;Large model&#34;] M1 --&gt; AG[&#34;Agent logic&lt;br/&gt;reflection · write actions&#34;] M2 --&gt; AG AG --&gt; OG[&#34;Output guardrails&#34;] OG --&gt; U subgraph OBS[&#34;Monitoring and observability&#34;] MET[&#34;Metrics&#34;] LOG[&#34;Logs and traces&#34;] FB[&#34;User feedback&#34;] end IG -.-&gt; OBS CTX -.-&gt; OBS GW -.-&gt; OBS OG -.-&gt; OBS Monitoring and observability# Monitoring tells you that something is wrong; observability lets you find out why from the outside, without shipping new code. Design for observability from the start. Three numbers frame incident handling: MTTD (time to detect), MTTR (time to resolve) and CFR (change

b: Simple definition# Once Claude Code can check its own work, it no longer needs you at the keyboard. Automation means starting runs from a script, a timer or an event (claude -p, GitHub Actions, /schedule). Parallel work means running several Claude workers at once — sub-agents inside a session, background sessions in agent view, coordinated agent teams, or a scripted dynamic workflow — usually each in its own git worktree. Version noteSource and date From the official pages on headless mode, GitHub Actions, scheduled tasks, /goal, running agents in parallel, agent teams, dynamic workflows and worktrees, read on 7 November 2026. Agent view and agent teams are research previews / experimental. The unattended-run contract# Before anything runs without you, answer five questions for that task — the harness, not the prompt, should hold the answers where possible. A safe unattended run: define done, bound it, check it, sign it off · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. &copy; 2026 Samir Kumar Sahoo, all rights reserved. Open full screen ↗ Question Answer with What does done look like? /goal condition, SPEC.md, a failing test to turn green How does it check its work? Test suite, Stop hook, /code-review, a reviewer sub-agent What may it touch? --allowedTools, --permission-mode dontAsk, sandbox, a worktree, one pushable branch What stops it? --max-turns, --max-budget-usd, an organisation spend limit Who signs off? A PR, branch protection, a person approving merge or deploy Scripts and CI: print mode# claude -p runs once and exits. In scripts you almost always add: Flag Why --bare Ignore the machine&rsquo;s hooks, skills, plugins, MCP and CLAUDE.md — same behaviour everywhere. Auth must come from ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, an apiKeyHelper, or cloud credentials --settings, --mcp-config, --append-system-prompt Pass in exactly what the run needs (hooks passed via --settings don&rsquo;t run under --bare) --allowedTools + --permission-mode dontAsk Pre-approve the tools; refuse everything else --max-turns, --max-budget-usd Hard stops --output-format json or stream-json --verbose Parse the result or stream events --json-schema Validated structured output # Fan out a migration, one bounded run per file for file in $(cat files.txt); do claude --bare -p &#34;Migrate $file to the new logger API and commit. Reply OK or FAIL.&#34; \ --allowedTools &#34;Read,Edit,Bash(git add *),Bash(git commit *)&#34; \ --permission-mode dontAsk --max-turns 20 done # Triage a log, get JSON back cat build.log | claude -p &#34;Classify the failure: flaky, infra or code. Return JSON.&#34; \ --output-format json --max-turns 3 Auto mode also works with -p (--permission-mode auto): a classifier block denies that one action and the run continues — it does not pause for a human. For long-lived CI credentials on a subscription, use claude setup-token. For programmatic control in Python or TypeScript, use the Agent SDK. GitHub, GitLab and pull requests# Integration What it does Set up Claude Code GitHub Actions Responds to @claude in issues and PR comments; turns issues into PRs; runs any prompt in a workflow /install-github-app, or add anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 Code Review (Team/Enterprise) Reviews every PR, verifies findings, comments inline Admin enables it; billed through usage credits /code-review --comment Local review posted as inline PR comments In a session /autofix-pr Cloud session that watches a PR and pushes fixes for CI failures and review comments Needs a claude.ai login GitLab CI/CD Same patterns in GitLab pipelines GitLab CI/CD guide name: Claude Code on: issue_comment: { types: [created] } pull_request_review_comment: { types: [created] } jobs: claude: if: contains(github.event.comment.body, &#39;@claude&#39;) runs-on: ubuntu-latest permissions: { contents: write, pull-requests: write, issues: write, id-token: write } steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v6 with: { fetch-depth: 1 } - uses: anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 with: anthropic_api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }} claude_args: &#34;--max-turns 30 --model sonnet&#34; The action follows the repo&rsquo;s CLAUDE.md on every run, so keep it concise and the same conventions apply in CI as on laptops. Keep the API key in secrets, give the job the least GitHub permissions it needs, and protect main so the bot cannot merge its own work. Keeping one session working# Mechanism Next turn starts when Stops when Use for Auto mode — (approves tools within a turn) Claude judges the work done Fewer prompts, not more turns /goal &lt;condition&gt; The previous turn finishes A separate evaluator confirms the condition, or judges it impossible Migrations, design docs with acceptance criteria, backlog burn-down Stop hook The previous turn finishes Your script passes Deterministic &ldquo;done&rdquo; for every session /loop [interval] &lt;prompt&gt; An interval elapses (or Claude self-paces 1 min–1 h) You stop it, or after 7 days Babysitting CI, polling a deploy Write goal conditions as something Claude&rsquo;s own output can demonstrate: one measurable end state, the check that proves it, constraints that must hold, and a bound — /goal all tests in test/auth pass and lint is clean; don't modify other test files; or stop after 20 turns. The evaluator reads the transcript; it doesn&rsquo;t run commands itself. Scheduling work# /loop Desktop scheduled task Cloud scheduled task (/schedule) Runs on Your machine, in the session Your machine Anthropic cloud (or self-hosted environment) Needs machine on / session open Yes / Yes Yes / No No / No Local files Yes Yes No — fresh clone Permissions Inherits session Per task Auto mode by default Minimum interval 1 minute 1 minute (1 hour in forms) 1 hour Triggers Time Time Time, GitHub events, API WarningBefore a cloud task runs alone Protect main with a branch rule the task cannot bypass, and watch the first few runs. A /loop in a long conversation resends that whole conversation every iteration — start it in a fresh

b: Simple definition# This playbook covers the practical path from &ldquo;we should use agents&rdquo; to an agent that works in production: find the right opportunity, score and prioritise it, design the agent with a structured framework, and implement it with principles that avoid the most common failures. It complements agentic AI strategy, which covers the portfolio and operating model. Key conceptThe one idea to keep Agents automate tasks, not roles. A person may own five processes; you may need five small, well-defined agents — and a human — to cover the same work. Step 1 — Find the sweet spot# Good agent opportunities sit where three things overlap: The sweet spot for agentic opportunities flowchart TB I[&#34;High business impact&#34;] --&gt; SS((&#34;Sweet spot&#34;)) F[&#34;Feasible with current&lt;br/&gt;technology and data&#34;] --&gt; SS E[&#34;Reasonable&lt;br/&gt;implementation effort&#34;] --&gt; SS SS --&gt; C[&#34;Candidate for an agent&#34;] And they are processes that agents are actually good at. Keep with people the work that depends on genuine creativity, strategic judgement, empathy or accountability that cannot be delegated. Score impact# Rate each criterion from 1 to 5: Criterion 1 3 5 Time investment Under an hour per week Several hours per week Hours every day Strategic value of freed time Little better use for it Moderate Unblocks high-value strategic work Error-reduction potential Errors are rare Occasional significant errors Frequent or costly errors Scalability One-off task Moderately repeatable Repeats across the organisation Score feasibility# Criterion 1 3 5 Process standardisation Ad hoc, no standard approach Some documentation; relies on experience Fully documented steps, decision rules and exceptions Data and system access Data locked in legacy systems or paper Available but needs significant preparation Structured data, modern APIs Prioritise# Plot each candidate by impact and feasibility. Low feasibility High feasibility High impact Strategic projects — fix the process or data first, then automate Quick wins → start here Low impact Avoid Opportunistic — do if cheap; good for learning Then choose the right level of automation: deterministic, standardised, zero-error-tolerance work suits intelligent automation; variable, unstructured, judgement-heavy work suits an agentic workflow. See level 2 or level 3? TipProve it manually first Never automate a process that has not been done successfully by hand. Existing process documentation — steps, tools, decision trees, worked examples — is the best raw material for an agent&rsquo;s instructions and evaluation set. Step 2 — Design with the A.G.E.N.T. framework# A.G.E.N.T. is a checklist of five design areas. Each answers one question. Component Key question Elements Actions A — Agent identity Who is the agent? Purpose, role, scope Write a one-sentence mission; state boundaries and responsibilities; align with the intended use G — Gear and brain What powers it? Model, tools, knowledge sources Choose the model for quality and cost; implement the needed tools and APIs; curate high-quality knowledge E — Execution and workflow How does it work? Inputs and outputs, workflow, triggers Standardise input/output formats; define the workflow; set triggers (schedule, event, request) N — Navigation and rules How does it decide? Processing rules, safety mechanisms, transparency Filtering and prioritisation rules; rate limits, circuit breakers, human escalation; decision logs T — Testing and trust How do we improve and scale it? Real-world testing, feedback, monitoring, scalability Simulate real cases and edge cases; collect feedback; monitor logs; plan for scale How it maps to the rest of this handbook: A.G.E.N.T. Read more Agent identity What is an agent?, Agent identity and access Gear and brain Model selection, Tool calling, MCP, RAG Execution and workflow Workflow patterns, Planning Navigation and rules Reliability and guardrails, AI security Testing and trust Agent evaluation, User feedback Example: a newsletter team of agents# A daily industry newsletter is a classic first multi-agent project: clear steps, low risk, measurable output. A team of specialised agents for a daily newsletter flowchart LR M[&#34;Manager agent&lt;br/&gt;coordinates and delivers&#34;] --&gt; S[&#34;Search agent&lt;br/&gt;finds relevant articles&#34;] S --&gt; SU[&#34;Summarisation agent&lt;br/&gt;key points per article&#34;] SU --&gt; E[&#34;Email agent&lt;br/&gt;daily digest to editor&#34;] E --&gt; H{&#34;Editor selects&lt;br/&gt;articles&#34;} H --&gt; C[&#34;Compiler agent&lt;br/&gt;organises selected content&#34;] C --&gt; F[&#34;Formatting agent&lt;br/&gt;prepares the newsletter&#34;] F --&gt; M Each agent has one job and few tools; the human editor stays in the loop at the point of judgement. See multi-agent systems. Step 3 — Implementation principles# Grouped by phase, these are the lessons that most often separate working agents from abandoned pilots. Defining the agent# Precise instructions win. Invest in the purpose, role and scope. Examples teach more than descriptions; put the most important instructions where the model weighs them most (often at the end). The simpler, the better. Every extra agent, tool or task adds cost and maintenance. Start minimal and grow. Few tools per agent. A narrowly scoped agent with one or two tools is more reliable than a multi-purpose one. Divide and conquer. Build one component at a time instead of the whole system at once. Designing for success# Design for collaboration with people. Augment rather than replace; keep humans in the loop for quality and strategic decisions. Integrate where users already work — the chat tool, CRM or ticketing system they use. An inconvenient agent is unused. Let agents check their own results — give them tools to verify that an action succeeded. Standardise inputs and outputs with strict schemas to avoid errors from mismatched data. Separate knowledge from actions. Keep

b: Simple definition# For a team, Claude Code configuration has three owners. The repository carries shared conventions, permissions, hooks, skills, agents and MCP servers, committed like any other code. Each developer keeps personal preferences in local and user files. The organisation sets policy through managed settings that no one else can override, and watches usage and spend through analytics and telemetry. Version noteSource and date From Anthropic&rsquo;s Set up Claude Code for your organization, Settings, Costs, Analytics, Monitoring usage and Plugin marketplaces, read on 7 November 2026. How team, personal and managed settings combine — and where usage goes · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. &copy; 2026 Samir Kumar Sahoo, all rights reserved. Open full screen ↗ What to commit to the repository# Path Purpose Notes CLAUDE.md Commands, misleading code, decisions not in the repo Under 200 lines; CLAUDE.local.md for personal notes (gitignored) .claude/rules/*.md Path-scoped rules (paths: frontmatter) Load only when matching files are touched .claude/settings.json Permissions, hooks, env, enabled plugins, marketplaces deny/ask apply at once; allow, hooks, marketplaces and most env wait for each developer&rsquo;s workspace trust .claude/skills/ Team procedures: release, incident runbook, API docs style disable-model-invocation: true for anything with side effects .claude/agents/ Shared sub-agents (a read-only reviewer, a test writer) Restrict tools; use model: haiku for simple jobs .mcp.json Team MCP servers Each developer approves project servers; keep secrets in env vars .worktreeinclude Gitignored files new worktrees need Small files only TipBootstrap a teammate /team-onboarding turns your last 30 days of sessions, commands and MCP usage into a guide a new teammate can paste as their first message. /insights shows how you use Claude Code and where it goes wrong. Settings precedence# Highest first — a key set higher overrides the same key lower down: Managed settings — server-delivered, MDM/registry, or managed-settings.json. Nothing below can override them. Command line — --settings &lt;file|json&gt; for one session. Project local — .claude/settings.local.json (yours, gitignored). Shared project — .claude/settings.json (committed). User — ~/.claude/settings.json. Arrays merge across scopes. permissions.allow and permissions.deny collect entries from every level, so developers can add to managed lists but not remove from them. Permission rules combine by kind, not only by level: a local allow doesn&rsquo;t outrank a project or managed ask. Deny always wins. A few restrictive keys (for example blockWritesOutsideWorkingDirectories: true) are honoured from any scope even if managed settings say otherwise. /status shows which sources are active (Setting sources). Managed settings: delivery# Mechanism Where Priority Server-managed Claude admin console (Team/Enterprise), or a self-hosted Claude apps gateway Highest; fetched at start, refreshed hourly OS policy macOS plist com.anthropic.claudecode; Windows HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\ClaudeCode High; admin-only, tamper-resistant File /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/, /etc/claude-code/, C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\ → managed-settings.json Medium Windows user registry HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\ClaudeCode Lowest; a convenience default, not enforcement WSL reads only the Linux path unless wslInheritsWindowsSettings: true is set in an admin-only Windows source. Mixed providers: server-managed for claude.ai users plus a file or OS-policy fallback for everyone else. Managed settings: what admins can enforce# Control Keys Permission rules, and make managed the only source permissions.allow/deny, allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly Ban --dangerously-skip-permissions; remove auto mode; set starting mode permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode, permissions.disableAutoMode, permissions.defaultMode OS sandbox with a network allowlist sandbox.enabled, sandbox.network.allowedDomains MCP servers allowed, denied or provided allowedMcpServers, deniedMcpServers, allowManagedMcpServersOnly, managedMcpServers Plugin and marketplace sources strictKnownMarketplaces, blockedMarketplaces, disableSideloadFlags Customisations only from plugins or policy strictPluginOnlyCustomization Hooks allowManagedHooksOnly, allowedHttpHookUrls Login method, organisation and provider login enforcement keys, allowedProviders Models and effort availableModels, enforceAvailableModels, maxEffortLevel Versions minimumVersion, requiredMinimumVersion, requiredMaximumVersion Background agents disableAgentView, or processWrapper for a corporate launcher Telemetry to Anthropic off env.CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1 Organisation-wide guidance Managed-policy CLAUDE.md (advice, not enforcement) { &#34;permissions&#34;: { &#34;deny&#34;: [&#34;Read(./.env)&#34;, &#34;Read(./.env.*)&#34;, &#34;Read(**/secrets/**)&#34;, &#34;Bash(curl * | bash)&#34;], &#34;disableBypassPermissionsMode&#34;: &#34;disable&#34; }, &#34;sandbox&#34;: { &#34;enabled&#34;: true, &#34;network&#34;: { &#34;allowedDomains&#34;: [&#34;github.com&#34;, &#34;*.internal.example.com&#34;] } }, &#34;maxEffortLevel&#34;: &#34;xhigh&#34;, &#34;minimumVersion&#34;: &#34;2.1.300&#34; } WarningPermissions and sandbox are different layers Denying WebFetch blocks Claude&rsquo;s fetch tool, but if Bash is allowed, curl can still reach any URL. Only the sandbox&rsquo;s domain allowlist enforces network limits at the OS level. Use both. Choosing a provider# Provider Choose when Watch out Claude for Teams / Enterprise Default: one per-seat subscription for Claude Code and claude.ai, nothing to run — Claude Console (API) API-first, pay-as-you-go No cloud sessions, scheduled cloud tasks, Code Review, Remote Control or Chrome without a claude.ai login Amazon Bedrock / Google Cloud Agent Platform / Microsoft Foundry Inherit existing cloud compliance and billing Same feature gaps; org model and effort

b: Simple definition# User feedback is every signal users give — deliberately or not — about whether the application helped them. It is the one data source competitors cannot copy. Collected well, it drives evaluation (are we getting better?), development (what should we train or fix next?) and personalisation (what does this user prefer?). Key conceptThe one idea to keep Design feedback collection into the product from the first release. Every conversation is a free evaluation sample — if you capture it. Explicit and implicit feedback# Type Examples Strength Weakness Explicit Thumbs up/down, star ratings, &ldquo;was this helpful?&rdquo;, choosing between two answers, written comments Clear meaning Sparse — most users never click; skewed towards strong opinions Implicit Copying the answer, accepting a code suggestion, editing the output, abandoning the session, asking again Plentiful, honest Noisy; its meaning depends on context Conversational interfaces make implicit feedback especially rich, because users express satisfaction and frustration in natural language. Signals hidden in conversations# Natural-language feedback# Signal What it looks like Likely meaning Early termination User stops generation, closes the app, or interrupts mid-answer The answer was going wrong, too slow or too long Error correction &ldquo;No, I meant…&rdquo;, &ldquo;That&rsquo;s wrong, the deadline is Friday&rdquo;, rephrasing the same request The model misunderstood or erred — the follow-up shows the right answer, a valuable training pair Complaints &ldquo;That&rsquo;s not what I asked&rdquo;, &ldquo;too long&rdquo;, &ldquo;you keep repeating yourself&rdquo; Specific failure categories you can count Sentiment Frustration, thanks, sarcasm Overall satisfaction trend User edits to a generated draft are a particularly strong signal: the edited version is a preferred response, and (original, edited) is a ready-made preference pair. Other conversational signals# Signal Interpretation Regeneration The first answer was unsatisfactory — or the user wanted options; compare which answer they keep Conversation organisation Renaming, sharing, bookmarking or deleting a conversation shows its value Conversation length Ambiguous: long can mean engaged (a companion app) or stuck (a support bot) — interpret per product Dialogue diversity Many distinct turns suggest progress; repeated similar turns suggest the user is looping on a failure TipDefine what &ldquo;good&rdquo; means per product A long conversation is success for a tutoring app and failure for a password-reset bot. Decide which signals indicate success for your use case before building dashboards. Feedback design# When to collect feedback# Moment Example In the beginning Ask a few preference questions at onboarding to personalise; make them optional When something goes wrong After an error or a complaint: let users flag, correct, or hand off to a human When the model has low confidence Show two candidate answers and ask which is better; ask a clarifying question instead of guessing After a meaningful outcome Task completed, ticket resolved — ask briefly Never interrupt the user&rsquo;s flow for feedback that does not change anything. Feedback requests should be rare, quick and optional. How to collect feedback# Integrate it into the workflow. The best feedback is a by-product of normal use — accepting a suggestion, choosing an option, editing a draft. Make it effortless. One click beats a form. Offer an optional comment box after a thumbs-down. Make the meaning unambiguous. &ldquo;Thumbs down&rdquo; can mean wrong, unhelpful, rude or slow; offer short reason chips. Show the effect. Users give more feedback when they see it change something. Respect privacy. Tell users what is collected and how it is used; let them opt out; keep it out of training sets unless they agree. See AI governance. Feedback in the product loop flowchart LR U[&#34;User&#34;] --&gt; A[&#34;AI response&#34;] A --&gt; S[&#34;Signals&lt;br/&gt;explicit ratings,&lt;br/&gt;edits, regenerations,&lt;br/&gt;early stops, complaints&#34;] S --&gt; L[&#34;Logged with trace&lt;br/&gt;prompt version, model,&lt;br/&gt;context, output&#34;] L --&gt; E[&#34;Evaluation&lt;br/&gt;dashboards, slices,&lt;br/&gt;regression sets&#34;] L --&gt; D[&#34;Training data&lt;br/&gt;preference pairs,&lt;br/&gt;corrections&#34;] L --&gt; P[&#34;Personalisation&lt;br/&gt;per-user preferences&#34;] E --&gt; I[&#34;Improve prompts,&lt;br/&gt;retrieval, models&#34;] D --&gt; I I --&gt; A The data flywheel# More users → more feedback → better data → better product → more users. Feedback-derived data improves prompts, retrieval, routing and fine-tuning, and becomes the private evaluation set that keeps you honest. This is the most durable form of AI product defensibility. To make the flywheel turn, store feedback joined to the full trace of the request — without the prompt, context and model version, a thumbs-down cannot be acted on. Feedback limitations# Biases# Bias Effect Mitigation Leniency bias Users rate higher than they feel, to be polite or avoid friction Use comparative choices and implicit signals, not only ratings Randomness Users click without reading, especially when asked often Ask rarely; weight by engagement Position bias Users favour the first option shown Randomise order in comparisons Preference bias Users favour longer, more confident or more flattering answers — not necessarily more correct Combine with correctness checks; do not optimise on preference alone Selection bias Only very happy or very unhappy users give explicit feedback Correct with implicit signals and sampling Degenerate feedback loops# When predictions influence the feedback that trains future predictions, the system can amplify its own biases: Content that is shown more gets more clicks, so it is shown even more (popularity bias). Optimising for user approval can teach the model to flatter and agree rather than be correct — sycophancy. Counter it by

b: Simple definition# Deployment topology decides where each part of a GenAI system runs: the model, the retrieval index, the orchestration code and the logs. On-premise means inference runs on hardware you operate; hybrid means some workloads run on your hardware or private cloud and others call cloud-hosted models, with one control plane deciding which request goes where. The architect&rsquo;s job is not to pick &ldquo;cloud&rdquo; or &ldquo;on-prem&rdquo; once. It is to make the choice per data class and per workload, and to make that choice enforceable. Why it matters# Five drivers push enterprises away from &ldquo;call the public API for everything&rdquo;: Driver Typical source Data sovereignty and residency GDPR transfer rules, banking secrecy, public-sector and defence classification, customer contracts Regulatory operational resilience EU DORA, PRA/EBA outsourcing rules: concentration risk, exit plans, audit rights over critical third parties Cost at high steady volume Per-token pricing loses to amortised GPUs once utilisation is high and predictable Latency and availability Plant floors, branches, ships, field devices; no dependency on internet links Control and customisation Fine-tuned open-weight models, pinned versions, no surprise model deprecations And three forces pull the other way: frontier quality (still mostly API-only), zero GPU operations, and speed of adoption. Hybrid exists because both lists are true at the same time. The deployment spectrum# From most managed to most controlled flowchart LR A[&#34;Public provider API&lt;br/&gt;shared endpoints&#34;] --&gt; B[&#34;Cloud-managed models&lt;br/&gt;Bedrock, Azure AI Foundry,&lt;br/&gt;Vertex AI, private endpoints&#34;] B --&gt; C[&#34;Dedicated capacity&lt;br/&gt;provisioned throughput,&lt;br/&gt;single-tenant deployments&#34;] C --&gt; D[&#34;Sovereign / national cloud&lt;br/&gt;local operator, local staff,&lt;br/&gt;local jurisdiction&#34;] D --&gt; E[&#34;On-premise self-hosted&lt;br/&gt;open-weight models on&lt;br/&gt;your GPUs and Kubernetes&#34;] E --&gt; F[&#34;Air-gapped&lt;br/&gt;no network path out;&lt;br/&gt;offline model updates&#34;] Option Data path Model choice You operate Best for Public API Leaves your network over TLS; contractual retention terms Full frontier range Nothing but the client Public and internal data, prototypes Cloud-managed, private networking Stays in your cloud tenancy and region; private link, no internet Frontier + hosted open-weight, per-region availability IAM, networking, quotas Most confidential enterprise workloads Dedicated capacity As above, with reserved, isolated throughput Usually a subset Capacity planning Predictable latency at steady volume Sovereign cloud Local legal entity and operations Narrower catalogue, often lagging As above Public sector, regulated sectors with jurisdiction rules On-premise Never leaves your data centre Open-weight only (plus some vendors&rsquo; licensed on-prem offerings) GPUs, drivers, serving stack, scaling, upgrades Restricted data, very high volume, fine-tuned models Air-gapped No external connectivity at all Open-weight, imported through a controlled transfer Everything, including offline updates and evaluation Defence, critical infrastructure, classified data Edge / on-device Stays on the device Small models (1–8B, quantized) Fleet distribution Offline field work, low latency, privacy on device Key conceptThe quality gap is real but narrowing Open-weight models run on-premise are close to mid-tier proprietary models for RAG, extraction, summarisation and classification. The gap is widest for hard multi-step reasoning and long-horizon agentic work. Put the hard tasks where the best models are allowed, and the sensitive high-volume tasks where your data is allowed. Choosing per workload# Deployment decision guide flowchart TB Q1{&#34;Highest data class&lt;br/&gt;in the prompt or context?&#34;} Q1 --&gt;|&#34;Public / internal&#34;| A[&#34;Public API or&lt;br/&gt;cloud-managed&#34;] Q1 --&gt;|&#34;Confidential&#34;| Q2{&#34;Contract + region +&lt;br/&gt;private networking&lt;br/&gt;acceptable to DPO and risk?&#34;} Q2 --&gt;|&#34;Yes&#34;| B[&#34;Cloud-managed in-region,&lt;br/&gt;zero data retention,&lt;br/&gt;private endpoints&#34;] Q2 --&gt;|&#34;No&#34;| C[&#34;On-premise or sovereign&#34;] Q1 --&gt;|&#34;Restricted / secret&#34;| Q3{&#34;Any network path&lt;br/&gt;allowed?&#34;} Q3 --&gt;|&#34;Yes, internal only&#34;| C Q3 --&gt;|&#34;No&#34;| D[&#34;Air-gapped&#34;] B --&gt; Q4{&#34;Steady volume high enough&lt;br/&gt;to keep GPUs above ~50% busy?&#34;} Q4 --&gt;|&#34;Yes&#34;| E[&#34;Consider on-prem&lt;br/&gt;for cost, keep cloud&lt;br/&gt;for burst and frontier tasks&#34;] Q4 --&gt;|&#34;No&#34;| B Questions that settle most cases: What is the most sensitive data that can reach the model — including retrieved documents, tool results and conversation history, not just the user&rsquo;s question? Does the task need frontier reasoning, or does a 30–70B open-weight model pass your evaluation set? What is the steady and peak token volume, and how predictable is it? What does the regulator or customer contract require: region, jurisdiction, audit rights, exit plan? Can your organisation operate GPUs 24×7 — skills, on-call, hardware supply? Hybrid reference architecture# The defining component of a hybrid platform is an AI gateway that routes by data classification, not just by cost. Applications call one endpoint; the gateway decides which deployment is allowed to see the request. b: Simple definition# Using Claude across the software development lifecycle (SDLC) means giving it a defined job in each phase — not just autocomplete while coding. In every phase the pattern is the same: context in (the artefacts that phase needs), a specific task, a verification step, and a human decision where accountability sits. The lifecycle at a glance# Claude across the SDLC: Claude assists, checks enforce, humans decide · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. &copy; 2026 Samir Kumar Sahoo, all rights reserved. Open full screen ↗ Phase Claude&rsquo;s job Typical surface Model · effort Verification Human owns Discovery &amp; requirements Synthesise inputs, draft stories and acceptance criteria, find gaps Claude app, Projects Opus high Stakeholder review, traceability Scope and priority Architecture &amp; design Generate options, trade-offs, ADR drafts, threat models Claude app, Claude Code (plan mode) Opus/Fable high–xhigh Architecture review board The decision Build Implement features, refactor, explain code Claude Code Opus xhigh; Sonnet for routine Compile, tests, lint, run The merge Test Generate unit/integration/property tests, test data, find gaps Claude Code, CI Sonnet medium–high Mutation score, coverage of risky paths Test strategy Review &amp; security First-pass review, vulnerability analysis, dependency checks /code-review, /security-review, CI action Sonnet/Opus high Reproduce each finding Approval CI/CD &amp; release Write pipelines and IaC, explain failures, draft release notes Claude Code, headless in CI Sonnet medium Pipeline green, policy checks Go/no-go Operate &amp; incidents Summarise alerts and logs, propose hypotheses, draft post-mortems Agent with read-only MCP tools Sonnet; Haiku for triage Evidence from telemetry Incident command Maintain &amp; migrate Upgrades, framework migrations, dead-code removal, docs refresh Claude Code, batch + parallel worktrees Opus xhigh Full test suite, canary Rollout Discovery and requirements# Context in: interview notes, support tickets, process documents, existing API contracts, regulatory text. Turn raw notes into user stories with acceptance criteria in Given/When/Then form. Ask Claude to find ambiguities, contradictions and missing non-functional requirements (performance, availability, audit, data retention, accessibility). Generate edge cases from the business rules — these become test cases later. Use Claude Projects (or a shared knowledge base) so every conversation sees the same domain material. TipExample prompt &ldquo;Here are the refund policy, three support tickets and the current Refund API spec. Draft user stories with Given/When/Then acceptance criteria for partial refunds. Then list every question a product owner must answer before development can start, and every non-functional requirement the documents imply but do not state.&rdquo; Watch out: Claude will fill gaps with plausible assumptions. Ask it to mark assumptions explicitly, and have the product owner resolve them. Architecture and design# Context in: requirements, current architecture (C4 diagrams, ADRs), constraints (cloud, compliance, team skills), quality attribute targets. Generate options, not answers: ask for two or three designs with explicit trade-offs against your quality attributes. Draft ADRs in your template; draw diagrams as Mermaid or C4 from the codebase. Threat-model the design (STRIDE per component and data flow). Challenge a design: &ldquo;Act as the architecture review board. What fails first at 10× load? What is the blast radius of each dependency failing?&rdquo; — then check the answers against the review framework. In Claude Code, plan mode on the real repository grounds design in the code that exists. Watch out: models are persuasive. Treat a confident trade-off analysis as a hypothesis; validate key numbers (latency, cost, limits) with spikes and documentation. Build# Context in: the repository, CLAUDE.md, the story and acceptance criteria, related tests. Follow the explore → plan → implement → verify loop (Claude Code in practice). Give one task per session with a clear definition of done: &ldquo;Implement partial refunds per story PAY-412. Done when ./mvnw verify passes and the new endpoint is in openapi.yaml.&rdquo; Use test-first where possible: have Claude write failing tests from the acceptance criteria, review the tests, then implement. For refactoring, ask for behaviour-preserving steps with tests run after each. Use Claude to explain unfamiliar code before changing it — especially legacy modules with no documentation. Test# Unit and integration tests from acceptance criteria and from the code&rsquo;s branches. Property-based tests for business invariants (&ldquo;refund total never exceeds captured amount&rdquo;). Test data that respects schemas and privacy rules (synthetic, never copied production PII). Gap analysis: &ldquo;Which behaviours in RefundService have no test? Which tests would still pass if the logic were wrong?&rdquo; — then confirm with mutation testing. End-to-end and UI checks with browser automation where it pays off. Common mistakeTests that test the implementation Generated tests often mirror the code they were written from, so they pass even when the logic is wrong. Write tests from the requirements, review them before implementing, and use mutation testing to check they can fail. Code review and security# Run automated first-pass review on every PR (Claude Code action or /code-review): correctness, error handling, concurrency, API compatibility, adherence to CLAUDE.md rules. Run /security-review or a security sub-agent on changes that touch authentication, input handling, crypto, deserialisation or infrastructure. Ask for findings with evidence — file, line, failing scenario — and tell it to report nothing rather than style nits. Combine with deterministic tools (SAST, dependency and secret scanning, licence checks); Claude explains and prioritises their findings and
