b: Simple definition# LLMOps is the set of practices for building, deploying, monitoring and improving LLM applications in production. It extends DevOps and MLOps with things specific to LLMs: prompts as versioned artefacts, evaluation of non-deterministic output, token cost, safety guardrails and traces of multi-step chains and agents. Why it is different from normal operations# Traditional service LLM application Same input → same output Same input → different outputs Correctness tested with assertions Quality measured with evaluation datasets and judges Errors are exceptions and status codes Many failures are silent: fluent but wrong answers Cost is mostly infrastructure Cost is per request, per token, and can spike with one prompt change Behaviour changes when you deploy Behaviour can change when the provider updates a model The LLMOps lifecycle# Continuous improvement loop flowchart LR A[&#34;Design&lt;br/&gt;use case, metrics, risks&#34;] --&gt; B[&#34;Build&lt;br/&gt;prompts, RAG, tools&#34;] B --&gt; C[&#34;Evaluate offline&lt;br/&gt;golden dataset in CI&#34;] C --&gt;|&#34;pass&#34;| D[&#34;Deploy&lt;br/&gt;canary, shadow, A/B&#34;] C --&gt;|&#34;fail&#34;| B D --&gt; E[&#34;Monitor online&lt;br/&gt;traces, cost, feedback, drift&#34;] E --&gt; F[&#34;Analyse failures&lt;br/&gt;add cases to dataset&#34;] F --&gt; B The key habit: every production failure becomes a test case in the evaluation dataset. Observability: what to capture# Capture user signals too — ratings, edits, regenerations, early stops — joined to the trace; see user feedback. For drift sources and metric categories, see AI engineering architecture. One trace of a RAG request flowchart TB T[&#34;Trace: POST /ask 2.8 s $0.011&#34;] --&gt; S1[&#34;span: guardrail.input 40 ms&#34;] T --&gt; S2[&#34;span: retrieval 310 ms&#34;] S2 --&gt; S2a[&#34;embed query 60 ms&#34;] S2 --&gt; S2b[&#34;vector search top_k=20 90 ms&#34;] S2 --&gt; S2c[&#34;rerank → 5 150 ms&#34;] T --&gt; S3[&#34;span: chat claude-x 2.3 s&lt;br/&gt;in 5,120 tok · out 380 tok&lt;br/&gt;prompt v14 · temp 0.2&#34;] T --&gt; S4[&#34;span: guardrail.output 80 ms&#34;] T --&gt; S5[&#34;feedback: thumbs down&lt;br/&gt;reason: outdated&#34;] Record for every LLM call: Model name and version, parameters (temperature, max tokens), prompt template version. Input and output token counts, cost, TTFT and total latency, finish reason. Retrieved document IDs and scores; tool calls with arguments and results. User feedback and evaluation scores linked to the trace. Prompts and completions only according to data policy — they often contain personal data. Mask, sample, restrict access and set retention. OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions define standard attribute names (for example gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, gen_ai.usage.output_tokens). Spring AI emits Micrometer observations that follow them; see Spring AI in production. Dashboards and alerts# Metric Why Requests, error rate, 429s, timeouts Availability and provider health p50/p95 TTFT and total latency User experience Tokens and cost per request, per user, per feature Cost control, chargeback, anomaly detection Retrieval hit rate, empty-retrieval rate RAG health Online eval scores (faithfulness, relevance) on sampled traffic Quality drift Guardrail trigger rate, refusal rate Safety and over-blocking User feedback (thumbs, escalations to human) Real-world quality Evaluation in the pipeline# Offline (pre-release): run the golden dataset on every prompt, model, retrieval or code change; block release if scores drop below the baseline. Online (production): sample live traffic and score it with LLM-as-judge and heuristics; track user feedback; run A/B tests for changes. Regression on model updates: pin model versions where providers allow it; re-run the suite before moving to a new version. Details of metrics and judges: RAG evaluation and agent evaluation. Resilience patterns# LLM providers are remote dependencies with high latency, rate limits and occasional outages. Resilient model call flowchart LR A[&#34;Call&#34;] --&gt; T[&#34;Timeout&lt;br/&gt;per call&#34;] T --&gt; R[&#34;Retry&lt;br/&gt;backoff + jitter on 429/5xx&#34;] R --&gt; CB{&#34;Circuit breaker&lt;br/&gt;open?&#34;} CB --&gt;|&#34;closed&#34;| P[&#34;Primary model&#34;] CB --&gt;|&#34;open&#34;| F[&#34;Fallback model&lt;br/&gt;other provider or region&#34;] P --&gt;|&#34;fails&#34;| F F --&gt;|&#34;fails&#34;| D[&#34;Degraded mode&lt;br/&gt;cached answer, search results only,&lt;br/&gt;or &#39;try later&#39;&#34;] Also: bulkheads (separate thread pools/queues per feature), queue-based load levelling for batch work, idempotency for actions triggered by agents, and graceful degradation designed with the product owner. Cost control# Per-team budgets and quotas at the gateway; alerts on spend anomalies. Prompt caching, response caching (exact and semantic), batch APIs for offline work. Routing to smaller models; trimming retrieved context; limiting max output tokens. Agent step budgets: maximum iterations, tool calls and tokens per task. Deployment strategies# Strategy Use for Shadow New model/prompt runs on live traffic, outputs logged not shown; compare offline. Canary Small % of users get the change; watch metrics; roll forward or back. A/B test Measure business outcome (resolution rate, CSAT) between variants. Feature flags Switch prompts/models per tenant or segment without redeploying. AI incident handling# Typical AI incidents: harmful or wrong output reaching customers, prompt injection leading to data exposure, runaway agent cost, a provider model update causing quality regression. Runbook essentials: a kill switch per feature, the ability to roll back prompt and model versions independently of code, trace search by user/session, a process to notify risk and data-protection teams, and a post-incident review that adds test cases. Common mistakes# Common mistakeLogging full prompts with customer data everywhere Traces become

b: Simple definition# A GenAI adoption strategy decides where generative AI should create value, which capabilities the organisation buys or builds, which models and deployments it standardises on, how risk is governed, and how people and processes change — so that AI moves from scattered experiments to a measured, repeatable capability. It is the umbrella over the more specific agentic AI strategy: most enterprises adopt assistive GenAI first and agents second, on the same platform and governance. Why adoption stalls# Most enterprises do not fail at building a GenAI demo. They fail at the step after: Symptom Root cause Pilot purgatory — many pilots, few in production No shared platform, evaluation or governance path; each pilot is rebuilt from scratch Shadow AI — staff paste data into consumer tools No approved alternative that is as easy to use No measurable value Success defined as &ldquo;users like it&rdquo;, no baseline, no business owner Data not ready Documents without owners, permissions or quality; systems without APIs Risk blocks everything Governance designed as a one-off committee review instead of risk-tiered paved roads Cost surprises Token spend unmetered, no chargeback, largest model used everywhere A strategy exists to remove these causes in a deliberate order. Adoption maturity model# GenAI adoption maturity flowchart LR S1[&#34;1 · Explore&lt;br/&gt;individual use,&lt;br/&gt;policy, approved tools&#34;] --&gt; S2[&#34;2 · Experiment&lt;br/&gt;funded pilots,&lt;br/&gt;first evaluation sets&#34;] S2 --&gt; S3[&#34;3 · Formalise&lt;br/&gt;AI platform, gateway,&lt;br/&gt;governance tiers&#34;] S3 --&gt; S4[&#34;4 · Scale&lt;br/&gt;portfolio in production,&lt;br/&gt;reuse, chargeback&#34;] S4 --&gt; S5[&#34;5 · Transform&lt;br/&gt;processes and products&lt;br/&gt;redesigned around AI and agents&#34;] Stage What it looks like Exit criteria to move on 1 Explore Acceptable-use policy, an approved enterprise chat assistant and coding assistant, AI literacy training Shadow-AI usage measurably down; inventory of ideas 2 Experiment 3–6 funded pilots with business owners and baselines At least two pilots meet their success metric on an evaluation set 3 Formalise AI gateway, model catalogue, RAG starter, evaluation harness, risk-tiered approvals A new use case can reach production in weeks, not months 4 Scale Dozens of use cases on the platform; reusable components; cost per team visible Portfolio value reported quarterly; platform reuse &gt; 50% 5 Transform End-to-end processes redesigned; agents with progressive autonomy; AI in products Process KPIs (cycle time, cost to serve) shifted, not just task time saved Many large enterprises in 2026 sit between stages 3 and 4. Skipping stage 3 is the most common reason stage 4 never arrives. The strategic pillars# Pillars of GenAI adoption flowchart TB V[&#34;Value and use cases&lt;br/&gt;portfolio, business cases&#34;] subgraph Foundations P[&#34;Platform&lt;br/&gt;gateway, models, RAG,&lt;br/&gt;eval, LLMOps&#34;] D[&#34;Data&lt;br/&gt;ownership, quality,&lt;br/&gt;permissions, APIs&#34;] G[&#34;Governance&lt;br/&gt;risk tiers, policy,&lt;br/&gt;regulation&#34;] end subgraph Enablers O[&#34;Operating model&lt;br/&gt;CoE, platform team,&lt;br/&gt;domain teams&#34;] H[&#34;People and change&lt;br/&gt;literacy, roles,&lt;br/&gt;champions&#34;] end V --&gt; Foundations Foundations --&gt; Enablers Enablers -.-&gt;|&#34;feedback, new ideas&#34;| V Each pillar needs an owner. The architect usually owns the platform and contributes to data and governance; the value pillar must be owned by the business. Use-case discovery and prioritisation# GenAI use-case archetypes# Grouping ideas into archetypes reveals reuse: one platform capability serves many use cases. Archetype Examples Platform capability reused Knowledge retrieval and Q&amp;A Policy assistant, IT/HR helpdesk, product knowledge for agents RAG with permissions Summarisation Call notes, case histories, research digests Prompt templates, evaluation for faithfulness Extraction and classification Invoices, KYC documents, claims, email triage Structured output, small models Content generation Marketing drafts, RFP responses, reports Style guides, review workflows Code and IT Coding assistants, test generation, legacy code explanation, migration Coding agents, repository context Conversational front ends Customer chat, employee self-service Guardrails, handoff to humans Agentic process work Case handling, reconciliation, service desk resolution Agents, tools, approvals Scoring and the portfolio# Score each candidate on value, feasibility and risk, with weights agreed by the business sponsors. Weighted scoring example Use case Value (40%) Feasibility (35%) Risk, inverted (25%) Score IT helpdesk knowledge assistant 7 9 9 8.2 Invoice data extraction 8 8 7 7.8 Contract clause review for legal 9 6 5 7.0 Customer-facing advice chatbot 8 6 3 6.1 Automated credit decisions 9 4 1 5.3 Feasibility covers data availability and quality, integration effort and whether current models pass the task. Risk covers regulation (for example EU AI Act high-risk areas such as credit scoring), harm if wrong, and reversibility. Build a balanced portfolio: a few quick wins to earn trust, two or three strategic bets that justify the platform, and foundations work (data, APIs) for high-value cases that are not yet feasible. Start internal and assistive, then move to customer-facing and autonomous. From idea to scaled value# Every prioritised use case should follow the same paved road: risk tiering sets the depth of review, a pilot on the shared platform is measured against its baseline, and only evaluation evidence moves it to go-live. b: Simple definition# Using Claude intelligently means getting reliable, verified results at the lowest sensible cost and risk. It rests on five habits: give the right context, ask for a clear outcome, make the result verifiable, pick the right model and effort, and keep a human accountable for what ships. 1. Context engineering beats prompt tricks# Claude knows a lot about software in general and nothing about your system. Quality depends mostly on what you put in the context window (prompt and context engineering). Give it Example The goal and why &ldquo;We need partial refunds because finance reconciles daily; amounts must match the ledger to the cent.&rdquo; Constraints Framework versions, architecture rules, performance and compliance limits Definition of done Commands to run, behaviour to observe, files that must change Pointers, not dumps &ldquo;The refund flow starts in RefundController; rules are in domain/refund&rdquo; — let it read the rest Examples One good existing endpoint, test or ADR to imitate What not to do Paths not to touch, patterns the team has rejected, with the reason Key conceptExplain the why Current models generalise from reasons far better than from rules. &ldquo;Never log card numbers — logs are shipped to a third-party SaaS&rdquo; produces better behaviour across cases than &ldquo;NEVER LOG PAN&rdquo; in capitals. 2. Prompting current models# Be direct and specific. Say what you want, in what format, at what length. Ask for action (&ldquo;change the code&rdquo;) when you want action, and for analysis when you want options. Drop old workarounds. Shouting (ALWAYS, MUST), &ldquo;think step by step&rdquo;, role-play scaffolding and long rule lists were for weaker models; on current models they can make output worse. Use effort to control depth. Structure long inputs. Put large documents first and the question last; label sections (for example with XML-style tags) so instructions and data are not confused. Ask for uncertainty. &ldquo;If something is ambiguous, list the assumption you made&rdquo; or &ldquo;say you don&rsquo;t know rather than guess&rdquo;. Iterate on the prompt like code. Keep prompts in version control and evaluate changes on a fixed set of cases. 3. Verification is the multiplier# Claude&rsquo;s output is a draft until something checks it. The more automatic the check, the more you can delegate. Delegation follows verifiability flowchart LR A[&#34;Easy to verify automatically&lt;br/&gt;(tests, compiler, schema, linter)&#34;] --&gt;|&#34;delegate fully,&lt;br/&gt;review the diff&#34;| X[&#34;High autonomy&#34;] B[&#34;Verifiable by a human quickly&lt;br/&gt;(docs, small changes, summaries)&#34;] --&gt;|&#34;delegate,&lt;br/&gt;read before use&#34;| Y[&#34;Medium autonomy&#34;] C[&#34;Hard to verify&lt;br/&gt;(security design, legal, numbers&lt;br/&gt;without a source)&#34;] --&gt;|&#34;assist only,&lt;br/&gt;expert decides&#34;| Z[&#34;Low autonomy&#34;] Give Claude the means to check itself: test commands, a running app, browser automation, schemas. Ask it to show evidence: test output, quoted source lines, citations. For important answers, use an independent check — a second session reviewing the first, a different model as judge, or a deterministic tool. Be most sceptical of numbers, versions, API names and citations — the classic hallucination surface. Verify against source. 4. Delegation and parallelism# Right-size the task: one coherent outcome per session; split large work into reviewable pieces. Use sub-agents for broad reading and narrow specialist checks, so the main context keeps conclusions only; give them cheaper models and read-only tools where possible. Run independent tasks in parallel (worktrees, batch jobs) and merge through normal PR review. Give long tasks a budget and checkpoints: progress notes, a task list, intermediate commits — so a failed run can resume, not restart. 5. Cost control# Free wins first, trade-offs second: Order Lever Typical saving 1 Prompt caching for stable prefixes (system prompt, tools, documents) Large on repeated context; also faster 2 Input hygiene: send pointers and relevant extracts, not whole repositories; clear old tool results Proportional to context trimmed 3 Batches for anything not interactive 50% 4 Effort per route: low for chat and classification, higher only where measured Often several × on output tokens 5 Model per route: Haiku/Sonnet where they clear the bar Up to 40× between tiers 6 Loop hygiene in agents: stop conditions, task budgets, no retry storms Prevents runaway bills TipMeasure cost per completed task A cheaper request that needs three retries and a human fix is not cheaper. Track cost per successfully completed task, per route, from the usage fields you log. Set spend limits and alerts per workspace or team, and review the top routes by cost monthly. 6. Security, privacy and governance# Concern Practice Data use Know your agreement: commercial API and enterprise plans are not used for training by default; zero data retention (ZDR) is available for eligible features and organisations — some newer features and models require standard retention, so check before you design. Residency and hosting Use inference_geo, or run through Bedrock, Vertex AI or Foundry to stay inside existing regions, networks and contracts. Secrets Never paste secrets into prompts; deny agent access to .env and key stores; use workload identity instead of static keys. Prompt injection Treat web pages, tickets, emails, files and tool output as untrusted; least-privilege tools; human approval for irreversible actions (AI security). Code provenance AI-written code goes through the same review, scanning and licence checks as human code; record AI assistance in PR templates if your policy requires it. Access control SSO, role-based access, workspace separation, admin-managed settings and MCP allowlists for Claude Code. Audit and observability Central logging of API usage and Claude Code telemetry (OpenTelemetry);
d: The practices that separate effective from wasteful Claude use: context engineering, prompting current models, verification loops, delegation and sub-agents, cost control, enterprise security and governance, measuring productivity, and the anti-patterns to avoid — with a one-page checklist.

b: Simple definition# In financial services, hybrid AI means running each AI workload in the place its data, regulation and economics allow: frontier models through in-region cloud for tasks that need the best reasoning, open-weight or licensed models on the bank&rsquo;s own infrastructure for restricted data and high-volume work, and one governed control plane across both. This article applies the general patterns from On-premise and hybrid deployment to the decisions a bank, insurer or asset manager actually has to make. Why financial services is different# Constraint What it means for AI architecture Model risk management (US SR 11-7, UK PRA SS1/23, similar rules elsewhere) LLMs used in decisions are models: inventory, independent validation, ongoing monitoring, change control. A provider silently updating a model is a validation problem Outsourcing and operational resilience (EU DORA, EBA outsourcing guidelines) AI providers supporting critical functions need contracts with audit rights, sub-processor transparency, incident reporting, exit plans and tested alternatives Data protection and secrecy GDPR, banking secrecy, PCI DSS for card data, client confidentiality in private banking; cross-border transfer limits Record-keeping and conduct Communications with clients and advice must be retained and supervised (for example MiFID II, FINRA rules); AI-drafted client messages fall in scope Fair treatment and explainability Credit, pricing and claims decisions must be explainable and non-discriminatory; EU AI Act lists creditworthiness assessment and life/health insurance pricing as high-risk Market-abuse and information barriers Research, trading and deal teams sit behind Chinese walls; retrieval must respect them Legacy estate Core banking, mainframes and payment hubs with batch windows and limited APIs Key conceptThe deciding question is usually &ldquo;who can see the data and change the model?&rdquo; Quality and cost matter, but in a regulated firm the first filter is data access and model change control. Those two decide whether a workload can go to a cloud API at all, and if so, under what contract. Use cases and where they belong# Use case Typical tasks Highest data class Latency need Quality need Typical placement Analytics Natural-language questions over data, report narration, variance commentary, SQL generation over a semantic layer Confidential (aggregated) to restricted (client-level) Interactive seconds High for numbers; must be verifiable Cloud-managed frontier/mid-tier for reasoning over aggregates; on-prem for client-level data; numbers always computed by the database, never the model Customer service Agent assist, chat and voice self-service, complaint triage, call summarisation Confidential (client PII, account data) Real-time: sub-second for voice, a few seconds for chat Medium–high; tone and compliance Cloud-managed in-region with zero data retention, PII redaction at gateway; small on-prem models for intent and PII detection; strict human handoff Financial crime Alert triage, adverse-media screening, SAR/STR narrative drafting, KYC/EDD summaries, transaction-pattern explanation Restricted (SAR data has tipping-off restrictions) Batch to near-real-time High; auditable reasoning On-prem or sovereign; open-weight models fine-tuned on investigator narratives; LLM assists the investigator, rules and ML models still score Investment research Summarising filings, earnings calls and broker research, thematic screening, drafting notes, Q&amp;A over research library Internal to confidential; MNPI behind walls is restricted Interactive; long documents Highest: multi-step reasoning, long context Cloud-managed frontier models for public and licensed content; on-prem or walled tenant for MNPI and proprietary positions; licence checks on third-party content Document intelligence KYC onboarding packs, loan and mortgage files, trade confirmations, ISDA/CSA clause extraction, claims, invoices Confidential to restricted Batch, high volume High field accuracy; measurable straight-through rate On-prem or dedicated capacity for volume: OCR/layout models + small/mid open-weight LLMs with structured output; frontier models for rare complex documents Typical placement in a hybrid bank flowchart TB subgraph CloudRegion[&#34;Cloud tenancy, in-region, private endpoints&#34;] F[&#34;Frontier / reasoning models&lt;br/&gt;investment research, analytics reasoning,&lt;br/&gt;complex documents&#34;] M[&#34;Mid-tier models&lt;br/&gt;customer-service assist and chat&#34;] end subgraph OnPrem[&#34;Bank data centre / private cloud&#34;] O1[&#34;Open-weight 30–70B, fine-tuned&lt;br/&gt;financial crime narratives, KYC summaries&#34;] O2[&#34;Document models + small LLMs&lt;br/&gt;extraction at volume&#34;] O3[&#34;Small models&lt;br/&gt;PII detection, intent, routing, guardrails&#34;] IDX[(&#34;Restricted indexes&lt;br/&gt;SAR, MNPI, client files&#34;)] end GW[&#34;AI gateway + policy engine&lt;br/&gt;data-class routing, redaction,&lt;br/&gt;audit, quotas, model catalogue&#34;] GW --&gt; F GW --&gt; M GW --&gt; O1 GW --&gt; O2 GW --&gt; O3 O1 --- IDX Trade-offs across five dimensions# For each use case, compare the realistic options on the same five dimensions. Dimension Cloud frontier API (private endpoint) Cloud-hosted open-weight / dedicated On-prem open-weight On-prem licensed commercial model Quality Highest, especially reasoning and long context Mid-tier to near-frontier Mid-tier; improves with fine-tuning on your data Varies; often a generation behind the vendor&rsquo;s cloud model Latency Good, but network, shared capacity and region affect p99 Predictable with reserved capacity Best and most predictable when sized right As on-prem Compute None to manage; pay per token Reserved units; pay for idle You buy, power and run GPUs; utilisation is the economic lever As on-prem, plus licence fees Security Data leaves your perimeter under contract; provider controls weights In your tenancy; provider operates

b: The design brief# &ldquo;Design an AI agent for an e-commerce company that resolves customer-support requests — order status, returns, refunds, address changes — over chat and email, escalating to humans when needed.&rdquo; 1. Requirements# Functional Understand requests in chat and email, in 5 languages. Look up orders, shipments, customers and policies. Perform actions: change delivery address (before dispatch), create return labels, issue refunds, apply goodwill vouchers. Escalate to a human agent with a summary when unsure, when the customer asks, or for sensitive cases (complaints, legal threats, vulnerable customers). Full audit trail of every action. Non-functional Requirement Target Volume 40,000 conversations/day, peak 3× Latency First response &lt; 3 s in chat; email within 5 minutes Automation ≥ 60% resolved without a human, with CSAT ≥ human baseline Safety Zero unauthorised refunds; refunds &gt; €100 need human approval Availability 99.9%; degraded mode routes to humans Compliance GDPR; PCI scope excluded (agent never sees card numbers) 2. Estimates# 40,000 conversations × ~6 turns × ~2 LLM calls per turn ≈ 480,000 LLM calls/day. ~6,000 input tokens per call (system + tools + history + retrieved policy), ~250 output. ≈ 2.9B input + 120M output tokens/day. Prompt caching of the ~3,000-token static prefix (system prompt + tool definitions) cuts input cost substantially. Router on a small model handles ~30% (simple status questions) cheaply. Target cost: &lt; €0.15 per resolved conversation vs ~€4–6 for a human-handled contact. 3. Agent topology# Agent topology: router &#43; specialists &#43; human hand-off flowchart TB IN[&#34;Chat / email channel&#34;] --&gt; TRI[&#34;Triage &amp; router&lt;br/&gt;small model: intent, language,&lt;br/&gt;sentiment, risk flags&#34;] TRI --&gt;|&#34;status, tracking&#34;| SA[&#34;Order-status agent&lt;br/&gt;read-only tools&#34;] TRI --&gt;|&#34;returns, refunds&#34;| RA[&#34;Returns &amp; refunds agent&lt;br/&gt;read + write tools, limits&#34;] TRI --&gt;|&#34;account, address&#34;| AA[&#34;Account agent&#34;] TRI --&gt;|&#34;complaint, legal,&lt;br/&gt;vulnerable, angry&#34;| HUM[&#34;Human agent queue&#34;] SA --&gt;|&#34;handoff&#34;| RA RA --&gt;|&#34;needs approval&#34;| APR[&#34;Approval queue&lt;br/&gt;human supervisor&#34;] SA --&gt;|&#34;escalate&#34;| HUM RA --&gt;|&#34;escalate&#34;| HUM AA --&gt;|&#34;escalate&#34;| HUM Why this split: each specialist has a small tool set and a focused prompt; the read-only agent cannot change anything (security boundary); refunds are isolated with stricter limits; triage runs on a cheap model. 4. Architecture# Agentic customer-support platform · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. &copy; 2026 Samir Kumar Sahoo, all rights reserved. Open full screen ↗ 5. Tools (exposed via MCP servers owned by domain teams)# Tool Type Guardrails in code get_order(orderId) Read Order must belong to authenticated customer track_shipment(orderId) Read Same ownership check search_policy(query) Read RAG over approved policy documents change_address(orderId, address) Write Only before dispatch; address validation; idempotency key create_return(orderId, items, reason) Write Within return window; item eligibility issue_refund(orderId, amount, reason) Write, financial Amount ≤ order total − prior refunds; ≤ €100 automatic; above → approval; idempotency key; daily cap per customer apply_voucher(customerId, value) Write, financial ≤ €15; max 1 per 30 days escalate_to_human(summary, priority) Control Always allowed Customer identity comes from the authenticated session and is passed as tool context, never from model-provided arguments. 6. Conversation flow with a refund# Refund for a damaged item sequenceDiagram actor C as Customer participant T as Triage participant R as Refunds agent participant O as Orders MCP participant P as Policy RAG participant PAY as Payments MCP participant A as Approval service C-&gt;&gt;T: &#34;My blender arrived broken, order A-10293. I want my money back.&#34; T-&gt;&gt;R: intent=refund, sentiment=negative, lang=en R-&gt;&gt;O: get_order(A-10293) [customer from session] O--&gt;&gt;R: delivered 2 days ago, total €129, item: blender R-&gt;&gt;P: search_policy(&#34;damaged item refund&#34;) P--&gt;&gt;R: &#34;Damaged on arrival: full refund, no return needed under €150 with photo&#34; R--&gt;&gt;C: &#34;Sorry about that! Could you upload a photo of the damage?&#34; C-&gt;&gt;R: photo R-&gt;&gt;R: vision check: damage visible R-&gt;&gt;PAY: issue_refund(A-10293, 129.00, &#34;damaged&#34;) PAY--&gt;&gt;R: PENDING_APPROVAL (amount &gt; €100) R-&gt;&gt;A: approval request + evidence + reasoning R--&gt;&gt;C: &#34;I&#39;ve requested a full refund of €129. You&#39;ll get confirmation within 2 hours.&#34; A--&gt;&gt;R: approved by supervisor R-&gt;&gt;PAY: confirm refund (idempotency key) R--&gt;&gt;C: &#34;Your refund of €129 has been issued.&#34; 7. State and memory# Conversation state and checkpoints in PostgreSQL; the agent can pause for photos or approvals and resume on any pod. History management: running summary + last 6 turns + pinned facts (order ID, decision). Long-term memory: limited customer facts (preferred language, previous contacts summary) with retention limits. 8. Guardrails and security# Input: injection classifier on customer messages and email attachments; PII masking in logs. Actions: per-agent tool allow-lists; authorisation in every MCP server; financial limits in the payments service, not the prompt. Output: policy compliance (no promises outside policy), tone, no internal data leakage. Lethal-trifecta check: the agent reading untrusted email has no tool to send data to arbitrary external addresses. Kill switch per agent and per tool; anomaly alerts (refund volume spikes). 9. Evaluation and rollout# Offline: 500 scenario simulations with simulated customers and sandboxed MCP servers; metrics: task success, correct final state, policy violations
d: A complete system design for an AI agent that resolves customer-support requests end to end: requirements, estimates, architecture, agent topology, MCP tools, conversation flow with refunds and approvals, state, guardrails, evaluation, rollout and trade-offs.

b: Purpose# The Enterprise AI &amp; Agentic AI Knowledge Hub explains strategic AI architecture simply, for architects and senior engineers who design, build or govern AI systems — and for anyone who wants to review and test their understanding of enterprise AI. It is the companion to the Java &amp; Software Architecture Knowledge Hub. Structure# LLM Foundations &amp; the Enterprise AI Stack — how models work, cost, prompting, fine-tuning, model selection, reference architecture, LLMOps. RAG, Vector Databases &amp; GraphRAG — retrieval from basics to GraphRAG and evaluation, with a system design. Agentic AI, MCP &amp; Multi-Agent Systems — agents, tools, MCP, patterns, memory, reliability, with a system design. Spring AI, Security &amp; Governance — Java implementation with Spring AI 2.0, AI security and AI governance. Agent Frameworks &amp; Platforms — Python, TypeScript, JVM and .NET frameworks and managed agent platforms. Review — an architecture review framework, review questions and a quick-reference sheet. Editorial conventions# Every article follows the same shape: a simple definition, the problem, the core concepts with diagrams of architecture and flows, practical guidance, common mistakes, review questions with answers, a summary and references. Callouts mark key concepts, review tips, common mistakes and trade-offs. Diagrams are written in Mermaid inside the articles, so they live in version control next to the text and follow the light/dark theme. Versions# Spring AI examples target Spring AI 2.0 on Spring Boot 4.1 and Java 21; class and property names were checked against the Spring AI 2.0 source. Prices and model names are illustrative and change frequently — always check current provider documentation. Regulatory timelines (for example the EU AI Act) are summarised; verify current dates before relying on them. Author# Written and maintained by Samir Kumar Sahoo. b: Definitions are deliberately short. Follow the links for the full explanation. A# A2A (Agent2Agent protocol) An open protocol for agents to discover each other through agent cards and delegate tasks. See Multi-agent systems. AG-UI (Agent–User Interaction protocol) An open protocol streaming typed events between an agent and a user interface. See Agent protocol stack. Advisor (Spring AI) An interceptor around a ChatClient call, used for memory, RAG, logging, tool loops and custom concerns. See Spring AI fundamentals. Agent An LLM-driven system that loops — reason, act through tools, observe — until a goal is met. See What is an agent? Agent framework A library that runs the agent loop and adds state, tools, multi-agent coordination, guardrails and tracing. See Framework landscape. Agent harness Everything around the model that makes an agent reliable: loop, tools, permissions, context management, skills, checkpoints, verification. See Harnesses &amp; skills. Agent Skills Folders with a SKILL.md and resources that agents load on demand. See Agent protocol stack. AGENTS.md A Markdown file in a repository with instructions for coding agents. See Agent protocol stack. Agentic RAG RAG where an agent decides when and where to retrieve, possibly several times. See Advanced retrieval. AI gateway The single controlled entry point to all models: auth, quotas, guardrails, routing, caching, logging, cost. See Enterprise AI stack. ANN (approximate nearest neighbour) Search that finds most of the closest vectors quickly without comparing all of them. See Vector databases. Attention The transformer mechanism by which each token weighs and uses information from other tokens. See How LLMs work. AgentOps Operating agents like production services: SLOs, monitoring, incidents, cost and continuous evaluation. See Agentic AI strategy. Air-gapped deployment Running models with no network path to the outside; updates imported offline. See On-prem &amp; hybrid. A.G.E.N.T. framework A five-part agent design checklist: agent identity, gear and brain, execution and workflow, navigation and rules, testing and trust. See Agent building playbook. AI engineering Building applications on top of foundation models — adapting and evaluating an existing model rather than training one. See AI engineering fundamentals. Agentic AI progression Six levels from manual work (0) through rule-based and intelligent automation to agentic workflows (3), semi-autonomous (4) and fully autonomous agents (5). See Levels, SPAR &amp; keystones. B–C# BM25 A classic keyword relevance ranking function used in sparse/keyword search. See Advanced retrieval. Chunking Splitting documents into passages for retrieval. See Chunking and embeddings. Claude Code Anthropic&rsquo;s agentic coding tool for the terminal, IDEs, desktop, web and CI; it reads, edits, runs and verifies code. See Claude Code in practice. CLAUDE.md A project memory file loaded into every Claude Code session — commands, architecture rules and conventions. See Claude Code in practice. Computer-use agent An agent that operates graphical interfaces from screenshots with clicks and keystrokes. See Computer-use agents. Context engineering Deciding everything that goes into the context window on each call. See Prompt and context engineering. Context window The maximum tokens (input + output) a model processes per call. See How LLMs work. Contextual retrieval Prepending an LLM-written situating sentence to each chunk before indexing. See Advanced retrieval. Cross-encoder / reranker A model that scores a query and a document together for precise relevance. See Advanced retrieval. Data-classification routing An AI gateway choosing the allowed model deployment by the highest data class in the assembled prompt. See On-prem &amp; hybrid. Comparative evaluation Ranking models from pairwise &ldquo;which is better?&rdquo; judgements aggregated with Elo or Bradley–Terry. See Evaluation methodology. Continuous batching A serving scheduler that adds and removes requests from the running batch at every decode step. See Inference optimisation. D–E# Distillation Training a small model on a large model&rsquo;s outputs. See Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning. Effort (Claude) A per-request setting (low to max) controlling how thoroughly a Claude model thinks, calls tools and writes — the quality-versus-cost dial within one model. See Claude models and model selection. Embedding A vector representing the meaning of text. See Chunking and embeddings. EU AI Act The EU regulation classifying AI systems by risk tier with matching obligations. See AI governance. Evaluator–optimizer A loop where one LLM generates and another critiques until criteria are met. See Workflow patterns. Embabel A JVM agent framework on Spring AI that plans typed actions toward goals with GOAP. See JVM frameworks. Excessive agency An LLM system with more tools, permissions or autonomy than it needs. See AI security. Data contamination Benchmark or evaluation examples leaking into training data, inflating scores. See Evaluating AI systems. Data flywheel More users produce more feedback and data, which improve the product and attract more users. See User feedback. Dataset engineering Curating, synthesising, deduplicating and formatting the data used to fine-tune and evaluate models. See Dataset engineering. Degenerate feedback loop When a system&rsquo;s outputs shape the feedback that trains it, amplifying its own biases (popularity bias, sycophancy). See User feedback. DPO (direct preference optimisation) Preference fine-tuning directly on (preferred, rejected) response pairs, without a separate reward model. See Training, scaling &amp; sampling. Evaluation-driven development Defining evaluation criteria and data before building, like tests before code. See Evaluating AI systems. Functional correctness / pass@k Scoring outputs by whether they work — tests pass, SQL returns the right rows; pass@k is the chance at least one of k samples
d: Short definitions of the enterprise AI and agentic AI terms used across the handbook, with links to the articles that explain them.
